77: Copy pageCopy page
78: Find the base URL, headers, and data formats for Notion API requests.
79: Copy pageCopy page
80: Send requests over HTTPS to https://api.notion.com. To make your first request, follow the API quickstart.
81: Conventions
82: For requests to pages, databases, and other workspace resources, send an Authorization: Bearer header with your token and a Notion-Version header. The authentication reference lists the supported token types.
83: Most endpoints use JSON. Set Content-Type: application/json when you send a JSON body. Sending a file uses multipart form data instead.
84: JSON conventions
85: The object field identifies a resource, such as a page or user.
86: You can send page and database IDs with or without dashes.
87: Property names use snake_case.
88: Dates and timestamps use ISO 8601, such as 2026-03-11 or 2026-03-11T09:30:00.000Z.
89: To clear a URL page property, send null.
90: Code samples & SDKs
91: Use the JavaScript SDK, curl, or any client that can send HTTPS requests. Each endpoint reference lists its parameters and response fields. See status codes to interpret an error response.
92: Pagination
93: For lists with more than one page, pass the response’s next_cursor as start_cursor in the next request. See the pagination reference.

64: Internal connection auth flow set-up 65: Connection permissions 66: Making API requests with an internal connection 67: Personal access token authentication 68: OAuth integration auth flow set-up 69: How to make an OAuth integration 70: OAuth integration authorization overview 71: Step 1 - Navigate the user to the connection’s authorization URL 72: Prompt for a standard connection with no template option (Default) 73: Prompt for a connection with a Notion template option 74: Step 2 - Notion redirects the user to the connection’s redirect URI and includes a code parameter 75: Step 3 - Send the code in a POST request to the Notion API 76: Step 4 - Notion responds with an access_token , refresh_token, and additional information 77: Step 5 - The connection stores the access_token and refresh_token for future requests 78: Step 6 - Refreshing an access token 79: Authorization 80: Authorization 81: Copy pageCopy page 82: Authenticate Notion API requests with personal access tokens, internal connection tokens, or OAuth integration OAuth flows. 83: Copy pageCopy page 84: What is authorization? 85: Authorization is the process of granting a connection or token access to Notion data. Internal connections use a static credential called an internal connection API token, personal access tokens use a user-scoped static token, and OAuth integrations and public integrations use the OAuth 2.0 protocol. 86: Internal connection auth flow set-up 87: To use an internal connection, start by creating your connection in the Developer portal. 88: The internal connection will be associated with the workspace of your choice. You are required to be a workspace owner to create a connection. 89: Create a new connection from the Developer portal. 90: Once the connection is created, you can update its settings as needed under the Configuration tab and retrieve the API token in this tab. 91: The API token will be used to authenticate REST API requests. The connection sends the same token in every API request. 92: Find the API token in the Configuration tab. 93: Connection permissions 94: Before a connection can interact with your Notion workspace page(s), the page must be manually shared with the connection. To share a page with a connection, visit the page in your Notion workspace, click the ••• menu at the top right of a page, scroll down to Add connections, and use the search bar to find and select the connection from the dropdown list. 95: Once the connection is shared, you can start making API requests. If the page is not shared, any API requests made will respond with an error. 96: Never share your API tokenYour API token is a secret. To keep your connection secure, never store the token in your source code or commit it in version control. Instead, read the token from an environment variable. Use a secret manager or deployment system to set the token in the environment.Learn more: Best Practices for Handling API Keys 97: Making API requests with an internal connection 98: Any time your connection interacts with your workspace, include the API token in the Authorization header with every API request. However, if you are using Notion’s SDK for JavaScript to interact with the REST API, the token is set once when a client is initialized. 99: HTTP 100: GET /v1/pages/b55c9c91-384d-452b-81db-d1ef79372b75 HTTP/1.1 101: Authorization: Bearer {INTEGRATION_TOKEN} 102: JavaScript 103: const { Client } = require("@notionhq/client") 104: // Initializing a client 105: const notion = new Client({ 106: auth: process.env.NOTION_TOKEN, 107: }) 108: const getUsers = async () => { 109: const listUsersResponse = await notion.users.list({}) 110: } 111: If you are not using the Notion SDK for JavaScript, also set the Notion-Version and Content-type headers in all of your requests, like so: 112: JSON 113: headers: { 114: Authorization: `Bearer ${process.env.NOTION_TOKEN}`, 115: "Notion-Version": "2026-03-11", 116: "Content-Type": "application/json", 117: }, 118: If you receive an error response from the API, check if the connection has been properly added to the page. If this does not solve the problem, refer to our Status codes page for more information. 119: Personal access token authentication 120: Personal access tokens (PATs) are created directly by a Notion user in the Developer portal. There is no OAuth flow and no page picker. A PAT acts as the user who created it and uses that user’s permissions in the selected workspace. 121: Use a PAT when a script, CLI workflow, Worker, or trusted tool should act as you. Use an internal connection for team-owned workspace automations, or an OAuth integration when each user needs to authorize your app. 122: PATs use the same Authorization header as other credentials for the Notion API: 123: HTTP 124: GET /v1/users/me HTTP/1.1 125: Authorization: Bearer {PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN} 126: Notion-Version: 2026-03-11 127: See Personal access tokens for creation steps, workspace admin controls, tier defaults, and security guidance. 128: OAuth integration auth flow set-up 129: An OAuth integration can be installed in any Notion workspace within its installation scope — a specific set chosen at creation time for scoped integrations, or any workspace for public integrations. 130: An OAuth integration isn’t tied to a single workspace through an internal connection API token. Instead, OAuth integrations follow the OAuth 2.0 protocol to authorize a connection to interact with a workspace. 131: How to make an OAuth integration 132: Navigate to the Developer portal and create a new OAuth integration. 133: Fill out the form with your connection details, including your redirect URI(s) under the OAuth configuration section and the connection’s installation scope — either Any workspace or Or select 1 or more workspaces. This can’t be changed after creation. 134: The redirect URI is the URI your users will be redirected to after authorizing the OAuth integration. To learn more, read OAuth’s description of redirect URIs. 135: Marketplace listing details (such as descriptions, categories, and images) are managed separately through the Listings section. Refer to the List on the Marketplace guide to learn more. 136: OAuth integration authorization overview 137: Both scoped OAuth integrations and public integrations use this flow. You can start authorization as soon as you configure the integration’s client credentials and redirect URI; Marketplace submission or review is not required. 138: As an overview, the authorization flow includes the following steps. Each step will be described in more detail below. 139: 1 140: Navigate the user to the connection’s authorization URL. This URL is provided in the Developer portal. 141: 2 142: After the user selects which workspace pages to share, Notion redirects the user to the connection’s redirect URI and includes a code query parameter. The redirect URI is the one you specified in your Developer portal. 143: 3 144: Make a POST request to create an access token, which exchanges the temporary code for an access token. 145: 4 146: The Notion API responds with an access token and some additional information. 147: 5 148: Store the access token for future API requests. View the API reference docs to learn about available endpoints. 149: Step 1 - Navigate the user to the connection’s authorization URL 150: After creating an OAuth integration in the Developer portal, access the connection’s secrets in the Configuration tab. Similarly to the internal connections, these values should be protected and should never be included in source code or version control. 151: The Configuration tab provides the authorization URL for your OAuth integration 152: As an example, your .env file using these secrets could look like this: 153: Shell 154: #.env 155: OAUTH_CLIENT_ID= 156: OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET= 157: NOTION_AUTH_URL= 158: To start the authorization flow for an OAuth integration, direct the prospective user to the authorization URL. A common pattern is to include a hyperlink in the connection app that interacts with the Notion REST API. For example, an app that lets users create Notion pages in their workspaces should send users to the authorization URL first. 159: The following example shows an authorization URL made available through a hyperlink: 160: HTML 161: Add to Notion 162: The URL begins with https://api.notion.com/v1/oauth/authorize and has the following parameters: 163: ParameterDescriptionRequired 164: client_idAn identifier for your connection, found in the connection settings.✅ 165: redirect_uriThe URL where the user should return after granting access.✅ 166: response_typeAlways use code.✅ 167: ownerAlways use user.✅ 168: stateIf the user was in the middle of an interaction or operation, then this parameter can be used to restore state after the user returns. It can also be used to prevent CSRF attacks. 169: Once the authorization URL is visited, the user will be shown a prompt that varies depending on whether or not the connection comes with a Notion template option. 170: Prompt for a standard connection with no template option (Default) 171: In the standard connection permissions flow, a prompt describes the connection capabilities, presented to the user as what the connection would like to be able to do in the workspace. A user can either select pages to grant the connection access to, or cancel the request. 172: Prompt for authorizing a standard connection (no template option) 173: If the user presses Cancel, they will be redirected to the redirect URI with and error query param added. 174: www.example.com/my-redirect-uri?error=access_denied&state= 175: You can use this errorquery parameter to conditionally update your app’s state as needed. 176: If the user opts to Select pages, then a page picker interface opens. A user can search for and select pages and databases to share with the connection from the page picker. 177: The page picker only displays pages or databases to which a user has full access, because a user needs full access to a resource in order to be able to share it with a connection. 178: Page picker interface 179: Users can select which pages to give the connection access to, including both private and public pages available to them. Parent pages can be selected to quickly provide access to child pages, as giving access to a parent page will provide access to all available child pages. Users can return to this view at a later time to update access settings if circumstances change. 180: If the user clicks Allow access, they are then redirected to the redirect_uri with a temporary authorization code. If the user denies access, they are redirected to the redirect_uri with an error query parameter. 181: If the user clicks Allow access and the rest of the auth flow is not completed, the connection will not have access to the pages that were selected. 182: Prompt for a connection with a Notion template option 183: OAuth integrations offer the option of providing a public Notion page to use as a template during the auth flow. 184: To add a template to your workspace, complete the following steps: 185: Choose a public page in your workspace that you want users to be able to duplicate. 186: Navigate to your connection in the Developer portal and open the Configuration tab, then scroll to the Basic information section. 187: Scroll to the bottom of your distribution settings and add the URL of the Notion page you selected to the Notion URL for optional template input. 188: Notion URL for optional template input in connection settings. 189: Once this URL is added, your auth flow prompt appearance will be updated. 190: Going back to your prompt view, if the connection offers a Notion template option, the first step in the permissions flow will describe the connection capabilities. This is presented to the user as what the connection would be able to do in the workspace, and it prompts the user to click Next. 191: Prompt for a connection with a Notion template option 192: In the next step, a user can either choose to duplicate the template that you provided or to select existing pages to share with the connection. 193: A user can select to duplicate a template or to share existing pages with the connection 194: If the user chooses to duplicate the template, then the following happens automatically: 195: The connection is added to the user’s workspace. 196: The template is duplicated as a new page in the workspace. 197: The new page is shared with the connection. 198: If the user chooses to select pages to share with the connection, then they continue to the page picker interface that’s part of the prompt for a standard connection. 199: After a user authorizes an OAuth integration, only that user is able to interact or share pages and databases with the connection. Unlike internal connections, if multiple members in a workspace want to use an OAuth integration, each prospective user needs to individually follow the auth flow for the connection. 200: User authorization failures 201: User authorization failures can happen. If a user chooses to Cancel the request, then a failure is triggered. Build your connection to handle these cases gracefully, as needed. 202: In some cases, Notion redirects the user to the redirect_uri that you set up when you created the OAuth integration, along with an error query parameter. Notion uses the common error codes in the OAuth specification. Use the error code to create a helpful prompt for the user when they’re redirected here. 203: Step 2 - Notion redirects the user to the connection’s redirect URI and includes a code parameter 204: When you first created the OAuth integration, you specified a redirect URI. If the user follows the prompt to Allow access for the connection, then Notion generates a temporary code and sends a request to the redirect URI with the following information in the query string: 205: ParameterDescriptionRequired 206: codeA temporary authorization code.✅ 207: stateThe value provided by the connection when the user was prompted for access. 208: To complete the next step, retrieve the code query parameter provided in the redirect. The retrieval method varies depending on your app’s tech stack. 209: In a React component, for example, the query parameters are made available through the useRouter() hook: 210: JavaScript 211: export default function AuthRedirectPage() { 212: const router = useRouter(); 213: const { code } = router.query; 214: ... 215: } 216: Step 3 - Send the code in a POST request to the Notion API 217: The connection needs to exchange the temporary code for an access_token. 218: To set up this step, retrieve the code from the redirect URI. 219: Next, send the code as part of a POST request to Notion’s token endpoint: https://api.notion.com/v1/oauth/token. 220: This endpoint is described in more detail in the API reference docs for creating a token. 221: The request is authorized using HTTP Basic Authentication. The credential is a colon-delimited combination of the connection’s CLIENT_ID and CLIENT_SECRET, like so: 222: CLIENT_ID:CLIENT_SECRET 223: Find both of these values in the Developer portal. 224: Note that in HTTP Basic Authentication, credentials are base64 encoded before being added to the Authorization header. 225: The body of the request contains the following JSON-encoded fields: 226: FieldTypeDescriptionRequired 227: "grant_type"stringAlways use "authorization_code".✅ 228: "code"stringThe temporary authorization code received in the incoming request to the "redirect_uri".✅ 229: "redirect_uri"stringThe "redirect_uri" that was provided in the Authorization step.✅/❌* 230: * If the redirect URI was supplied as a query param in the Authorization URL, this field is required. If there are more than one redirect URIs included in your connection settings, this field is required. Otherwise, it is not allowed. Learn more in the Create a token page. 231: The following is an example request to exchange the authorization code for an access token: 232: HTTP 233: POST /v1/oauth/token HTTP/1.1 234: Authorization: Basic "$CLIENT_ID:$CLIENT_SECRET" 235: Content-Type: application/json 236: {"grant_type":"authorization_code","code":"e202e8c9-0990-40af-855f-ff8f872b1ec6", "redirect_uri":"https://example.com/auth/notion/callback"} 237: The Node-equivalent of this example would look something like this: 238: JavaScript 239: ... 240: const clientId = process.env.OAUTH_CLIENT_ID; 241: const clientSecret = process.env.OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET; 242: const redirectUri = process.env.OAUTH_REDIRECT_URI; 243: // encode in base 64 244: const encoded = btoa(`${clientId}:${clientSecret}`); 245: const response = await fetch("https://api.notion.com/v1/oauth/token", { 246: method: "POST", 247: headers: { 248: Accept: "application/json", 249: "Content-Type": "application/json", 250: Authorization: `Basic ${encoded}`, 251: }, 252: body: JSON.stringify({ 253: grant_type: "authorization_code", 254: code: "your-temporary-code", 255: redirect_uri: redirectUri, 256: }), 257: }); 258: ... 259: Step 4 - Notion responds with an access_token , refresh_token, and additional information 260: Notion responds to the request with an access_token, refresh_token, and additional information. The access_token will be used to authenticate subsequent Notion REST API requests. The refresh_token will be used to refresh the access token, which generates a new access_token. 261: The response contains the following JSON-encoded fields: 262: FieldTypeDescriptionNot null 263: "access_token"stringAn access token used to authorize requests to the Notion API.✅ 264: "refresh_token"stringA refresh token used to generate a new access token✅ 265: "bot_id"stringAn identifier for this authorization.✅ 266: "duplicated_template_id"stringThe ID of the new page created in the user’s workspace. The new page is a duplicate of the template that the developer provided with the connection. If the developer didn’t provide a template for the connection, then the value is null. 267: "owner"objectAn object containing information about who can view and share this connection. A user object is returned, representing the user who authorized the connection.✅ 268: "workspace_icon"stringA URL to an image that can be used to display this authorization in the UI. 269: "workspace_id"stringThe ID of the workspace where this authorization took place.✅ 270: "workspace_name"stringA human-readable name that can be used to display this authorization in the UI. 271: Token request failures 272: If something goes wrong when the connection attempts to exchange the code for an access_token, then the response contains a JSON-encoded body with an "error" field. Notion uses the common error codes from the OAuth specification. 273: Step 5 - The connection stores the access_token and refresh_token for future requests 274: Set up a way for your connection to store both the access_token and refresh_token that it receives. The access_token is used to make authorized requests to the Notion API, and the refresh_token is used to generate a new access_token. 275: Tips for storing and using token access 276: Setting up a database is a typical solution for storing access tokens. If you’re using a database, then build relations between an access_token, refresh_token, and the corresponding Notion resources that your connection accesses with that token. For example, if you store a Notion database or page ID, relate those records with the correct access_token that you use to authorize requests to read or write to that database or page, and the refresh_token for ongoing token lifecycle support.. 277: Store all of the information that your connection receives with the access_token and refresh_token. You never know when your UI or product requirements might change and you’ll need this data. It’s really hard (or impossible) to send users to repeat the authorization flow to generate the information again. 278: The bot_id returned along with your tokens identifies the Notion bot for the authorization. Store the token pair from each successful authorization response. This includes re-authorization of the same connection, where Notion may return a new access_token and refresh_token. 279: Step 6 - Refreshing an access token 280: Refreshing an access token will generate a new access token and a new refresh token. 281: Send the refresh_token provided from Step 4 as part of a POST request to Notion’s token endpoint: https://api.notion.com/v1/oauth/token. 282: This endpoint is described in more detail in the API reference docs for refreshing a token. 283: The request is authorized using HTTP Basic Authentication. The credential is a colon-delimited combination of the connection’s CLIENT_ID and CLIENT_SECRET, like so: 284: CLIENT_ID:CLIENT_SECRET 285: Find both of these values in the Developer portal. 286: Note that in HTTP Basic Authentication, credentials are base64 encoded before being added to the Authorization header. 287: The body of the request contains the following JSON-encoded fields: 288: FieldTypeDescriptionRequired 289: "grant_type"stringAlways use "refresh_token".✅ 290: "refresh_token"stringThe "refresh_token" returned in the Authorization step.✅ 291: The following is an example request to exchange the refresh_token for a new access token and new refresh token 292: HTTP 293: POST /v1/oauth/token HTTP/1.1 294: Authorization: Basic "$CLIENT_ID:$CLIENT_SECRET" 295: Content-Type: application/json 296: {"grant_type":"refresh_token","refresh_token":"nrt_4991090011501Ejc6Xn4sHguI7jZIN449mKe9PRhpMfNK"} 297: The Node-equivalent of this example would look something like this: 298: JavaScript 299: ... 300: const clientId = process.env.OAUTH_CLIENT_ID; 301: const clientSecret = process.env.OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET; 302: // encode in base 64 303: const encoded = btoa(`${clientId}:${clientSecret}`); 304: const response = await fetch("https://api.notion.com/v1/oauth/token", { 305: method: "POST", 306: headers: { 307: Accept: "application/json", 308: "Content-Type": "application/json", 309: Authorization: `Basic ${encoded}`, 310: }, 311: body: JSON.stringify({ 312: grant_type: "refresh_token", 313: refresh_token: "your-refresh-token", 314: }), 315: }); 316: ... 317: Share a connection 318: Previous 319: Secure API credentials 320: Next 321: xslack

67: Quickstart
68: Copy pageCopy page
69: Create a page in your Notion workspace with a personal access token and a single API request.
70: Copy pageCopy page
71: Build tools and automations that create pages, organize data, and share feedback in Notion. This guide walks you through creating your first page with the API. You need a Notion account and a terminal.
72: Step 1: Get a personal access token
73: A personal access token (PAT) lets you authenticate API requests as yourself without setting up a connection or completing an OAuth flow.
74: 1
75: Open Personal access tokens in the Developer portal.
76: 2
77: Select New token.
78: 3
79: Enter a name, select the Notion API capability, and then select Create token. If a workspace picker appears, select a workspace first.
80: 4
81: Copy the token and save it somewhere secure. You won’t be able to see it again.
82: Don’t see the option to create a token?On Business and Enterprise plans, PAT creation is restricted by default. Ask a workspace owner to enable it in Settings → Connections.See Who can create PATs.
83: Set the token as an environment variable so you can use it in the examples below. Set it again if you open a new terminal. Keep the token out of browser code and public repositories.
84: macOS / Linux
85: Windows (PowerShell)
86: export NOTION_API_KEY=ntn_...
87: $env:NOTION_API_KEY = "ntn_..."
88: Step 2: Create a page
89: Make a POST request to the Create a page endpoint with markdown content. The API creates a private page in your workspace, using the # heading as the page title automatically.
90: curl
91: HTTP
92: JavaScript
93: curl -X POST https://api.notion.com/v1/pages \
94: -H "Authorization: Bearer $NOTION_API_KEY" \
95: -H "Notion-Version: 2026-03-11" \
96: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
97: -d '{
98: "icon": { "emoji": "🚀" },
99: "markdown": "# Hello from the API\n\n## Welcome\n\nThis page was created with the Notion API. You just made your first request!\n\n- Read the [API reference](https://developers.notion.com/reference/intro)\n- Explore [examples](https://developers.notion.com/page/examples)"
100: }'
101: POST https://api.notion.com/v1/pages
102: Authorization: Bearer {PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN}
103: Content-Type: application/json
104: Notion-Version: 2026-03-11
105: {
106: "icon": { "emoji": "🚀" },
107: "markdown": "# Hello from the API\n\n## Welcome\n\nThis page was created with the Notion API. You just made your first request!\n\n- Read the [API reference](https://developers.notion.com/reference/intro)\n- Explore [examples](https://developers.notion.com/page/examples)"
108: }
109: // Save as quickstart.mjs after running: npm install @notionhq/client
110: import { Client } from "@notionhq/client";
111: const notion = new Client({
112: auth: process.env.NOTION_API_KEY,
113: notionVersion: "2026-03-11",
114: });
115: async function main() {
116: const page = await notion.pages.create({
117: icon: { emoji: "🚀" },
118: markdown: [
119: "# Hello from the API",
120: "",
121: "## Welcome",
122: "",
123: "This page was created with the Notion API. You just made your first request!",
124: "",
125: "- Read the [API reference](https://developers.notion.com/reference/intro)",
126: "- Explore [examples](https://developers.notion.com/page/examples)",
127: ].join("\n"),
128: });
129: console.log("Created page:", page.url);
130: }
131: main();
132: The markdown field accepts enhanced markdown — headings, lists, code blocks, links, and more. The API converts it to Notion blocks for you.
133: Under the hood: markdown → blocks
134: Notion pages are made up of blocks — headings, paragraphs, lists, and more. When you send markdown, the API converts it into this block structure automatically.You can also build this structure directly using the children field. Here’s what the same page looks like expressed as blocks:
135: {
136: "icon": { "emoji": "🚀" },
137: "properties": {
138: "title": [{ "text": { "content": "Hello from the API" } }]
139: },
140: "children": [
141: {
142: "object": "block",
143: "type": "heading_2",
144: "heading_2": {
145: "rich_text": [{ "text": { "content": "Welcome" } }]
146: }
147: },
148: {
149: "object": "block",
150: "type": "paragraph",
151: "paragraph": {
152: "rich_text": [
153: {
154: "text": {
155: "content": "This page was created with the Notion API. You just made your first request!"
156: }
157: }
158: ]
159: }
160: }
161: ]
162: }
163: The block model gives you precise control over every element — formatting, colors, toggles, and block types that markdown can’t express. Use markdown when you want simplicity, and children when you need that control.See Working with page content to learn more about the block model.
164: Check the result
165: A successful response returns a page object:
166: Response
167: {
168: "object": "page",
169: "id": "a1b2c3d4-e5f6-7890-abcd-ef1234567890",
170: "created_time": "2025-01-15T09:30:00.000Z",
171: "last_edited_time": "2025-01-15T09:30:00.000Z",
172: "icon": {
173: "type": "emoji",
174: "emoji": "🚀"
175: },
176: "parent": {
177: "type": "workspace",
178: "workspace": true
179: },
180: "properties": {
181: "title": {
182: "id": "title",
183: "type": "title",
184: "title": [{ "plain_text": "Hello from the API" }]
185: }
186: },
187: "url": "https://www.notion.com/Hello-from-the-API-a1b2c3d4e5f67890abcdef1234567890",
188: "public_url": null
189: }
190: To see your new page:
191: From the response: Copy the url value and open it in your browser.
192: From Notion: Look in Private in your sidebar for 🚀 Hello from the API.
193: Open the page and you should see your heading, paragraph, and bullet list inside.
194: Getting an error?
195: Error responses return a JSON object with a code and message:
196: {
197: "object": "error",
198: "status": 401,
199: "code": "unauthorized",
200: "message": "API token is invalid."
201: }
202: ErrorFix
203: unauthorizedDouble-check that your token is correct and hasn’t expired.
204: validation_errorCheck the request body against the Create a page reference.
205: For the full list of error codes, see Status codes.
206: Next steps
207: Now that you’ve made your first request, explore what else you can build.
208: Pages
209: Create, update, and retrieve page content.
210: Databases
211: Create a database and find its data sources.
212: Views
213: Create and configure database views programmatically.
214: Data sources
215: Manage data sources, properties, entries, and schemas.
216: File uploads
217: Upload and attach files to pages and databases.
218: Comments
219: Handle page and inline comments.
220: Content queries
221: Find pages and data sources by title.
222: Users
223: Read user profiles available to your connection.
224: For a team automation or an app others can install, compare connections and tokens.
225: API reference
226: Browse every endpoint, request parameter, and response field.
227: JavaScript SDK
228: Official client library for Node.js.

82: Copy pageCopy page
83: Connect Notion to your AI assistant through its connector library, Notion’s directory, or manual MCP setup.
84: Copy pageCopy page
85: The easiest way to connect is through your AI assistant’s connector or plugin library. You can also browse available connections in Notion under Settings → Notion MCP.
86: From your AI assistant
87: Find Notion in your assistant’s connector or plugin library.
88: From Notion
89: Browse the directory in Notion’s settings.
90: Manual setup
91: Add Notion MCP using a server URL or client configuration.
92: Connect from your AI assistant
93: Open your AI assistant’s connector or plugin library and search for Notion. Select it and follow the prompts to authorize access to your Notion workspace.
94: After you authorize the connection, your AI assistant can read and update content that you can access in the selected workspace.
95: If Notion isn’t listed, check whether your assistant supports adding a custom MCP server and follow manual setup.
96: Connect from Notion
97: In Notion, open Settings → Notion MCP and browse the directory. Select your AI assistant and follow its connection instructions.
98: Manual setup
99: Use these instructions if you’re adding Notion as a custom MCP server or configuring a client directly. The remote server URL is https://mcp.notion.com/mcp.
100: Codex
101: Claude Code
102: Cursor
103: fx
104: Hermes
105: Devin
106: Pi
107: VS Code
108: Antigravity
109: Other MCP clients
110: Codex (ChatGPT)
111: Codex is OpenAI’s coding agent. See the Codex MCP documentation for more details.
112: Install the Codex CLI before running the commands below. If you see command not found, make sure codex is on your PATH.
113: 1
114: Add the Notion server to your Codex configuration at ~/.codex/config.toml:
115: [mcp_servers.notion]
116: url = "https://mcp.notion.com/mcp"
117: 2
118: Authenticate by running:
119: codex mcp login notion
120: Complete the OAuth flow to connect your Notion workspace.
121: Project-level configuration
122: To share the Notion MCP configuration with your team, create a .codex/config.toml file in your project root with the same server configuration.
123: Claude Code
124: Claude Code is Anthropic’s agentic coding tool for the terminal. See the Claude Code MCP documentation for more details.
125: Install Claude Code before running the command below. If you see command not found, make sure claude is on your PATH.
126: Run this command in your terminal:
127: claude mcp add --transport http notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp
128: Then authenticate by running /mcp in Claude Code and following the OAuth flow.
129: Using --scope flag for different installation scopes
130: --scope local (default): Available only to you in the current project
131: --scope project: Shared with your team via .mcp.json file
132: --scope user: Available to you across all projects
133: Use the /mcp command to list and manage the MCP servers you have installed, and use the /context command to understand the context token usage of your current session, including the number of tokens used by each MCP server that’s enabled.
134: Install the Notion plugin for Claude Code to add the MCP server, Skills, and slash commands for common Notion workflows.
135: Cursor
136: Cursor is an AI code editor that can connect to MCP servers. See the Cursor MCP documentation for more details.
137: 1
138: Create a .cursor/mcp.json file in your project root:
139: {
140: "mcpServers": {
141: "notion": {
142: "url": "https://mcp.notion.com/mcp"
143: }
144: }
145: }
146: 2
147: Open Customize in Cursor’s sidebar, then enable Notion and complete the OAuth flow to connect your workspace.
148: Global configuration
149: To configure Notion across all projects, add the same server configuration to ~/.cursor/mcp.json:
150: {
151: "mcpServers": {
152: "notion": {
153: "url": "https://mcp.notion.com/mcp"
154: }
155: }
156: }
157: fx
158: fx is a CLI coding agent from Vercel Labs. See the fx MCP documentation for more details.
159: 1
160: Start an interactive fx session:
161: fx
162: 2
163: Add the Notion server:
164: /mcp add notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp
165: fx opens your browser to complete the OAuth flow. To sign in again later, run /mcp login notion.
166: JSON configuration
167: Add Notion MCP to ~/.fx/mcp.json:
168: {
169: "mcpServers": {
170: "notion": {
171: "type": "http",
172: "url": "https://mcp.notion.com/mcp"
173: }
174: }
175: }
176: A running fx session picks up the change on your next prompt or /mcp command. Then run /mcp login notion.
177: Hermes
178: Hermes is a coding agent from Nous Research that can be extended with MCP servers. See the Hermes MCP documentation for more details.
179: 1
180: Add the Notion server to ~/.hermes/config.yaml:
181: mcp_servers:
182: notion:
183: url: "https://mcp.notion.com/mcp"
184: auth: oauth
185: 2
186: Authenticate by running:
187: hermes mcp login notion
188: Complete the OAuth flow to connect your Notion workspace.
189: Global configuration
190: The ~/.hermes/config.yaml configuration above applies to all projects for the current Hermes profile. See the Hermes configuration documentation for more details.
191: Devin
192: Devin is an AI software engineering agent that can connect to custom MCP servers. See the Devin MCP documentation for more details.
193: 1
194: In Devin, go to Settings → Connections → MCP servers, then select Add a custom MCP.
195: 2
196: Enter Notion as the server name, select HTTP as the transport, and set the server URL to:
197: https://mcp.notion.com/mcp
198: 3
199: Select OAuth as the authentication method. Choose Personal access for an individual connection, or Organization access to share the connection with your organization.
200: 4
201: Save the server, then complete the OAuth flow when Devin prompts you.
202: With Organization access, members share one authenticated connection. Use a Notion service account rather than a personal account, and have someone with the Manage MCP Servers permission complete the OAuth flow. With Personal access, each member authenticates their own Notion account.
203: Pi
204: Pi is an open-source, terminal-based coding agent. It uses the third-party Pi MCP Adapter to connect to MCP servers.
205: 1
206: Install the adapter and restart Pi:
207: pi install npm:pi-mcp-adapter
208: 2
209: In Pi, run /mcp setup, then choose Notion to add the server.
210: 3
211: Authenticate by running /mcp-auth notion and completing the OAuth flow to connect your Notion workspace.
212: Global and team configuration
213: To use Notion in every Pi project, add this configuration to ~/.config/mcp/mcp.json. To share it with a team, commit the same configuration in a project-root .mcp.json; each teammate then completes the OAuth flow locally.
214: {
215: "mcpServers": {
216: "notion": {
217: "url": "https://mcp.notion.com/mcp",
218: "auth": "oauth"
219: }
220: }
221: }
222: VS Code (GitHub Copilot)
223: Visual Studio Code supports MCP servers in its agent customization experience. See the VS Code MCP documentation for more details.
224: 1
225: Create a .vscode/mcp.json file in your workspace:
226: {
227: "servers": {
228: "notion": {
229: "type": "http",
230: "url": "https://mcp.notion.com/mcp"
231: }
232: }
233: }
234: 2
235: Open the Command Palette (Cmd+Shift+P / Ctrl+Shift+P) and run MCP: List Servers
236: 3
237: Start the Notion server and complete the OAuth flow when prompted
238: User-level configuration
239: To configure Notion MCP across all workspaces, run MCP: Open User Configuration from the Command Palette and add the server configuration there.
240: Antigravity
241: Antigravity supports MCP servers across its products. See the Antigravity MCP documentation for more details.
242: We recommend connecting to Notion MCP as a custom server rather than using the pre-configured “Notion” connector in the Antigravity MCP gallery, which uses the deprecated notion-mcp-server package.
243: 1
244: Follow the Antigravity instructions for connecting custom MCP servers and add the following to your mcp_config.json:
245: {
246: "mcpServers": {
247: "notion": {
248: "serverUrl": "https://mcp.notion.com/mcp"
249: }
250: }
251: }
252: 2
253: Save the configuration. Antigravity will prompt you to complete the OAuth flow to connect your Notion workspace.
254: Other MCP clients
255: Add Notion as a remote MCP server with the Streamable HTTP transport and the URL https://mcp.notion.com/mcp.
256: Migrate from the legacy SSE endpoint
257: Notion will retire the legacy HTTP with Server-Sent Events (SSE) endpoint, https://mcp.notion.com/sse, on February 23, 2027. Update your client before that date.
258: In your client’s Notion server settings, change the transport from SSE to Streamable HTTP and replace the URL with https://mcp.notion.com/mcp. Save the settings, sign in again if prompted, and check that the client lists Notion tools. If your client only offers SSE, update it to a version that supports Streamable HTTP.
259: JSON configuration
260: If your client accepts a JSON configuration, start with Streamable HTTP:
261: Streamable HTTP
262: STDIO (via mcp-remote)
263: {
264: "mcpServers": {
265: "notion": {
266: "url": "https://mcp.notion.com/mcp"
267: }
268: }
269: }
270: {
271: "mcpServers": {
272: "notion": {
273: "command": "npx",
274: "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://mcp.notion.com/mcp"]
275: }
276: }
277: }
278: Use the STDIO configuration if your client doesn’t support remote HTTP connections.
279: Troubleshooting
280: An enterprise policy blocks the connection
281: An admin in your organization may restrict adding MCP servers. If you see an enterprise policy error, ask your admin whether Notion MCP is allowed in your AI assistant. Notion workspace owners can also manage access through admin controls.
282: My MCP client doesn't support remote MCP servers
283: Some MCP clients only support local stdio servers. You can still connect to Notion MCP using the mcp-remote bridge:
284: {
285: "mcpServers": {
286: "notion": {
287: "command": "npx",
288: "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://mcp.notion.com/mcp"]
289: }
290: }
291: }
292: As a last resort, you can run our open-source MCP server locally, though this package is no longer actively maintained.
293: Authentication issues
294: Complete the OAuth flow when prompted.
295: Disconnect and reconnect the client. Look for Clear authentication or Disconnect in its MCP settings.
296: Check your permissions in the Notion workspace that you’re trying to access.
297: My MCP client isn't listed here
298: See Other MCP clients for the Notion MCP endpoints and JSON configuration examples. If the client doesn’t support MCP, contact its developer.
299: FAQs
300: Can I use Notion MCP without interactive authorization?
301: Yes, on Business and Enterprise plans. A workspace owner can create an MCP token with New MCP token in the Developer portal. The MCP client sends the token as a bearer token to https://mcp.notion.com/mcp, with no browser sign-in.Enterprise workspaces that use SAML SSO can also use enterprise-managed authorization, where the company’s identity provider grants access without a consent screen.
302: Which Notion plans can use Notion MCP?
303: Notion MCP works on every plan. Some features depend on the workspace’s plan:
304: MCP tokens: Business and Enterprise. Only workspace owners can create them.
305: Enterprise-managed authorization: Enterprise, with SAML SSO.
306: Connected-source search with notion-connector-search: Business or Enterprise with Notion AI. notion-search searches Notion on every plan.
307: Database queries with notion-query-data-sources: querying a saved view works on every plan. SQL queries are unlimited on Business or Enterprise with Notion AI. Other plans get a limited number of SQL queries on one data source at a time.
308: Some search filters, such as last edited by and last edited date: Business and Enterprise. On other plans these filters are dropped, and the result says so.
309: Request limits: higher on Business and Enterprise. See rate limits.
310: Can workspace guests use Notion MCP?
311: No. Only workspace members can connect Notion MCP. A guest who tries to connect sees a message that guests can’t connect, and Notion refuses the authorization.
312: Does Notion MCP support file uploads?
313: Yes. Use the notion-create-file-upload tool to upload images and other files up to 20 MiB. Workspace file-size limits still apply.The tool returns a short-lived upload URL and the headers and form field that the MCP client must use to send the file. After the upload succeeds, pass the response’s suggested_markdown directly to notion-create-pages or notion-update-page, or include it on a separate line in notion-create-comment markdown to attach the file. For larger files, use the file upload API.
314: What's the difference between Notion MCP and the open-source server?
315: Notion MCP (https://mcp.notion.com/mcp) is our hosted, actively maintained server. It supports OAuth authorization and MCP tokens, and requires no infrastructure setup.The open-source server (notion-mcp-server) is no longer actively maintained. It authenticates with an integration token and requires you to manage your own connection and deployment.For most users, we recommend Notion MCP.
316: I'm building my own MCP client
317: If you’re integrating Notion MCP into your own application, see
318: Build an MCP client for Notion for OAuth
319: and connection requirements.
320: Overview
321: Previous
322: Build an MCP client for Notion
323: Next
324: xslack

1: Creating personal access tokens | Airtable Help Center
2: Contact support
3: Sign up for free
4: All Collections›Integrating with Airtable›API
5: Creating personal access tokens
6: Last updated 9 days ago
7: Plan availability
8: All plan types. Certain features are only available to Enterprise Scale or Business plan customers.
9: Permissions
10: The scopes and access that you can set up with personal access tokens will reflect the permissions that you have in the various workspaces and bases connected to your Airtable account.
11: Platform(s)
12: Web/Browser, Mac app, and Windows app
13: Related reading
14: Scopes developer documentation - More technical information related to scopes in Airtable.
15: Service accounts overview - Help article that explains how Airtable admins can set up non-user accounts that can access Airtable's APIs.
16: Third-party integrations via OAuth overview - Help article that discusses the broader ways to manage which third-party integrations have access to your Airtable data.
17: What are personal access tokens?
18: Personal access tokens (PATs) allow users to create multiple access tokens that allow for a wide range of access to the information held in Airtable bases. For example, on the narrow end, you can create a PAT that only has a single scope to a single base in Airtable. On the deep end, however, you could have a "main/overarching" token that has access to all workspaces and bases with all available scopes included. Further, admins can adopt user role access on workspaces and bases in their enterprise for which they are not direct collaborators.
19: PATs allow admins access to workspaces and bases added to their organization. The admin who owns the PAT does not need to be a direct collaborator on every workspace and base within the organization. Instead, the PAT adopts the user role permissions for those bases and workspaces.
20: Accessing personal access tokens
21: Open the developer hub.
22: Click Personal access tokens under the “Developers” section.
23: Creating personal access tokens
24: Open the developer hub.
25: Click Create token.
26: Name your token.
27: Click + Add a scope.
28: Check out developer documentation to learn more about scopes.
29: Click + Add all resources/+ Add a base to select your token’s access level.
30: Options include choosing a single base, multiple bases—including bases from different workspaces—all current and future bases in a workspace you have access to, or even all of the bases in every workspace you have access to, including bases and workspaces added in the future. What the token can do in each base still depends on your permission level there.
31: In the resource picker you can search for a base or workspace by its ID as well as by its name. This is useful when several bases share a similar name, or when you already have the base ID from a URL or an API response.
32: Updating personal access tokens
33: Open the developer hub.
34: Scroll or search for the name of the PAT that you want to update/edit.
35: Click the token's name.
36: Alternatively, click the … icon to the far side of the PAT, then click Edit token.
37: Update the name, scopes, or access for the PAT.
38: Click Save changes.
39: Regenerating or deleting personal access tokens
40: Open the developer hub.
41: Scroll or search for the name of the PAT that you want to regenerate or delete.
42: Click the … icon to the far side of the PAT.
43: Click Regenerate token or Delete token.
44: Regenerating a token will cause a warning message to appear. Remember that any services currently using this token will need to be updated with the new token that is generated.
45: Limiting a token to a specific set of bases
46: You can't scope a personal access token to a managed app or to any other custom group of bases. Tokens can be scoped to individual bases, to workspaces, to all of your workspaces, or, for enterprise admins, to an entire organization. To give a token access to a specific set of bases—including bases added later—keep those bases in a dedicated workspace and add that workspace to the token.
47: Create a workspace for the bases the token needs to reach.
48: Move the bases into that workspace, or create them there.
49: Add the account that will own the token to the workspace. For integrations, this is usually a service account.
50: Open the developer hub while signed in as that account, and create a new token or open an existing one.
51: Click + Add a base, then select the workspace.
52: The token checks which workspace a base is in each time it's used. Bases created in or moved into the workspace later are covered automatically, and a base moved out of the workspace loses access right away. You don't need to own the workspace to add it to a token, but the token can only do what your permission level allows in each base—for example, Editor to update records and Creator to change fields and tables. If your organization's admin has turned on "Block API access to organization-owned bases and workspaces," the account must also be on the API access allowlist.
53: FAQs
54: What can my personal access tokens access?
55: Unlike legacy API keys, which have the same access as your Airtable account, you can limit and configure the access of your personal access tokens. You can do this by selecting the scopes (what endpoints the token can use) and access/resources (which bases and workspaces the token can access) when creating or updating a token.
56: Regardless of the scopes and access a user selects for their token, the token will only be able to perform actions that the user creating it is allowed to do. For example, to create a new field in a base via the API, the user must be a Creator collaborator in the base and the token must have the schema.bases:write scope and the base added as a resource.
57: For more information about how scopes and access work, see the Authentication developer reference. For more information about configuring your token's access, refer to the personal access tokens guide.
58: How do I find my API key?
59: On Jan 18, 2023, we began the deprecating user API keys, completing the deprecation process on Feb 1, 2024, meaning:
60: API Keys can no longer access the Airtable API.
61: Webhooks created with user API keys will not expire, but can no longer be created.
62: All users should migrate to personal access tokens for individual use and OAuth for third-party integrations. To access your PATs:
63: Open the developer hub.
64: Click Personal access tokens under the “Developers” section.
65: Why might I be seeing the "INVALID_PERMISSIONS_OR_MODEL_NOT_FOUND" error?
66: Typically, this error type indicates either:
67: A permissions-related issue, in which case you’ll want to:
68: Check your PAT scopes
69: Check your permissions level in the base you are referencing
70: See if field and table permissions might also be causing the invalid permissions error.
71: An issue with the base referenced, in which case you’ll want to:
72: Double-check that the base id referenced is correct
73: Confirm that the base has not been deleted
74: More common API troubleshooting information is available here.
75: I’m not able to access the enterprise scopes. What might be occurring?
76: The ability to add enterprise. scopes is restricted to Enterprise Scale plans. This feature is not available on Business plans. Upgrading to an Enterprise Scale plan is required to use this functionality.
77: Do personal access tokens expire?
78: By default, no. A personal access token has no expiration window of its own and stays active until it is deleted, regenerated, or modified. One exception applies: on enterprise organizations, an admin can set a policy that caps the maximum lifetime of a personal access token. When a token passes that cap, requests using it fail with UNAUTHORIZED - Invalid authentication token. If you're on an enterprise organization and a token that previously worked stops being accepted, ask your admin whether a token lifetime policy is in effect. If no lifetime policy applies and a PAT stops working, the cause is one of the following rather than expiration:
79: The token was regenerated, which invalidates the previous token value, so any service still using the old string will fail until updated with the new one.
80: The token was deleted, or its scopes or base/workspace access were changed.
81: If a PAT failure is happening in the environment or application consuming the token, check there, and with that platform's support, if Airtable shows the token as active.
82: You can review your tokens any time in the developer hub under Personal access tokens.
83: I have checked my scopes and IDs and still get an INVALID_PERMISSIONS_OR_MODEL_NOT_FOUND error. What else could cause it?
84: If your scopes, workspace/base IDs, and access all check out and you're on an enterprise organization, the most likely cause is an org-level API restriction set in the admin panel, not your token. When an admin enables "Block API access to organization-owned bases and workspaces" (under Settings → Integrations & development), only users on the API access allowlist can use personal access tokens against organization-owned resources — and requests from anyone not on the allowlist return INVALID_PERMISSIONS_OR_MODEL_NOT_FOUND, even with fully correct scopes and IDs. To resolve it, ask one of your internal Airtable admins to add you (or your service account) to the allowlist for that setting. If the admin needs guidance, point them to Settings – Airtable admin panel. The other documented causes remain worth ruling out: field/table editing permissions and an incorrect or inaccessible base/workspace ID.
85: Can I use a personal access token to write to a synced table?
86: No. You can't create or delete records in a synced table, or edit its synced fields, with a personal access token, whatever scopes the token has. A synced table takes its values from its source, so Airtable returns an error such as Your record could not be created because the underlying table is externally synced.
87: This also applies indirectly: a write to a linked record field fails if it would need to create a new record in a synced table. You can still write to fields you've added to the synced table yourself. Automations can't write to one-way synced tables; with two-way sync, automation actions (but not scripts) can make the edits the sync allows.
88: Can I limit a personal access token to a single interface?
89: No, you cannot scope a personal access token to an interface or to an individual view. Token access is granted per base and per workspace, so a token can reach any table or interface in a base it has access to, within the limits of its scopes. If your team works only in interfaces and you need to narrow what a token can reach in the underlying data, use Airtable field and table editing permissions on the tables and fields themselves. Those permissions are honored by API requests, just as they are in the Airtable UI.
90: Why does my personal access token return "UNAUTHORIZED - Invalid authentication token"?
91: This error means Airtable did not accept the credential sent in your request's Authorization header. It returns HTTP status 401 with this body:
92: {"error":{"type":"UNAUTHORIZED","message":"Invalid authentication token"}}
93: It is a different error from AUTHENTICATION_REQUIRED, which means no credential reached Airtable at all, and from INVALID_PERMISSIONS_OR_MODEL_NOT_FOUND, which means the token was accepted but doesn't have the scopes or resource access the request needs. A token that is rejected here never got as far as a scope or base check, so re-checking scopes and base access won't resolve it.
94: Work through these causes in order:
95: Only the token ID was sent. A complete token is a 17-character ID, a period, then a 64-character secret. The secret is displayed only once, at creation. If you no longer have it, regenerate the token and copy the whole value.
96: The secret was truncated or altered between copying and sending. Check for missing characters, added whitespace, or a line break introduced by the tool storing the token.
97: The token was deleted, regenerated, or had its access modified after you copied it. Confirm it still appears in the developer hub.
98: The token has passed a maximum lifetime set by an admin. On enterprise organizations, an admin policy can cap how long a personal access token stays valid. Once a token is past that cap, every request using it returns this error even though the token still looks correct and still appears in your token list. Ask one of your Airtable admins whether a token lifetime policy applies to your organization.
99: The endpoint doesn't accept personal access tokens. A small number of endpoints accept only other credential types, and a personal access token sent to one returns this error regardless of its scopes.
100: To narrow down which of these applies, repeat the request with response headers shown — for example, curl -i instead of curl -s:
101: If the response includes a WWW-Authenticate header containing error="invalid_token", Airtable recognized the value as a personal access token and rejected it during validation. The cause is one of the token-specific items above.
102: If that header is absent, the value wasn't recognized as a personal access token at all. Look for a malformed or truncated credential, or an endpoint that doesn't accept personal access tokens.
103: For error codes beyond authentication, see Airtable API: Common troubleshooting.
104: Never paste a complete token into a support ticket, community post, or chat conversation. Redact everything after the period, and regenerate any token whose secret you've shared.
105: Related Articles

107: Airtable Web API - Using filterByFormula or sort parameters
108: Service accounts overview
109: Airtable API: Common troubleshooting
110: Managing API call limits in Airtable

sources.numbered_text:
1: Using the Airtable MCP server | Airtable Help Center
2: Contact support
3: Sign up for free
4: All Collections›Airtable AI
5: Using the Airtable MCP server
6: Last updated 13 days ago
7: Plan availability
8: All plans
9: Permissions
10: Your MCP permissions mirror the same permission level(s) that you have have been granted in Airtable.
11: Owner, Creator, or Editor - Can set up OAuth integrations and manage MCP access. Can read and update records they have permission to access.
12: Additionally, workspace owners or creators can create new bases via MCP. Note that base-level creator permissions will not be able to create a new base.
13: Commenter or Read-only - Can read data via MCP for bases they have access
14: Platform(s)
15: Works with AI assistants that support Model Context Protocol (Claude, ChatGPT, and other MCP-compatible tools)
16: Airtable’s MCP server lets you connect AI tools directly to your Airtable bases. This integration allows you to ask questions about your data, create and update records, and analyze information—all through natural conversation with AI tools like Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, and more.
17: Setup instructions, client quickstart guides, and full technical documentation are available at Airtable developer docs: MCP server overview. Start there to connect Claude, ChatGPT, Claude Code, Cursor, or any other MCP-compatible tool.
18: What is Model Context Protocol (MCP)?
19: Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that allows AI tools to securely connect to external data sources. With MCP, AI tools can query your Airtable data, perform actions on your behalf, and present structured information—all while respecting your existing permissions and security settings.
20: What you can do with MCP?
21: The Airtable MCP Server enables several types of interactions between your AI tools and your data. Below is a brief list of capabilities, but you can find more information in the developer docs here.
22: Search and analyze data - "Show me all customers from our CRM base who haven't been contacted in the last 30 days."
23: Create records - "Add these 5 new project tasks to my 'Project Tracker' base."
24: Update existing records - "Update the status of task #123 to 'Complete'."
25: Create bases - "Create a new base called 'Q3 Campaign Tracker' in my Marketing workspace."
26: Access interface data - "Show me the records from the 'Q1 Pipeline' page." (This works even with interface-only permissions, on supported page layouts)
27: Create interfaces and interface pages - "Create an interface page to track my open tasks."
28: Read and edit record detail pages - "Add the Owner and Due date fields to the record detail page on my 'Q1 Pipeline' page, and group them under 'Ownership'."
29: Create and edit custom elements - "Build me a modern, sleek visual read out of the weekly data for our team's sprints from the 'Sprint' table."
30: Build forms - "Create one form to intake feedback from an internal audience and another one from an external audience in the 'Product feedback' table."
31: Submit forms on your behalf - "I found a bug in our software. I've attached screenshots and several logs of the issue, use that to file the request on my behalf to this form: {Insert a link to the Airtable form here}."
32: Work with automations - “What automations are configured in my 'Project Tracker' base?”
33: MCP prerequisites
34: Before setting up the Airtable MCP Server, you'll need:
35: An MCP-enabled Host (Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, etc)
36: Data stored in Airtable bases
37: Permission to use third-party integrations in your Airtable organization (if you don’t have permission, an Airtable admin at your organization may need to allow-list a new integration)
38: Tips for optimal MCP usage
39: Get the most out of your MCP integration with these tips:
40: Be specific: When asking about data, mention the base name or describe what you're looking for clearly
41: Use natural language: You don't need to know field names or table IDs—describe what you want in plain English. Sometimes you may want to describe the base in more detail before asking for data from a table.
42: Check permissions: If you can't access certain data via MCP, verify that you have the appropriate permissions in Airtable.
43: Think about what data you’re giving your AI tool: Your tool will be able to read and make edits to your Airtable data on your behalf. Make sure you trust the tools you’re using or any other data sources you connect to.
44: Setting up a quick MCP connection
45: All setup paths—pre-built connectors, plugins, manual OAuth configuration, and personal access tokens—are documented in the developer docs:
46: MCP server overview and setup
47: Claude quickstart steps
48: Claude Code quickstart steps
49: ChatGPT quickstart steps
50: Before setting up, you'll need an MCP-enabled AI tool, data stored in Airtable bases, and permission to use third-party integrations in your Airtable organization. If you don't have permission, an Airtable admin may need to allowlist the integration—see the FAQs below.
51: Managing your MCP integration
52: After setup, you can control which bases your AI assistant can access:
53: Go to your third-party integrations page.
54: Alternatively, click your user profile in Airtable, then click Integrations and Third-party integrations.
55: Select your MCP integration.
56: Add or remove bases and apps as needed. You can also add apps where you have interface-only access.
57: Limitations and dependencies
58: Keep these limitations in mind while using the MCP Server:
59: Rate limits: MCP server calls are subject to standard Airtable API rate limits.
60: Batch size: Creating records is limited to 10 records per request.
61: Change policy: Tool names, behaviors, and capabilities may change
62: Permission requirements: The MCP server respects your existing Airtable permissions—you can only access data you normally have permission to view or modify.
63: Third-party integrations: If you are an enterprise user and your admin has enabled restrictions on third-party integrations, they'll need to allowlist the MCP integration.
64: Automation activation: MCP can create and update automation drafts, but turning an automation on (deploy) is done in the Airtable UI.
65: Automations with Script actions: MCP can create and update automation drafts, but automations containing a Script action can't be created or edited via MCP. You will need to add or modify Script actions directly in the Airtable UI.
66: Interface filters: MCP can't add filters to an Interface (for example, a Current User filter). You will need to configure Interface filters directly in Interface Designer.
67: Editing existing Interfaces: Some page types, including inbox and legacy layouts, can only be edited in Interface Designer by a user, manually.
68: MCP can edit pages in an existing Interface directly. It can change settings on grid, list, kanban, calendar, gallery and timeline pages, and it can edit dashboards, standalone forms and record detail pages.
69: On record detail pages it can add or remove fields, add groups, change the title field and how fields are displayed, and make the page read-only.
70: To make bigger structural changes to an interface page, such as changing its type, replace its layout through MCP or use Interface Designer.
71: Interface page layouts: The page-read tools support most, but not all, interface page layouts. If a page's layout isn't supported yet, the request fails, and your AI assistant may report that no matching records were found rather than that the page type isn't supported.
72: Ask for a record list or grid page sourced from the same data, or ask a base Owner or Creator to grant you read-only base access so your assistant can use the table and view tools instead.
73: Troubleshooting MCP connection problems
74: If your AI tool can't connect to the Airtable MCP server, work through the checks below before contacting support.
75: Your client reports "authentication required" and lists no tools
76: Your client reached the server but hasn't finished the OAuth login. Run your client's MCP login command and complete the Airtable authorization in your browser. If the authorization page returns an error instead, see the next section.
77: Authorization fails with "invalid client_id or mismatched redirect_uri"
78: The full error reads: "This third-party app failed to properly construct a request to Airtable: invalid client_id or mismatched redirect_uri."
79: Some MCP clients register themselves with Airtable using Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD) rather than dynamic client registration, and that path can be rejected at authorization. Airtable's OAuth metadata advertises a dynamic client registration endpoint, so telling your client to use dynamic client registration resolves the error.
80: In Codex CLI, force dynamic client registration when you log in:
81: codex mcp login airtable --oauth-client-registration dcr
82: In other clients, look for an equivalent OAuth setting that selects dynamic client registration — sometimes labeled DCR — as the registration method. If your client doesn't expose that option, connect with a personal access token instead; see the MCP server overview in the developer docs.
83: This workaround was reported against Codex CLI 0.166.0 on macOS. Other clients and operating systems may name the setting differently.
84: Your client isn't one of the documented quickstarts
85: The developer docs carry step-by-step quickstarts for a few clients, but any tool that supports remote MCP servers over HTTP can connect. Point it at the server URL https://mcp.airtable.com/mcp and choose OAuth as the authentication method, then follow the error guidance above if authorization fails.
86: Your admin hasn't allowlisted the integration
87: If your organization restricts third-party integrations, the MCP integration must be allowlisted before you can connect. See "How can admins enable a blocked MCP integration?" in the FAQs below.
88: If the connection still fails after these steps, see Troubleshooting disconnected OAuth integrations in Airtable.
89: FAQs
90: Can I use MCP with any base I have access to?
91: If you have base-level access, you can use MCP to access the data stored within that base. The MCP server respects your existing Airtable permissions. If you have read-only or comment-only access to a base, you'll be able to read that data via MCP, but you won't be able to create or update records.
92: What AI assistants work with Airtable's MCP Server?
93: Any AI assistant that supports the Model Context Protocol can connect to Airtable's MCP Server. This includes Claude, ChatGPT, and other MCP-compatible tools. Check your AI assistant's documentation to confirm MCP support.
94: How do I revoke access if I no longer want my AI assistant to access my bases?
95: Navigate to your user profile > Integrations > Third-party Integrations, find the MCP integration, and either remove specific bases or delete the integration entirely.
96: Does using MCP count against my Airtable limits?
97: MCP uses our public API under the hood and will count against any existing API rate limits. Any records created using MCP will count against existing base limits.
98: Can I use MCP to access Airtable Interfaces?
99: Yes, for supported page layouts. If you have interface-only access to a base, you can use MCP to discover your interface pages (list_pages_for_base), list records shown on a page (list_records_for_page), and drill into record details (get_record_for_page). The data returned respects the same permissions as your interface—you'll only see data that your interface pages make available to you. Not every interface page layout is supported yet. If a page's layout isn't supported, the request fails and your assistant may say that no matching records were found. See "Limitations and dependencies" above.
100: What happens if I try to update a field I don't have permission to modify?
101: The MCP server will return an error, just as the Airtable API would. Your AI assistant should communicate this limitation to you.
102: Are there additional costs for using MCP?
103: No. The MCP integration is currently included with your current Airtable plan. There are no additional Airtable charges for MCP usage, but existing API rate limits remain.
104: How can admins enable a blocked MCP integration?
105: For Airtable admins to enable a blocked integration:
106: Navigate to Admin Panel > Settings > Integrations & development > Third party integration allowlist.
107: Click Allow integration.
108: Enter the client ID provided by your user.
109: Click Save.
110: Can I create new bases using MCP?
111: Yes. You can use the create_base tool to create a new base in any workspace where you have Creator-level permissions. You can optionally define tables and fields during creation. Use list_workspaces first to find the workspace ID where you want to create the base.
112: Can the Airtable MCP connect to development apps (part of the managed apps and components feature) and update those apps in the same way as regular Airtable bases?
113: No. Calls to a development base will return a 403 permissions error. However, API/MCP calls can be made to bases where a managed app or component has been installed (i.e., the child/production bases). So the restriction is specifically on the development base itself, not on installed instances.
114: How do I connect Claude Code to Airtable?
115: The recommended approach is to run claude mcp add --transport http airtable https://mcp.airtable.com/mcp in your terminal, then run /mcp inside Claude Code to authenticate with your Airtable account through your browser. Alternatively, you can connect using a personal access token if you prefer. See Airtable developer docs: MCP server overview for instructions.
116: Who at my organization can enable third-party integrations or MCP, and can Airtable tell me who my admin is?
117: Allowlisting a third-party integration is handled by an admin at your own organization. Typically that person is a super admin, org unit admin, or an integration admin with access to the “Settings → Integrations & development” in the admin panel. For the exact steps, see "How can admins enable a blocked MCP integration?" above.
118: For privacy and security reasons, Airtable Support does not share the names or contact details of admins within an enterprise account. To find the right person, reach out to your internal IT team or whoever manages your organization's Airtable account. If your first contact isn't able to make an organization-wide decision, they can usually point you to the person who can.
119: I have Editor permissions but can only create an "Interface only" token. Why?
120: If you are only able to create "Interface only" tokens, that usually means you have Editor access to an interface, not to the underlying base. Interface access and base access are separate in Airtable, and full-access tokens — including the kind needed to connect an MCP client like Claude in edit mode — require base-level access.
121: To resolve it, ask a base owner, creator, or an admin in your organization to grant you Editor (or higher) access to the base itself, not just the interface. Base access is shared through a base invite link, which works differently from interface sharing — see Creating Airtable base share links. Once you have base-level access, the full-access token option will become available.
122: How do I limit write access when setting up an MCP connection?
123: For a read-only connection, so your AI tool can view data but can't create, update, or delete records, include only these scopes:
124: data.records:read
125: schema.bases:read
126: data.recordComments:read
127: workspacesAndBases:read
128: Enterprise admins can use a service account for this setup. See Airtable developer docs: MCP server overview.
129: Can I create or edit automations using MCP?
130: Yes. You can list and inspect automations, create draft automations, update draft configuration, and delete inactive automations. New and updated automations are saved as drafts—open the automation in Airtable to review and turn it on. To delete an automation that is currently on, turn it off in Airtable first.
131: Related Articles
132: Using Airtable AI in fields
133: AI Field agent - Build prototype
134: Using Omni AI in Airtable
135: Using Airtable AI in Slack
136: AI-generated interface elements in Airtable
