42: OAuth 2.0 authentication
43: Linear supports OAuth2 authentication, which is recommended if you’re building applications to integrate with Linear.
44: It is highly recommended you create a workspace for the purpose of managing the OAuth2 Application, as each admin user will have access.
45: All OAuth2 applications were migrated to the new refresh token system on April 1, 2026.
46: Specifically for CI and scheduled automation, refer to Client credentials token.
47: Token lifetimes and renewal⁠
48: The grant type determines how credentials are renewed. The actor determines whose identity the application uses. Using actor=app with an authorization-code grant does not remove the refresh-token requirement.
49: Grant type
50: Actor
51: Access-token lifetime
52: Renewal
53: Authorization code
54: user or app
55: 24 hours by default
56: Exchange the refresh token for a new token pair.
57: Client credentials
58: app
59: 30 days
60: Request a new access token. No refresh token is issued.
61: Use expires_in from the token response to track when the access token expires. Tokens can also be revoked or replaced before they expire, so handle authentication failures even when the expected expiration time has not passed.
62: Create an OAuth2 application⁠
63: Create a new OAuth2 Application and configure the redirect callback URLs to your application.
64: Redirect user access requests to Linear⁠
65: When authorizing a user to the Linear API, redirect to an authorization URL with correct parameters and scopes:
66: GET https://linear.app/oauth/authorize HTTP/1.1
67: Name
68: Description
69: client_id
70: (required) Client ID provided when you create the OAuth2 Application
71: redirect_uri
72: (required) Redirect URI
73: response_type=code
74: (required) Expected response type
75: scope
76: (required) Comma separated list of scopes:
77: read - (Default) Read access for the user’s account. This scope will always be present.
78: write - Write access for the user’s account. If your application only needs to create comments, use a more targeted scope
79: issues:create - Allows creating and updating issues, creating their attachments, subscribing and unsubscribing from issues, and uploading files and images.
80: comments:create - Allows creating new issue comments and uploading files and images. Does not allow editing comments.
81: timeSchedule:write - Allows creating and modifying time schedules
82: admin - User actor only. Grants access to admin-level endpoints. Request it only when needed.
83: oauth:create - Allows creating OAuth applications.
84: customer:read - App actor only. Allows reading customer data.
85: customer:write - App actor only. Allows writing customer data.
86: initiative:read - App actor only. Allows reading initiatives.
87: initiative:write - App actor only. Allows writing initiatives.
88: customView:read - App actor only. Allows reading workspace-wide shared views, not team, project, or initiative views.
89: app:mentionable - App actor only. Allows users to mention the app.
90: app:assignable - App actor only. Allows users to delegate issues to the app. It does not enable ordinary issue assignment.
91: See App authentication for agent-specific scopes such as app:assignable or app:mentionable.
92: state
93: (optional, recommended) Prevents CSRF attacks and should always be supplied. Read more about it here.
94: prompt=consent
95: (optional) The consent screen is displayed every time, even if all scopes were previously granted. This can be useful if you want to give users the opportunity to connect multiple workspaces.
96: actor
97: Selects the identity the application acts as. The actor is not a permission; request permissions using scope:
98: user - (Default) Resources are created as the user who authorized the application. This option should be used if you want each user to do their own authentication
99: app - Resources are created as the application. Use this for agents and service accounts.
100: PKCE⁠
101: Linear supports the PKCE flow. To use this flow, you’ll need to include two additional parameters as part of your /authorize request:
102: Name
103: Description
104: code_challenge
105: (required) Code challenge you generated
106: code_challenge_method
107: (required) Either plain or S256, depending on whether the challenge is the plain verifier string or the SHA256 hash of the string
108: Example⁠
109: GET https://linear.app/oauth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&redirect_uri=YOUR_REDIRECT_URL&state=SECURE_RANDOM&scope=read HTTP/1.1
110: GET https://linear.app/oauth/authorize?client_id=client1&redirect_uri=http%3A%2F%2Flocalhost%3A3000%2Foauth%2Fcallback&response_type=code&scope=read,write HTTP/1.1
111: GET https://linear.app/oauth/authorize?client_id=client1&redirect_uri=http%3A%2F%2Flocalhost%3A3000%2Foauth%2Fcallback&response_type=code&scope=read,write&code_challenge=challenge&code_challenge_method=S256 HTTP/1.1
112: GET https://linear.app/oauth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&redirect_uri=YOUR_REDIRECT_URL&state=SECURE_RANDOM&scope=read,comments:create HTTP/1.1
113: GET https://linear.app/oauth/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&redirect_uri=YOUR_REDIRECT_URL&state=SECURE_RANDOM&actor=app&scope=read,customer:read HTTP/1.1
114: The last two examples show a comment-only integration (read access plus comment creation, without general write access) and a read-only customer integration using the app actor.
115: Handle the redirect URLs you specified in the OAuth2 Application⁠
116: Once the user approves your application they will be redirected back to your application, with the OAuth authorization code in the URL params.
117: Any state parameter you specified in step 2 will also be returned in the URL params and must match the value specified in step 2. If the values do not match, the request should not be trusted.
118: Example⁠
119: GET https://example.com/oauth/callback?code=9a5190f637d8b1ad0ca92ab3ec4c0d033ad6c862&state=b1ad0ca92 HTTP/1.1
120: Exchange code for an access token⁠
121: After receiving the code, you can exchange it for a Linear API access token:
122: POST https://api.linear.app/oauth/token HTTP/1.1
123: Pass parameters in body as URL-encoded form submission, where the Content-Type header must be application/x-www-form-urlencoded.
124: Parameter
125: Description
126: code
127: (required) Authorization code from the previous step
128: redirect_uri
129: (required) Same redirect URI which you used in the previous step
130: client_id
131: (required) Application’s client ID
132: client_secret
133: (required) Application’s client secret
134: grant_type=authorization_code
135: (required)
136: PKCE⁠
137: If you are using the PKCE flow, the parameters required by the /token endpoint are different:
138: Name
139: Description
140: code
141: (required) Authorization code from the previous step
142: redirect_uri
143: (required) Same redirect URI which you used in the previous step
144: client_id
145: (required) Application’s client ID
146: client_secret
147: (optional) Application’s client secret
148: code_verifier
149: (required) The code verifier for the PKCE request that you originally generated before the authorization request
150: grant_type=authorization_code
151: (required)
152: Response⁠
153: After a successful request, a valid access token and refresh token will be returned in the response. The access token is valid for 24 hours and will need to be refreshed when it expires. Example response:
154: {
155: "access_token": "00a21d8b0c4e2375114e49c067dfb81eb0d2076f48354714cd5df984d87b67cc",
156: "token_type": "Bearer",
157: "expires_in": 86399,
158: "scope": "read write",
159: "refresh_token": "sz0c8ffy95zj2ff6bh1hiausauw3dbfsu4gly1z4p49b5odqv8l7owunb654vg1f",
160: }
161: Note: OAuth apps created prior to Dec 1, 2023 will instead return scope as an array of strings in the token response.
162: Refresh an access token⁠
163: Each refresh token expires 30 days after issuance. A successful refresh returns a new access token and refresh token, with a new 30-day refresh-token lifetime. API requests do not extend either lifetime.
164: Refresh before the access token expires to avoid interrupted requests. An expired access token can still be renewed while its refresh token remains valid.
165: Save the returned credentials together and coordinate refreshes across processes sharing an authorization. If the current refresh token expires or is revoked, complete authorization again.
166: For authorization, you have two options:
167: Use HTTP basic authentication by passing a Base64-encoded client_id:client_secret string as an authorization header: Authorization: Basic <base64(client_id:client_secret)>
168: Pass client_id and client_secret as parameters
169: If your access token was generated using PKCE, you can simply pass client_id as a parameter.
170: If a refresh succeeds but its response is lost, retry with the same refresh token within 30 minutes of the original successful refresh to recover the replacement credentials. Retrying does not extend this window. Save and use the returned credentials rather than continuing to use the old refresh token. This retry window does not restore explicitly revoked credentials or credentials replaced through an installation update.
171: POST https://api.linear.app/oauth/token HTTP/1.1
172: Pass parameters in body as URL-encoded form submission, where the Content-Type header must be application/x-www-form-urlencoded.
173: Parameter
174: Description
175: refresh_token
176: (required) Refresh token from the previous step
177: grant_type=refresh_token
178: (required)
179: client_id
180: (optional if you’re using HTTP basic authentication) Application’s client ID
181: client_secret
182: (optional if you’re using HTTP basic authentication or refreshing a token generated using PKCE) Application’s client secret
183: Response⁠
184: After a successful request, a new valid access token and a new refresh token will be returned in the response:
185: {
186: "access_token": "fxra4u0msw3bagb9rdn2i641bs52m9zo8ksoxljouygcu31nh8s2jf8fygbepy16",
187: "token_type": "Bearer",
188: "expires_in": 86399,
189: "scope": "read write",
190: "refresh_token": "qjmj51q8f8fnwe188702jarfqxwhdy6r5ivqy4yjuhw2crubm5e7nyu84un3marx",
191: }
192: Make an API request⁠
193: Once you have obtained a valid access token, you can make a request to Linear’s GraphQL API. You can initialize the Linear Client with the access token:
194: const client = new LinearClient({ accessToken: response.access_token })
195: const me = await client.viewer
196: Or pass the token as an authorization header: Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>
197: curl https://api.linear.app/graphql \
198: -X POST \
199: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
200: -H 'Authorization: Bearer <ACCESS_TOKEN>' \
201: --data '{ "query": "{ viewer { id name } }" }' \
202: When credentials become invalid⁠
203: Tokens can become invalid before their reported expiry. Choose the recovery path that matches the grant and the event.
204: Expiration. Refresh an expired access token using a valid refresh token, or request a new client-credentials token. If the refresh token has expired, complete authorization again. See refresh an access token.
205: Revocation. An authorization can be revoked before its tokens expire. Refreshing cannot restore revoked credentials. An already-revoked historical token is not a reliable way to revoke the current credentials. Use the current authorization’s credentials and the revocation endpoint.
206: Installation updates. Updating an authorization-code app installation replaces its current access and refresh credentials. Follow the installation update flow and update every process that shares the credentials.
207: Client-credentials scope changes. Requesting different scopes replaces existing app-actor credentials for that app in that workspace, not across all workspaces. Keep scope sets consistent across processes. See client credentials tokens.
208: Switching grants. A client-credentials request replaces an existing authorization-code app installation. To switch back to an authorization-code installation, revoke the existing authorization first.
209: Secret rotation. Rotating the client secret revokes client-credentials tokens, but does not revoke authorization-code access and refresh token pairs. Refresh requests that require a secret must use the current secret. See rotating your client secret.
210: Token cleanup. The 1,000-token limit is enforced through asynchronous cleanup, not a strict issuance ceiling. Cleanup retains the most recently used unexpired client-credentials tokens per app and workspace; unused tokens fall back to creation time. Request new credentials if cleanup invalidates a token.
211: App deletion. Deleting the OAuth app revokes its related tokens. Refreshing cannot restore access.
212: Revoke an access token⁠
213: To revoke a user’s access, call the revocation endpoint and include the token to be revoked in the token form field of the request body.
214: If available, include token_type_hint (access_token or refresh_token) to help the server identify the token.
215: POST https://api.linear.app/oauth/revoke HTTP/1.1
216: Note: For backwards compatibility, we still accept revocation via the Authorization header or the legacy access_token / refresh_token form fields. New integrations should use the token field. The token field must not be combined with legacy fields.
217: Response⁠
218: Expected HTTP status:
219: 200 - token was revoked
220: 400 - unable to revoke token (e.g. token was already revoked)
221: 401 - unable to authenticate with the token
222: Rotating your client secret⁠
223: If your application’s credentials are ever exposed (for example, in a security incident on your own infrastructure) you can generate a new client secret or webhook signing secret without re-registering your application.
224: From your application’s settings page in Linear, under Settings → API, select Rotate secret next to the credential you want to replace. Your client secret and your webhook signing secret each have their own control.
225: Rotating your client secret immediately invalidates any client credentials tokens issued for your application. It does not revoke access or refresh tokens already granted to individual workspaces — those keep working, and will use your new secret the next time they’re refreshed. If you need to revoke those as well, do so separately (see “Revoking access tokens” above).
226: Rotating your webhook signing secret takes effect immediately. Update your webhook handler to verify incoming payloads with the new secret at the same time you rotate it.
227: Client credentials tokens⁠
228: We support the client_credentials grant type for OAuth2 apps that use tokens for server-to-server communication and cannot support a user-initiated OAuth flow involving refresh tokens.
229: Client-credentials tokens use the app actor, are valid for 30 days, and do not include a refresh token. Reuse the token across API requests and request a replacement shortly before it expires, using expires_in to track expiration. Handle authentication failures as well, since tokens can be revoked before they expire.
230: You must first toggle on client credentials tokens for your OAuth2 app when creating or editing the app in Linear
231: The token generated using this grant type will be an app actor token that has access to all public teams in the workspace and is valid for 30 days. You can learn more about app actor tokens here.
232: The app user’s team access can be modified through the app details page for your app at any point after the token is generated. Since there is no refresh token paired with this access token, your server is expected to fetch a new token if it receives a 401 error when making a request with the previous token.
233: Multiple client-credentials tokens can coexist when they request the same scopes. Keep scope sets consistent across processes. Scope changes, switching grants, and asynchronous cleanup can invalidate existing credentials. See when credentials become invalid for workspace scope, renewal, and recovery guidance.
234: For increased security, we will also invalidate your app’s client credentials tokens if its client secret is rotated.
235: Request⁠
236: For authorization, you have two options:
237: Use HTTP basic authentication by passing a Base64-encoded client_id:client_secret string as an authorization header: Authorization: Basic <base64(client_id:client_secret)>
238: Pass client_id and client_secret as parameters
239: POST https://api.linear.app/oauth/token HTTP/1.1
240: Name
241: Description
242: grant_type=client_credentials
243: (required)
244: scope
245: (required) Comma-separated list of scopes
246: client_id
247: (optional if you’re using HTTP basic authentication) Application’s client ID
248: client_secret
249: (optional if you’re using HTTP basic authentication) Application’s client secret
250: Response⁠
251: After a successful request, a new valid access token will be returned in the response:
252: {
253: "access_token": "fxra4u0msw3bagb9rdn2i621bs52m9zo8ksoxljouygcu31nh8s2jf8fygbepy16",
254: "token_type": "Bearer",
255: "expires_in": 2591999,
256: "scope": "read write",
257: }
258: If your OAuth2 app does not have client credentials tokens enabled, you will receive an error response:
259: {
260: "error":"Error",
261: "error_description":"Client does not support the client_credentials grant type"
262: }

64: MCP server
65: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) server provides a standardized interface that allows any compatible AI model or agent to access your Linear data in a simple and secure way.
66: Connect to our MCP server natively in Claude, Cursor, and other clients or use the mcp-remote module for backwards compatibility with clients that do not support remote MCP.
67: Linear’s MCP server follows the authenticated remote MCP spec, so the server is centrally hosted and managed. The Linear MCP server has tools available for finding, creating, and updating objects in Linear like issues, projects, and comments — with more functionality on the way, and feedback on its functionality is welcomed.
68: For help getting started after setup, see some of our example prompts.
69: Setup⁠
70: General⁠
71: Our MCP server uses Streamable HTTP as the primary transport, accessible at the following address. The interactive setup flow uses OAuth 2.1 with dynamic client registration. You can also authenticate directly with a bearer token or Linear API key — see the FAQ for details.
72: Read-write access is provided through https://mcp.linear.app/mcp by default.
73: For read-only access, you have two options:
74: Connect to https://mcp.linear.app/mcp/readonly, which only ever exposes read tools.
75: Use the standard /mcp endpoint, but only request the read OAuth scope. Clients that request read are granted read-only access, and the underlying token can’t reach write APIs.
76: For instructions for specific clients, read on. Dedicated setup pages are also available for Claude, Cursor, VS Code, Windsurf, and Zed.
77: Claude⁠
78: Team, Enterprise (Claude.ai)
79: Navigate to the connectors page and connect Linear.
80: Free, Pro (Claude desktop)
81: From Claude settings > Connectors you can add the Linear connector.
82: Enterprise-managed authorization⁠
83: If you use Okta, first configure SAML for Linear using Okta’s OIN. Then enable MCP enterprise managed authentication from the bottom of your Okta identity provider settings in Linear.
84: Once this is toggled on, copy the Issuer URI for the authorization server from Okta’s side and paste this into your Linear settings:
85: e.g. https://your-org.okta.com
86: This allows supported external MCP clients such as Claude to authenticate users automatically using your Okta-managed access policies.
87: Claude auto-connect (beta)⁠
88: Claude auto-connect lets members with matching Linear accounts on Business or Enterprise plans connect automatically, without a separate sign-in or consent screen. Members retain their existing Linear permissions. Setup requires a Claude Team or Enterprise plan and admin access in both Claude and Linear.
89: In Claude, go to Organization settings → Connectors → Linear and select Set up next to Managed authorization.
90: Under Identity source, select Claude-issued and copy the issuer URL shown in Claude.
91: In Linear, go to Workspace settings → Security, enable Claude-issued authentication for MCP, and enter the URL in Claude issuer URL.
92: Copy the Tenant ID from Linear and paste it into Tenant ID in Claude.
93: Select Run test. Once all checks pass, select Enable and continue and choose who gets the connector.
94: Members’ Claude and Linear email addresses must match. Test with a few members before rolling this out. To turn it off, disable managed authorization in Claude and Claude-issued authentication for MCP in Linear.
95: Claude Code⁠
96: claude mcp add --transport http linear-server https://mcp.linear.app/mcp
97: Then run /mcp once you’ve opened a Claude Code session to go through the authentication flow.
98: Codex⁠
99: The setup steps for the MCP server are the same regardless of whether you use the IDE Extension or the CLI since the configuration is shared.
100: Configuration via CLI:
101: Run the following command in Terminal:
102: codex mcp add linear --url https://mcp.linear.app/mcp
103: This will automatically prompt you to log in with your Linear account and connect it to your Codex.
104: Note: If this is the first time you are using an MCP in Codex you will need to enable the rmcp feature for this to work. Add the following into your ~/.codex/config.toml:
105: [features]
106: experimental_use_rmcp_client = true
107: Configuration through environment variables:
108: Open the ~/.codex/config.toml file in your preferred editor
109: Add the following:
110: [features]
111: experimental_use_rmcp_client = true
112: [mcp_servers.linear]
113: url = "https://mcp.linear.app/mcp"
114: Run codex mcp login linear to move through the authentication flow.
115: Cursor⁠
116: To add the MCP to Cursor, you can install by clicking here, or searching for Linear from Cursor’s MCP tools page.
117: fx⁠
118: In fx, add Linear’s MCP server:
119: /mcp add linear https://mcp.linear.app/mcp
120: Then run:
121: /mcp login linear
122: Follow the prompts in your browser to authorize access to Linear.
123: For more configuration options, see the fx MCP documentation.
124: Visual Studio Code⁠
125: {
126: "mcpServers": {
127: "linear": {
128: "command": "npx",
129: "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://mcp.linear.app/mcp"]
130: }
131: }
132: }
133: CTRL/CMD P and search for MCP: Add Server.
134: Select Command (stdio)
135: Enter the following configuration, and hit enter.
136: npx mcp-remote https://mcp.linear.app/mcp
137: Enter the name Linear and hit enter.
138: Activate the server using MCP: List Servers and selecting Linear, and selecting Start Server.
139: v0 by Vercel⁠
140: To add the MCP to v0, you can install from the connections page.
141: Windsurf⁠
142: CTRL/CMD , to open Windsurf settings.
143: Under Scroll to Cascade -> MCP servers
144: Select Add Server -> Add custom server
145: Add the following:
146: {
147: "mcpServers": {
148: "linear": {
149: "command": "npx",
150: "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://mcp.linear.app/mcp"]
151: }
152: }
153: }
154: Zed⁠
155: CMD , to open Zed settings.
156: Add the following:
157: {
158: "context_servers": {
159: "linear": {
160: "source": "custom",
161: "command": "npx",
162: "args": ["-y", "mcp-remote", "https://mcp.linear.app/mcp"],
163: "env": {}
164: }
165: }
166: }
167: Others⁠
168: Hundreds of other tools now support MCP servers, you can configure them to use Linear’s MCP server with the following settings:
169: Command: npx
170: Arguments: -y mcp-remote https://mcp.linear.app/mcp
171: Environment: None
172: Common use cases⁠
173: The MCP server lets you work with your Linear data from any compatible AI client. To help get started with the Linear MCP tooling, feel free to copy some example prompts into your own client to explore what’s possible.
174: Roadmap planning
175: Use case
176: Use this workflow to turn a planning document into a structured Linear project, with issues, milestones, and relationships that make the work easier to organize and track.
177: Example prompt
178: You are helping turn a planning document into a well-structured Linear project.
179: Read the document, create a project that reflects its objective, scope, and timeline, then create the issues needed to represent the work with clear titles and populated descriptions. Each issue should make the work actionable by capturing the problem, the goal, the proposed approach when one is provided, and any open questions that remain. Organize issues into milestones when the document clearly implies phases, deliverables, or checkpoints, and add related relationships where issues are meaningfully connected, but do not invent dependencies or structure that the source material does not support.
180: If the document is too vague or ambiguous to produce high-quality work, flag the uncertainty and return a proposed outline for review instead of guessing.
181: Before creating anything, show the proposed project, milestones, issues, relationships, and any decisions that need review.
182: Standup note automation
183: Use case
184: Use this workflow to turn standup notes into clear updates on the relevant Linear issues, so progress and blockers stay documented without extra manual work.
185: Example prompt
186: You are helping turn live standup notes into updates on existing Linear issues.
187: Read the notes, identify any issues mentioned by ID, title, owner, or clear surrounding context, and match each note only when the connection is strong.
188: For every confident match, add a concise comment that captures what changed, the current status or blocker, and the next step if one is mentioned. Keep each comment factual and specific to that issue. If a note is ambiguous or you cannot confidently match it, do not guess or create work from it; return it as unmatched with a short explanation.
189: Before applying any changes, show which issues you plan to update and the exact comment you would post to each one, then apply the comments and separately list any notes you skipped.
190: Standup notes: [Paste the notes’ raw text here or attach the transcript as a document]
191: Incoming bug investigation
192: Use case
193: Use this workflow to investigate a reported bug from an existing Linear issue, identify a likely root cause, and capture the findings back on the issue for the team.
194: Example prompt
195: You are helping investigate a bug that is already tracked in Linear.
196: Start from the referenced issue, use its description and any linked context as the starting point, and search for the most likely root cause by following relevant technical, product, or workflow clues.
197: Focus on producing a clear, evidence-based explanation of what is happening, what changed if that is relevant, and what the likely cause appears to be. Do not guess when the evidence is weak; instead, call out uncertainty and explain what additional context would help.
198: Once you have enough information, write a concise summary of the findings and post that summary as a comment on the issue so the investigation is documented for the team.
199: Linear issue to investigate: [LIN-123]
200: Team cycle summarization
201: Use case
202: Use this workflow to summarize what a team completed during a specific cycle or timeframe, making it easier to review progress and communicate outcomes.
203: Example prompt
204: You are helping summarize work completed during a specific Linear cycle or timeframe.
205: Identify the most recently completed cycle to analyze for the selected team or teams, gather the relevant issues, and produce a concise summary of what was accomplished. Focus on the work that was actually completed, the main themes across that work, and any notable patterns such as bugs resolved, projects advanced, or areas of concentrated effort.
206: Keep the summary clear and useful for sharing with others, and avoid overstating progress where the underlying work is still in flight.
207: Team identifiers: [LIN, FEA]
208: Timeline generation
209: Use case
210: Use this workflow to build a historical timeline of work in Linear around a topic, so teams can understand how a project, incident, or theme evolved over time.
211: Example prompt
212: You are helping document the history of work in Linear around a specific topic.
213: Gather the relevant issues and projects connected to that topic, review their historical activity, and produce a timeline that shows the key developments in chronological order.
214: Focus on meaningful milestones such as when work was created, when direction changed, when major decisions or updates were recorded, and when important work was completed.
215: Keep the timeline factual and grounded in the underlying activity, and call out any gaps or ambiguity rather than inferring events that are not clearly supported.
216: Topic: [Insert a specific topic from your workspace]
217: Implementation plan
218: Use case
219: Use this workflow to turn an initial idea into a reviewed implementation plan, then create the corresponding Linear work and delegate execution to the right people or agents.
220: Example prompt
221: You are helping plan and structure a development effort in Linear.
222: Start by designing an approach based on the provided context, with enough detail to explain the proposed solution, major workstreams, and any important tradeoffs or open questions. Treat that initial plan as a draft that can be reviewed and edited before any work is created.
223: Once the plan is approved, create a parent issue that captures the overall goal and create sub-issues for the concrete pieces of work needed to execute it.
224: Keep the breakdown clear and actionable, and assign or delegate work only when the requested owners or agents are explicitly specified.
225: Context: [Insert enough context to help orient the agent]
226: FAQ⁠
227: Why am I seeing an internal server error when trying to connect?
228: Enter the following in the Terminal to clear saved auth info: rm -rf ~/.mcp-auth then try again to connect.
229: Additionally you may need to update to a newer version of node if required.
230: Can I authenticate with multiple Linear workspaces?
231: The Linear MCP server authenticates each session via OAuth. Because reconnecting alone does not switch the workspace within an existing auth session, each workspace needs its own separate authentication context.
232: If your client or the mcp-remote module supports a configuration directory (for example via MCP_REMOTE_CONFIG_DIR), point each workspace to a different path:
233: MCP_REMOTE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.mcp-auth/workspace-a npx mcp-remote https://mcp.linear.app/mcp
234: MCP_REMOTE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.mcp-auth/workspace-b npx mcp-remote https://mcp.linear.app/mcp
235: Authenticate each configuration separately. For clients that manage their own auth storage, check the client’s documentation for workspace-switching options.
236: Can I authenticate with my own API keys or OAuth access tokens?
237: The MCP server supports passing OAuth token and API keys directly in the Authorization: Bearer <yourtoken> header instead of using the interactive authentication flow.
238: You can use this to interact with the MCP server as an app user, provide read-only access through a restricted API key, or integrate with an existing Linear OAuth application without an extra authentication hop.
239: For an alternative read-only approach with your own API key, create a Linear API key with only the Read permission enabled.
240: What about the SSE endpoint?
241: The SSE endpoint at https://mcp.linear.app/sse is a deprecated fallback for clients that do not support Streamable HTTP.
242: For all new setups, use the primary Streamable HTTP endpoint at https://mcp.linear.app/mcp.
243: My remote MCP connection dropped or isn't responding
244: Remote MCP connections can occasionally need a reconnect in some client setups. Try disconnecting and reconnecting the server from your client’s MCP settings. This is a routine client-side reset and does not affect your Linear data or authentication session.
245: I'm using WSL on Windows, and seeing an error
246: The default connection uses Streamable HTTP at https://mcp.linear.app/mcp. If that does not work in WSL, use this SSE fallback instead (/sse is a legacy path for clients that do not support Streamable HTTP):
247: {"mcpServers": {"linear": {"command": "wsl","args": ["npx","-y","mcp-remote","https://mcp.linear.app/sse","--transport sse-only"]}}}
248: When do I need to reconnect my MCP client to Linear?
249: Standard MCP OAuth connections start with a 25-day refresh window. That window can renew when your client refreshes its credentials, so you don’t necessarily need to reconnect every 25 days.
250: If the MCP server returns HTTP 401 with error="invalid_token" in the WWW-Authenticate header, the token is no longer valid. The response doesn’t tell your client whether the token expired or was revoked. If your client can’t refresh its credentials, reconnect it to Linear.

64: API and Webhooks
65: Linear’s GraphQL API and webhooks lets you extend Linear’s functionality beyond what we provide out of the box.
66: Overview⁠
67: Linear’s public API is built using GraphQL. It’s the same API we use internally for developing our applications.
68: Linear’s webhooks allow you to receive HTTP(S) push notifications whenever data is created or updated. This allows you to build integrations on top of Linear.
69: Basics⁠
70: API⁠
71: You own your data in Linear and our GraphQL API lets you query that data. In addition to querying, Linear has full support for mutating all entities. Any mutations you make via the API are observed in real-time by all clients.
72: Go to the API section under Account > Security & Access settings and read the linked API documentation for more information. Our GraphQL schema is available here.
73: For more in depth documentation visit developers.linear.app. If you have a question the docs don’t answer, post it in the #api channel in our Slack community.
74: API Keys⁠
75: Admins can choose whether or not Members can create their own API keys from Settings > Administration > API > Member API keys. This setting will not apply to Admins who can always create API keys.
76: Existing API keys for your workspace can be viewed from the same menu and revoked if needed.
77: Admins and permitted Members can create personal API keys from Settings > Account > Security & Access. For each key you create, you can choose to give it full access to the data your user can access, or restrict it to certain permissions (Read, Write, Admin, Create issues, Create comments). You can also limit an API key’s access to specific teams in your workspace.
78: Webhooks⁠
79: Our webhooks support data change events for Issues, Comments, Issue attachments, Documents, Emoji reactions, Projects, Project updates, Cycles, Labels, Users and Issue SLAs.
80: Consider using webhooks to trigger CI builds, perform calculations on issue data or send messages on specific conditions. Creating and managing webhooks requires admin permissions. Read more in our webhook documentation.
81: The configured URL will be called whenever any issue or comment in that team is created or updated. You’ll receive the entire data object as the payload. We’ll also let you know what the previous values for all changed properties were.
82: Create a webhook⁠
83: Create and manage webhooks and OAuth applications in Settings > Administration > API. Admin permissions in your workspace are necessary to view this page.
84: Third-party apps⁠
85: Third-party integrations created for Linear can be found on our integrations directory.

153: About
154: Postman Collection
155: OpenAPI
156: The Jira REST API enables you to interact with Jira programmatically. Use this API to
157: build apps, script interactions with
158: Jira, or develop any other type of integration. This page documents the REST resources available in Jira Cloud, including
159: the HTTP response codes and example requests and responses.
160: Version
161: This documentation is for version 3 of the Jira Cloud platform REST API, which is the latest
162: version. Version 2 and
163: version 3 of the API offer the same collection of operations. However, version 3 provides support for
164: the Atlassian Document Format
165: (ADF) in:
166: body in comments, including where comments are used in issue, issue link, and transition resources.
167: comment in worklogs.
168: description and environment fields in issues.
169: textarea type custom fields (multi-line text fields) in issues. Single line custom fields
170: (textfield) accept a string and don't handle Atlassian Document Format content.
171: Authentication and authorization
172: Forge apps
173: For Forge apps, REST API scopes
174: are used when authenticating with Jira Cloud platform. See Add scopes to call an Atlassian REST API for more details.
175: The URIs for Forge app REST API calls have this structure:
176: /rest/api/3/<resource-name>
177: For example, /rest/api/3/issue/DEMO-1
178: Connect apps
179: For Connect apps, authentication (JWT-based) is built into the Connect libraries. Authorization is implemented using either
180: scopes (shown as App scope required for operations on this page) or user impersonation. See
181: Security for Connect apps
182: for details.
183: The URIs for Connect app REST API calls have this structure:
184: https://<site-url>/rest/api/3/<resource-name>
185: For example, https://your-domain.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/issue/DEMO-1
186: Other integrations
187: For integrations that are not Forge or Connect apps, use OAuth 2.0 authorization code grants (3LO) for security
188: (3LO scopes are shown as for operations OAuth scopes required). See
189: OAuth 2.0 (3LO) apps
190: for details.
191: The URIs for OAuth 2.0 (3LO) app REST API calls have this structure:
192: https://api.atlassian.com/ex/jira/<cloudId>/rest/api/3/<resource-name>
193: For example, https://api.atlassian.com/ex/jira/35273b54-3f06-40d2-880f-dd28cf8daafa/rest/api/3/issue/DEMO-1
194: Ad-hoc API calls
195: For personal scripts, bots, and ad-hoc execution of the REST APIs use basic authentication. See Basic auth for REST APIs for details.
196: The URIs for basic authentication REST API calls have this structure:
197: https://<site-url>/rest/api/3/<resource-name>
198: For example, https://your-domain.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/issue/DEMO-1
199: Permissions
200: Operation permissions
201: Most operations in this API require permissions. The calling user must have the required permissions for an operation to
202: use it. Note that for Connect apps, the app user must have the required permissions for the operation and the app must
203: have scopes that permit the operation.
204: A permission can be granted to a group, project role, or issue role that the user is a member of, or granted directly to a user.
205: See Permissions overview for details. The most common permissions are:
206: Administer the Cloud site: Users in the site-admins group have this
207: permission. See Manage groups for details.
208: Administer Jira: Granted by the Jira Administrators global permission. There is a default group for this permission.
209: See Manage groups and Managing global permissions for details.
210: Administer a project in Jira: Granted by the Administer projects project permission for a project. This can be
211: granted to a user, a group, a project role, and more.
212: See Managing project permissions for details.
213: Access a project in Jira: Granted by the Browse projects project permission for a project. This can be
214: granted to a user, a group, a project role, and more.
215: See Managing project permissions for details.
216: Access Jira: Granted by the Jira Users global permission. Users in the default product access group (for example,
217: jira-software-users-acmesite) have this permission.
218: See Manage groups and
219: Managing global permissions for details.
220: Anonymous access
221: Some operations provide support for anonymous access. However, anonymous access is only available if
222: the Jira permission needed to access the object or records returned by the operation is granted to
223: the Public group. See Allowing anonymous access to your project
224: for details.
225: If an operation is called anonymously and anonymous access is not available, the operation will return
226: an error. Note that not all operations that correspond to objects that can be given public access
227: provide for anonymous access.
228: Expansion, pagination, and ordering
229: Expansion
230: The Jira REST API uses resource expansion, which means that some parts of a resource are not returned unless specified
231: in the request. This simplifies responses and minimizes network traffic.
232: To expand part of a resource in a request, use the expand query parameter and specify the object(s) to be expanded.
233: If you need to expand nested objects, use the . dot notation. If you need to expand multiple objects, use a
234: comma-separated list.
235: For example, the following request expands the names and renderedFields properties for the JRACLOUD-34423 issue:
236: GET issue/JRACLOUD-34423?expand=names,renderedFields
237: To discover which object can be expanded, refer to the expand property in the object.
238: In the JSON example below, the resource declares widgets as expandable.
239: 1
240: 2
241: 3
242: 4
243: 5
244: 6
245: 7
246: 8
247: 9
248: {
249: "expand": "widgets",
250: "self": "https://your-domain.atlassian.net/rest/api/3/resource/KEY-1",
251: "widgets": {
252: "widgets": [],
253: "size": 5
254: }
255: }
256: Pagination
257: The Jira REST API uses pagination to improve performance. Pagination is enforced for operations that could return a large
258: collection of items. When you make a request to a paginated resource, the response wraps the returned array of values in
259: a JSON object with paging metadata. For example:
260: 1
261: 2
262: 3
263: 4
264: 5
265: 6
266: 7
267: 8
268: 9
269: 10
270: 11
271: 12
272: {
273: "startAt" : 0,
274: "maxResults" : 10,
275: "total": 200,
276: "isLast": false,
277: "values": [
278: { /* result 0 */ },
279: { /* result 1 */ },
280: { /* result 2 */ }
281: ]
282: }
283: startAt is the index of the first item returned in the page.
284: maxResults is the maximum number of items that a page can return. Each operation can have a different limit for
285: the number of items returned, and these limits may change without notice. To find the maximum number of items
286: that an operation could return, set maxResults to a large number—for example, over 1000—and if the returned value of maxResults is less than the requested value, the returned value is the maximum.
287: total is the total number of items contained in all pages. This number may change as the client
288: requests the subsequent pages, therefore the client should always assume that the requested page can be empty. Note
289: that this property is not returned for all operations.
290: isLast indicates whether the page returned is the last one. Note that this property is not returned for all operations.
291: Ordering
292: Some operations support ordering the elements of a response by a field. Check the documentation for the operation to
293: confirm whether ordering of a response is supported and which fields can be used. Responses are listed in ascending order
294: by default. You can change the order using the orderby query parameter with a - or + symbol. For example:
295: ?orderBy=name to order by name field ascending.
296: ?orderBy=+name to order by name field ascending.
297: ?orderBy=-name to order by name field descending.
298: Timestamps
299: By default, top-level timestamps (e.g. updated and created) are returned in ISO 8601 format, in the system default user time zone.
300: To return date time data in the logged in user's timezone, please refer to renderedFields property under the expand query parameter in relevant APIs.
301: Special headers
302: The following request and response headers define important metadata for the Jira Cloud REST API resources.
303: X-Atlassian-Token (request): Operations that accept multipart/form-data must include the X-Atlassian-Token: no-check
304: header in requests. Otherwise the request is blocked by cross-site request forgery (CSRF/XSRF) protection.
305: X-Force-Accept-Language (request): controls how the standard HTTP Accept-Language header is processed.
306: By default Accept-Language is ignored and the response is in the language configured in the user's profile or,
307: when no language is configured for the user, the default Jira instance language. For the response to recognize
308: Accept-Language send X-Force-Accept-Language = true as well. If Accept-Language requests a language that Jira
309: can return the response is in that language, otherwise Jira returns the response in the default language. If
310: Accept-Language is not specified the response is in the default language.
311: X-AAccountId (response): This response header contains the Atlassian account ID of the authenticated user.
312: Anonymous operations
313: Jira provides for all permissions, except the global permission Administer Jira, to be assigned to Anyone. Once a permission is assigned to Anyone, anyone knowing a project's URL is able to use the features in Jira enabled by the permission. However, the Jira REST API does not enable anonymous access for operations by default. This means that an anonymous user who may be able to perform an action through Jira, may not be able to perform the same action where it's enabled by the REST API.
314: The operations that provide anonymous access are annotated "This operation can be accessed anonymously."
315: Asynchronous operations
316: Some Jira REST API operations may trigger long-running or computationally expensive tasks. In these cases, the operation
317: will schedule an asynchronous task and return a 303 (See Other) response, indicating the location of the queued task
318: in the Location header. You can query this task to get progress updates.
319: When the task finishes, the response object will contain the result field. The content of the field is specific to the
320: operation that created the task. Refer to the operation’s documentation for more information.
321: Note that asynchronous tasks are not guaranteed to be run in order. In other words, if you need your tasks to execute
322: in a certain order, you should start a task only after the prerequisite task(s) have finished.
323: Experimental features
324: Features and methods marked as experimental may change without notice. Feedback on experimental functionality is welcome.
325: Report issues to Developer and Marketplace support (preferred) or use the
326: Give docs feedback link at the top of this page.
327: Status codes
328: The Jira Cloud platform REST API uses the standard HTTP status codes.
329: Operations that return an error status code may also return a response body containing details of the error or errors.
330: The schema for the response body is shown below:
331: 1
332: 2
333: 3
334: 4
335: 5
336: 6
337: 7
338: 8
339: 9
340: 10
341: 11
342: 12
343: 13
344: 14
345: 15
346: 16
347: 17
348: 18
349: 19
350: 20
351: 21
352: 22
353: 23
354: 24
355: 25

357: 27

359: "id": "https://docs.atlassian.com/jira/REST/schema/error-collection#",
360: "title": "Error Collection",
361: "type": "object",

69: This page shows you how REST clients can authenticate themselves using
70: basic authentication with an Atlassian account email address
71: and API token.
72: Authentication using passwords has been deprecated.
73: Basic authentication is not as secure as other methods. We recommend using it for simple scripts and
74: manual calls to the REST APIs. Otherwise, consider building an app:
75: Forge apps and Connect apps use more secure methods for authentication: OAuth 2.0 and JWT respectively.
76: In addition, authentication is built into the app frameworks, so you don't need to configure it.
77: See Security for Forge apps and Security for Connect apps.
78: OAuth 2.0 apps (integrations) created in the developer console can use
79: OAuth 2.0 authorization code grants (3LO), which
80: is also more secure than basic auth.
81: Overview
82: Important notice for apps using 3LO or API tokens
83: Apps that collect API tokens or instruct customers to create individual 3LO apps don't comply with our Security requirements for cloud apps and Acceptable use policy.
84: Follow these best practices:
85: Build a single, distributable 3LO app for your integration.
86: Clearly identify your app in the Marketplace (recommended).
87: Work with customers to transition away from custom 3LO apps or API tokens.
88: Read our blog post for full details
89: The Jira REST API is protected by the same restrictions that apply in the standard Jira web interface.
90: These restrictions mean that if you don't log in, you access Jira anonymously. If you log in and don't
91: have permission to view something in Jira, you won't be able to view it using the Jira REST API either.
92: In most cases, the first step in using the Jira REST API is to authenticate a user account with your
93: Jira site. This page provides a simple example of basic authentication.
94: Get an API token
95: Basic auth requires API tokens. You generate an API token for your Atlassian account and use
96: it to authenticate anywhere where you would have used a password. This enhances security because:
97: you're not saving your primary account password outside of where you authenticate
98: you can quickly revoke individual API tokens on a per-use basis
99: API tokens will allow you to authenticate even if your Atlassian Cloud organization has two-factor
100: authentication or SAML enabled.
101: See the Atlassian Cloud Support API tokens article to discover
102: how to generate an API token.
103: Simple example
104: Most client software provides a simple mechanism for supplying a user name (in our case, the email address)
105: and API token that the client uses to build the required authentication headers. For example, you can
106: specify the -u argument in cURL as follows:
107: 1
108: 2
109: 3
110: 4
111: 5
112: 6
113: curl -D- \
114: -u fred@example.com:freds_api_token \
115: -X GET \
116: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
117: https://your-domain.atlassian.net/rest/api/2/issue/createmeta
118: Supply basic auth headers
119: You can construct and send basic auth headers. To do this you perform the following steps:
120: Generate an API token for Jira using your Atlassian Account.
121: Build a string of the form useremail:api_token.
122: BASE64 encode the string.
123: Linux/Unix/MacOS:
124: 1
125: 2
126: echo -n "user@example.com:api_token_string" | base64
127: Windows 7 and later, using Microsoft Powershell:
128: 1
129: 2
130: 3
131: 4
132: 5
133: $Text = ‘user@example.com:api_token_string’
134: $Bytes = [System.Text.Encoding]::UTF8.GetBytes($Text)
135: $EncodedText = [Convert]::ToBase64String($Bytes)
136: $EncodedText
137: Supply an Authorization header with content Basic followed by the encoded string. For example, the string fred:fred encodes to ZnJlZDpmcmVk in base64, so you would make the request as follows:
138: 1
139: 2
140: 3
141: 4
142: 5
143: 6
144: curl -D- \
145: -X GET \
146: -H "Authorization: Basic ZnJlZDpmcmVk" \
147: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
148: "https://your-domain.atlassian.net/rest/api/2/issue/QA-31"
149: Advanced topics
150: Authentication challenges
151: Because Jira permits a default level of access to anonymous users, it does not supply an authentication
152: challenge. Some HTTP clients expect to receive an authentication challenge before they send
153: an authorization header. This means that a client may not behave as expected. In this case,
154: configure the client to supply the authorization header, as described above, rather than
155: relying on its default mechanism.
156: CAPTCHA
157: A CAPTCHA is 'triggered' after several consecutive failed log in attempts, and requires the user to
158: interpret a distorted picture of a word and type that word into a text field with each subsequent log
159: in attempt. If CAPTCHA has been triggered, you cannot use Jira's REST API to authenticate with the Jira site.
160: You can check this in the error response from Jira. If there is an X-Seraph-LoginReason header with
161: a value of AUTHENTICATION_DENIED, the application rejected the login without even checking the password.
162: This is the most common indication that Jira's CAPTCHA feature has been triggered.

68: OAuth 2.0 (3LO) apps
69: This page shows you how to configure OAuth 2.0 (3LO) (also known as "three-legged OAuth" or "authorization
70: code grants") apps. OAuth 2.0 (3LO) allows external applications and services to access
71: Atlassian product APIs on a user's behalf. OAuth 2.0 (3LO) apps are created and managed in the
72: developer console.
73: This page only applies to OAuth 2.0 apps (integrations) created in the developer console.
74: For Forge apps and Connect apps, you don't need to configure authentication it is built into the app frameworks.
75: See Security for Forge apps and Security for Connect apps.
76: For simple scripts or to make REST API calls yourself, see Basic auth for REST APIs.
77: Overview
78: Important notice for apps using 3LO or API tokens
79: Apps that collect API tokens or instruct customers to create individual 3LO apps don't comply with our Security requirements for cloud apps and Acceptable use policy.
80: Follow these best practices:
81: Build a single, distributable 3LO app for your integration.
82: Clearly identify your app in the Marketplace (recommended).
83: Work with customers to transition away from custom 3LO apps or API tokens.
84: Read our blog post for full details
85: OAuth 2.0 (3LO) involves three parties:
86: An Atlassian site (resource)
87: A user (resource owner)
88: An external application/service (client).
89: For example, a Jira or Confluence site (resource), an Atlassian user (resource owner), and Gmail (client).
90: Underlying the authorization interactions between these three parties is an authorization server.
91: To the user, the authorization process looks like this:
92: The app directs the user to an Atlassian screen that prompts them to grant access to their data
93: on the Atlassian site. The screen displays the access being requested in the Atlassian product.
94: The user grants (or denies) access to their data on the Atlassian site, via the screen.
95: The user is directed back to the external service. If the user granted access, the external service
96: can now access data (within the specified scopes) from the Atlassian site on the user's behalf.
97: Underlying this process are a number of interactions between the external service, the app, and the
98: authorization server. The full process is described in more detail below.
99: Note, this process assumes that the external service has registered an app with Atlassian that can
100: use OAuth 2.0 (3LO).
101: The user, in the external service, uses a feature that requires data from an Atlassian product.
102: The external service seeks authorization to access the product's APIs, within the specified scopes,
103: on behalf of the user.
104: The user is directed to the Atlassian account login screen, if they are not already logged in,
105: and prompted to log in.
106: The user is directed to the authorization URL for the authorization server. This displays a screen
107: that prompts the user to grant access to their data.
108: If the user grants access, the user is directed to the callback URL with an authorization code.
109: The app makes a POST to the token URL for the authorization server, exchanging the authorization
110: code for an access token.
111: The access token can now be used to access the APIs for the authorized Atlassian site on behalf
112: of the user. This can be used until the token expires or is revoked.
113: Creating OAuth 2.0 (3LO) Apps
114: From any page on developer.atlassian.com, select your profile
115: icon in the top-right corner, and from the dropdown, select Developer console.
116: In the Developer console, select the Create dropdown and choose OAuth 2.0 integration to
117: create an OAuth 2.0 (3LO) app.
118: Enter an app name and choose the OAuth 2.0 (3LO) grant type for your app.
119: When you create an OAuth 2.0 (3LO) app, you can choose between two grant types:
120: Account-level grant: The user’s consent applies at the Atlassian account level. A single grant can cover access to
121: multiple sites where your app is installed, subject to the scopes you request.
122: Resource-level grant: The user’s consent is limited to the specific site(s) they select on the consent screen.
123: The resulting tokens can only be used with those selected site(s).
124: Enabling OAuth 2.0 (3LO)
125: Before you can implement OAuth 2.0 (3LO) for your app, you need to enable it for your app using the
126: developer console.
127: From any page on developer.atlassian.com, select your profile
128: icon in the top-right corner, and from the dropdown, select Developer console.
129: Select your app from the list (or create one if you don't already have one).
130: Select Authorization in the left menu.
131: Next to OAuth 2.0 (3LO), select Configure.
132: Enter the Callback URL. Set this to any URL that is accessible by the app. When you implement
133: OAuth 2.0 (3LO) in your app (see next section), the redirect_uri must match this URL.
134: Click Save changes.
135: Note, if you haven't already added an API to your app, you should do this now:
136: Select Permissions in the left menu.
137: Next to the API you want to add, select Add.
138: Implementing OAuth 2.0 (3LO)
139: Once you have enabled OAuth 2.0 (3LO) for your app, you can implement it in your app's code.
140: There are a number of key parts to this:
141: Direct the user to the authorization URL to get an authorization code
142: Exchange the authorization code for an access token
143: Authorize any calls to the product APIs using the access token
144: Check site access for the app
145: 1. Direct the user to the authorization URL to get an authorization code
146: As described in the Overview above, your app should start the authorization flow by directing the
147: user to the authorization URL:
148: 1
149: 2
150: 3
151: 4
152: 5
153: 6
154: 7
155: 8
156: 9
157: https://auth.atlassian.com/authorize?
158: audience=api.atlassian.com&
159: client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&
160: scope=REQUESTED_SCOPE_ONE%20REQUESTED_SCOPE_TWO&
161: redirect_uri=https://YOUR_APP_CALLBACK_URL&
162: state=YOUR_USER_BOUND_VALUE&
163: response_type=code&
164: prompt=consent
165: Use the authorization URL in a GET request. You can get this URL by going to your app in the
166: developer console, selecting Authorization in the left menu, and
167: selecting Configure next to OAuth 2.0 (3LO). Alternatively, you can
168: construct the URL manually (for example, if you want to specify scopes from multiple products).
169: The query parameters for the authorization URL are described below:
170: audience: (required) Set this to api.atlassian.com.
171: client_id: (required) Set this to the Client ID for your app. Find this in Settings
172: for your app in the developer console.
173: scope: (required) Set this to the desired scopes:
174: Separate multiple scopes with a space.
175: Only choose from the scopes that you have already added to the APIs for your app in the developer console.
176: You may specify scopes from multiple products.
177: redirect_uri: (required) Set this to the callback URL configured in Authorization
178: for your app in the developer console.
179: state: (required for security) Set this to a value that is associated with the user you are
180: directing to the authorization URL, for example, a hash of the user's session ID. Make sure that this is a
181: value that cannot be guessed. You may be able to generate and validate this value automatically, if
182: you are using an OAuth 2.0 client library or an authentication library with OAuth 2.0 support. For
183: more information, including why this parameter is required for security, see What is the state parameter used for? below.
184: response_type: (required) Set to code as you are requesting an authorization code (not a token).
185: prompt: (required) Set to consent so that the screen prompting the user to grant access will display.
186: If successful, the user will be redirected to the app's callback URL, with an authorization code provided
187: as a query parameter called code. This code can be exchanged for an access token, as described in step 2.
188: When a user authorizes an OAuth 2.0 (3LO) app for the first time, the app connects to the selected site.
189: Organization admins and site administrators can see who authorized the app and when on the
190: Connected apps page at admin.atlassian.com.
191: Determining the scopes required for an operation
192: To find out which scopes an operation requires, check the OAuth scopes required field
193: in the relevant API documentation:
194: Jira Cloud platform REST API documentation
195: Jira Service Management Cloud REST API documentation
196: Jira Software Cloud REST API documentation
197: Confluence Cloud REST API documentation
198: If the operation has the statement Apps can't access this REST resource, you can't use it with
199: OAuth 2.0 (3LO).
200: Note, the permissions held by the user an app is acting for always constrain the app, regardless
201: of the app's scopes. For example, if a Jira app has the manage:jira-project scope but the user
202: does not have the Administer Jira permission, the app can not create projects.
203: 2. Exchange authorization code for access token
204: 1
205: 2
206: 3
207: 4
208: 5
209: curl --request POST \
210: --url 'https://auth.atlassian.com/oauth/token' \
211: --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
212: --data '{"grant_type": "authorization_code","client_id": "YOUR_CLIENT_ID","client_secret": "YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET","code": "YOUR_AUTHORIZATION_CODE","redirect_uri": "https://YOUR_APP_CALLBACK_URL"}'
213: client_id: (required) Set this to the Client ID for your app. Find this in Settings
214: for your app in the developer console.
215: client_secret: (required) Set this to the Secret for your app. Find this in Settings
216: for your app in the developer console.
217: code: (required) Set this to the authorization code received from the initial authorize call (described above).
218: redirect_uri: (required) Set this to the callback URL configured for your app in the developer console.
219: If successful, this call returns an access token similar to this:
220: 1
221: 2
222: 3
223: 4
224: 5
225: 6
226: 7

229: HTTP/1.1 200 OK
230: Content-Type: application/json
231: {
232: "access_token": <string>,
233: "expires_in": <expiry time of access_token in second>,
234: "scope": <string>
235: }
236: This access token can be used to make API calls,
237: as described below.
238: 3. Make calls to the API using the access token
239: Your app now has an access token that it can use to authorize requests to the APIs for the Atlassian
240: site. To make requests, do the following:
241: Get the cloudid for your site.
242: Construct the request URL using the cloudid.
243: Call the API, using the access token and request URL.
244: 3.1 Get the cloudid for your site
245: Make a GET request to https://api.atlassian.com/oauth/token/accessible-resources passing the access
246: token as a bearer token in the header of the request. For example:
247: 1
248: 2

252: curl --request GET \
253: --url https://api.atlassian.com/oauth/token/accessible-resources \
254: --header 'Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN' \
255: --header 'Accept: application/json'
256: This will retrieve the sites that have scopes granted by the token (see
257: Check site access for the app below for details). Find your site in the response and
258: copy the id. This is the cloudid for your site.

344: 3.2 Construct the request URL
345: Requests that use OAuth 2.0 (3LO) are made via api.atlassian.com (not https://your-domain.atlassian.net).
346: Construct your request URL using the following structure:
347: Jira apps:
348: https://api.atlassian.com/ex/jira/{cloudid}/{api}
349: Confluence apps:
350: https://api.atlassian.com/ex/confluence/{cloudid}/{api}
351: where:
352: {cloudid} is the cloudid for your site that you obtained in the previous step. For example,
353: 11223344-a1b2-3b33-c444-def123456789.
354: {api} is the base path and name of the API. For example:
355: /rest/api/2/project for the project endpoint in the Jira REST API.
356: /rest/servicedeskapi/request for the request endpoint in the Jira Service Management REST API.
357: /rest/api/space for the space endpoint in the Confluence REST API.
358: Your request URL should look something like this (using the example cloudid and Jira API above):
359: https://api.atlassian.com/ex/jira/11223344-a1b2-3b33-c444-def123456789/rest/api/2/project
360: Note that if you are copying the examples in the API documentation, you will need to amend the example
361: URLs as they currently use https://your-domain.atlassian.net/{api} rather than the request URLs shown above.
362: 3.3 Call the API
363: Make the API call passing the access token as a bearer token in the header of the request. This will authorize the request on the user's behalf.

383: 4. Check site access for the app
384: An authorization grant is when a user consents to your app. For OAuth 2.0 (3LO) apps, the consent
385: is valid for all sites the app is installed in, as long as the scopes used by your app's APIs
386: don't change. A user's grant can change when either of the following occur:
387: The user revokes the grant. The app cannot work anywhere after a user has revoked their consent
388: to the app.
389: The user consents to a new grant of the app. The scopes in the new grant override the scopes
390: in the existing grant.
391: Therefore, since a grant can change over time, it's important that you check that the user
392: has granted the app the scopes it requires and that your app has correct access to a site and its APIs.
393: To check this, call the accessible-resources endpoint on
394: https://auth.atlassian.com (you used this endpoint in a previous step to get the cloudid

451: Using accessible-resources with different grant types
452: The GET /oauth/token/accessible-resources endpoint always returns the sites (resources) that the
453: current access token can be used with, but the result set depends on the grant type:
454: Account-level grants
455: The response can include multiple sites.
456: Sites may be added to the same grant over time when the user later consents for additional
457: sites using the same app and Atlassian account.
458: Existing access tokens can then be used with all sites that are part of the account-level
459: grant (subject to scopes and token expiry).
460: Resource-level (site-restricted) grants
461: The response only includes the specific site(s) the user selected on the consent screen when
462: they created the grant.
463: Tokens derived from this grant cannot be used with any site that is not listed in the
464: accessible-resources response.
465: Your app should always:
466: Call GET /oauth/token/accessible-resources with the current access token.
467: Determine which site(s) are available for that token.
468: Use the returned id (the cloudid) to construct API URLs, for example:
469: https://api.atlassian.com/ex/jira/{cloudid}/{api}
470: https://api.atlassian.com/ex/confluence/{cloudid}/{api}
