519: Each item in the response describes a container (for example, a Jira site) that your app has access to,
520: the scopes associated with that access, and metadata such as the name and avatar URL (if any). It's
521: important to understand that this endpoint won't tell you anything about the user's permissions, which
522: may limit the resources that your app can access via the site's APIs.
523: Note, the id is not unique across containers (that is, two entries in the results can have the same
524: id), so you may need to infer the type of container from its scopes.
525: Managing your OAuth 2.0 (3LO) apps
526: You can securely manage all your OAuth 2.0 (3LO) and Forge
527: apps in one place using the Atlassian developer console.
528: The console lets you view information about your apps, including their environments and scopes.
529: To access the console:
530: From any page on developer.atlassian.com, select your profile
531: icon in the top-right corner.
532: From the dropdown, select Developer console.
533: Your existing OAuth 2.0 (3LO) and Forge apps are listed in the order they were created.
534: OAuth 2.0 (3LO) apps are displayed with a 3LO lozenge.
535: Connect apps are not listed in the console. To learn more about platform and framework options for
536: building apps, see
537: Cloud development platform overview.
538: The following details are listed:
539: App name: the name of your app
540: Distribution status:
541: Sharing: your app can be shared via link
542: Not sharing: your app can't be shared via link
543: Updated on: the time and date you created your app or updated its settings
544: You can search for an app using the search bar above the app table.
545: View app details
546: Select any app on the My apps page to get more information about the app, including app ID,
547: description, authorization, and permissions.
548: The Overview page displays the following panels:
549: App details
550: App ID: the identifier for your app
551: Description: the description of your app
552: Distribution
553: Distribution status: whether your app can be used by others
554: Permissions
555: API scopes: which scopes are currently defined in your app
556: Authorization
557: Authorization type: the authorization configured for your app
558: Select Settings in the left menu to view your app's authentication details, or to change your
559: app's name, description, or avatar.
560: View app permissions
561: You can view the level of access your Forge app has to an Atlassian user's account by selecting
562: Permissions in the left menu, or selecting the Permissions panel.
563: The Permissions page lists the APIs included in your app.
564: To add or remove individual scopes for an API, select Configure, and in the list of scopes,
565: select Add or Remove. Note that users who previously consented to the scopes will need
566: to re-consent to the new scopes.
567: Delete your app
568: You can only delete an app if it's not installed anywhere.
569: If your app is currently installed on a site, uninstall it.
570: Select Settings in the left menu, and select Delete app.
571: Distributing your OAuth 2.0 (3LO) apps
572: When you create an OAuth 2.0 (3LO) app, it's private by default. This means that only you can
573: install and use it. If you want to distribute your app to other users, you must enable sharing.
574: From any page on developer.atlassian.com, select your profile
575: icon in the top-right corner, and from the dropdown, select Developer console.
576: Select your app from the list.
577: Select Distribution in the left menu.
578: Enable sharing using the toggle switch in the Enable sharing section.
579: Select Authorization in the left menu, and under OAuth 2.0 (3LO), select Configure.
580: Copy the Authorization URL(s) and distribute to your users.
581: Users trying to install an unapproved OAuth 2.0 integration are warned that the app has not yet been reviewed by Atlassian. To get your integration reviewed and approved, follow the steps on Listing a third party integration on the Atlassian Marketplace. Note, you don't need an informative Atlassian Marketplace listing to submit your integration for approval.
582: Note that:
583: You'll have to send the link to all the users you want to grant access to.
584: Enabling sharing doesn't make your app available on the
585: Atlassian Marketplace.
586: Although OAuth 2.0 (3LO) apps can be listed on the Atlassian Marketplace,
587: they will appear as informational listings only, with limited Marketplace features.
588: Known issues
589: We are aware of the following issues with OAuth 2.0 (3LO). Some of the issues have workarounds, which
590: are described below. Others do not have workarounds, but are listed so that you are aware of them. If
591: you discover an issue that is not listed below, please report it to
592: Developer and Marketplace support.
593: Implicit grant flow not supported
594: Site-scoped grants limitations
595: Apps cannot declare searchable entity properties
596: Implicit grant flow not supported
597: OAuth 2.0 (3LO) currently supports the code grant flow only. It does not support the implicit grant
598: flow. We understand that this is preventing people from using OAuth 2.0 (3LO) for standalone mobile
599: apps and web/JavaScript (Chrome, Electron) apps and we are investigating ways to address this.
600: Grant limitations
601: Historically, OAuth 2.0 (3LO) only supported account grants, where the user consents to the
602: app at the Atlassian account level and a single grant can cover multiple sites where the app is installed.
603: OAuth 2.0 (3LO) now also supports resource-level (site-restricted) grants, which limit access to
604: specific site(s).
605: This further means:
606: a user consents to the app making requests on their behalf for only the sites they have access to,
607: and the app can make requests on their behalf for only the sites where the app is installed.
608: There are a few limitations to this:
609: The consent screen currently requires the user to select the site where they want to install the app.
610: This can be confusing for users who want to install the app into multiple sites. To do this,
611: the user would need to repeat the installation process multiple times.
612: An admin can't revoke a user's access to an app through the Connected Apps user screen. This is
613: because the OAuth grant given by the user is between the app and the user. An admin can only choose
614: to uninstall the app to restrict a user's access.
615: (Jira only) Apps cannot declare searchable entity properties
616: Jira apps can store and read the values of entity properties (issue properties and project properties)
617: using the REST API. However, in the current implementation of OAuth 2.0 (3LO), Jira apps cannot declare
618: searchable entity properties.
619: This means that if your app uses OAuth 2.0 (3LO), it won't be able to refer to entity properties in JQL queries.
620: Frequently asked questions
621: How do I get a new access token, if my access token expires or is revoked?
622: What happens if a user grants access to more than one Atlassian site for an app?
623: What is the state parameter used for?
624: How do I retrieve the public profile of the authenticated user?
625: Is CORS whitelisting supported?
626: How do I configure the refresh token behavior?
627: How do I get a new access token, if my access token expires or is revoked?
628: You have two options:
629: Initiate the entire authorization flow from the beginning again.
630: Use a refresh token to get another access token and refresh token pair.
631: Use a refresh token to get another access token and refresh token pair
632: Refresh tokens are implemented using rotating refresh tokens.
633: Rotating refresh tokens issue a new, limited life refresh token each time they are used.
634: This mechanism improves on single persistent refresh tokens by reducing the period
635: in which a refresh token can be compromised and used to obtain a valid access token.
636: These are the configuration options for a rotating refresh token:
637: TermDefaultDescription
638: Inactivity expiry time90 daysA rotating refresh token expires if the user is inactive for this period. Each new rotating refresh token resets the inactivty expiry time and allocates another 90 days.
639: Reuse interval or leeway10 minutesWithin this period, the breach detection features don't apply when exchanging a refresh token multiple times. This interval helps avoid network concurrency issues.
640: To get a refresh token in your initial authorization flow, add offline_access
641: to the scope parameter of the authorization URL. Once you have the refresh token,
642: exchange it for an access token by calling the token URL.
643: Use the following values to construct the request body:
644: grant_type: Set to refresh_token.
645: client_id: (required) Set this to the Client ID for your app. Find this in Settings
646: for your app in the developer console.
647: client_secret: (required) Set this to the Secret for your app. Find this in Settings
648: for your app in the developer console.
649: refresh_token: The refresh token that you obtained with your original access token.
650: 1
651: 2
652: 3
653: 4
654: 5
655: curl --request POST \
656: --url 'https://auth.atlassian.com/oauth/token' \
657: --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
658: --data '{ "grant_type": "refresh_token", "client_id": "YOUR_CLIENT_ID", "client_secret": "YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET", "refresh_token": "YOUR_REFRESH_TOKEN" }'
659: If successful, a new access token is returned that you use to make calls to the
660: product API. You receive a new refresh
661: token as well and the refresh token you used for the request is disabled.
662: This is an example response with a refresh token:
663: 1
664: 2
665: 3
666: 4
667: 5
668: 6
669: 7
670: 8
671: 9
672: 10
673: HTTP/1.1 200 OK
674: Content-Type: application/json
675: {
676: "access_token": <string>,
677: "refresh_token": <string>,
678: "expires_in": <expiry time of access_token in second>,
679: "scope": <string>
680: }
681: Otherwise, if an error is returned, see the list below for possible causes:
682: 403 Forbidden with {"error": "invalid_grant", "error_description": "Unknown or invalid refresh token."
683: This error is returned for the following reasons:
684: The user's Atlassian account password has been changed. Change the password back to the original
685: password, or initiate the entire authorization flow from the beginning again.
686: Your app is using rotating refresh tokens and the exchange of refresh token failed because:
687: Your refresh token has expired. Users need to initiate the entire authorization flow from the
688: beginning to get a new refresh token.
689: Your app is not replacing the previous refresh token with the new refresh token returned
690: during access token request.
691: What happens if a user grants access to more than one Atlassian site for an app?
692: Only one grant exists per app for a given Atlassian account. If a user grants access to more than one
693: Atlassian site for this app, then the additional sites are added to the same grant. This means that
694: existing access tokens will give you access to all sites and scopes that a user has granted your app
695: access to.
696: What is the state parameter used for?
697: The primary use for the state parameter is to associate a user with an authorization flow. This makes
698: the authorization flow more secure, as the authorization flow cannot be hijacked to associate a user's
699: account with another user's token. Consider the following example scenario using Jira:
700: An application, named Incidents_Application, has a Jira integration that implements OAuth 2.0
701: authorization code grants but does not specify a state parameter.
702: A malicious actor, Mallory, initiates a Jira authorization flow for herself. This could be via the
703: Incidents_Application or by crafting an authorization URL that includes the Incidents_Application's client_id.
704: Mallory blocks the request to the Incidents_Application's callback URL during the authorization flow.
705: She records the URL, including the code parameter.
706: Mallory tricks another user, Edward, into visiting the callback URL in his browser.
707: The Incidents_Application handles the callback and exchanges Mallory's code for an access token to Jira.
708: Edward is logged into the Incidents_Application and the callback request came from Edward's browser, so
709: Mallory's token is now linked to Edward's account.
710: Mallory now has access to information sent to Edward by the Incidents_Application via the Jira
711: integration. For example, the Incidents_Application may create a Jira ticket about a confidential
712: incident, where the ticket is intended to be restricted to Edward but is restricted to Mallory instead.
713: If the Incidents_Application integration had used a state parameter, the Incidents_Application
714: would have known that the callback URL belonged to Mallory and ignored the request.
715: Other uses for the state parameter include:
716: Acting as a key for keeping track of specific details about the flow.
717: Returning the user to the right step in their workflow after sending them through the authorization flow.
718: How do I retrieve the public profile of the authenticated user?
719: The User Identity API is used to retrieve the public profile of the authenticated user. If you
720: want to use this API, do the following:
721: Add the User Identity API to your app in the developer console.
722: Add the read:me scope to the authorization URL for your app.
723: An example of a request to retrieve the public profile of the authenticated user is shown below:

769: Is CORS whitelisting supported?
770: CORS whitelisting is supported for api.atlassian.com. CORS whitelisting allows OAuth 2.0 authorization
771: code grants to work for browser-based XHR or fetch requests subject to cross-origin restrictions, such
772: as Chrome or Electron apps.
773: How do I configure the refresh token behavior?
774: Each time they are used, rotating refresh tokens issue a new limited life refresh token that
775: is valid for 90 days. This mechanism improves on single persistent refresh tokens by reducing the period
776: in which a refresh token can be compromised and used to obtain a valid access token.
777: If your refresh token expires, your user will need to complete the
778: entire authorization flow from the beginning again.
779: Every new refresh token returned invalidates the refresh token used to get the new access token. Your code should
780: replace the existing refresh token with the new refresh token. See
781: Use a refresh token to get another access token and refresh token pair for more details.

1: atlassian-mcp-server | Official remote MCP server for Atlassian. Securely connect Jira, Confluence, Jira Service Management, Bitbucket, and Compass to Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code, and other AI tools using OAuth 2.1 or API tokens.
2: atlassian-mcp-server
3: Atlassian MCP Server
4: The official Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for Atlassian: a cloud-hosted bridge that gives your AI tools secure, real-time access to Jira, Confluence, Jira Service Management, Bitbucket, Compass, Loom, and the wider Atlassian platform — powered by your Teamwork Graph.
5: Getting started ·
6: Supported tools ·
7: Security & admin ·
8: Community
9: The official Atlassian MCP Server is a cloud-based bridge between your Atlassian Cloud site and compatible external tools. Once configured, it enables those tools to interact with Jira, Confluence, Jira Service Management, Bitbucket, Compass, Loom, and Atlassian platform data (Projects, Goals, Teams, Focus, Talent, and the Teamwork Graph) in real time. Authentication uses OAuth 2.1 or API tokens, so every action respects the user’s existing access controls.
10: With the Atlassian MCP Server, you can:
11: Summarize and search Jira, Jira Service Management, Confluence, Bitbucket, Projects, Goals, and more without switching tools.
12: Retrieve and review recordings of videos and meetings from Loom.
13: Create and update work items or pages based on natural language commands.
14: Automate repetitive work, like generating work items from meeting notes or specs.
15: Connect once, then describe what you want — no tab switching and no copy-pasting. Your AI selects and runs the right actions.
16: It’s built for developers, content creators, and project teams who work in IDEs or AI tools and want to use Atlassian data without constantly switching context.
17: [!IMPORTANT]
18: v2 is now the recommended version. New setups should use https://mcp.atlassian.com/v2/mcp, which exposes more tools and more products. Existing v1 connections automatically start to expose and use v2 tools; incompatible clients may need to clear cached client IDs or .well-known credentials to keep authenticating. For setup steps, see Getting started with the Atlassian MCP Server.
19: One-click setup
20: Pick your AI client below to install the official Atlassian MCP Server. Each button uses your client’s native install link, so you don’t need to edit any JSON config by hand.

186: Product-specific conditions:
187: delete_jira and manage_jira are disabled by default and must be enabled by an admin before they can be used.
188: Bitbucket Cloud tools are only available if your Bitbucket workspace is linked to an organization. Workspaces that aren’t linked to an organization can’t be selected when authenticating.
189: Jira Service Management tools only support authentication via API token, and are only available if an organization admin has enabled API token authentication.
190: Loom tools are only available for Loom workspaces linked to an Atlassian site.
191: Teamwork Graph tools can retrieve data from third-party services connected to Jira, such as linked pull requests, builds, and deployments. For GitHub for Atlassian, full access means tools retrieve GitHub data based on the user’s GitHub permissions, while limited access means they retrieve data based on the user’s Jira permissions. Azure DevOps, GitLab, Jenkins, and Spinnaker connectors follow the limited access model.
192: [!NOTE]
193: For the complete, current tool reference, including the required scope for each permission group, see Supported tools.
194: How the server exposes tools
195: Rather than sending every tool definition to the AI client at connection time, the Atlassian MCP Server exposes a small set of the most-used tools and lets the client discover the rest on demand. Tools marked Primary are visible directly to agents.
196: This has two benefits:
197: Your client’s context stays free for the task at hand instead of being filled with tool definitions.
198: New tools become available without the client needing to reconnect.
199: MCP gateways
200: If you’re using an MCP gateway, or otherwise need every tool available up front rather than using the discovery and execute methods, use the tools=all override to expose all tools as a paginated flat tool list:
201: https://mcp.atlassian.com/v2/mcp?tools=all
202: Before you start
203: Check that your environment meets these requirements before you set up the server.
204: Prerequisites
205: The requirements depend on how you connect:
206: For supported clients
207: An Atlassian Cloud site with one or more of Jira, Confluence, Jira Service Management, Bitbucket, or Compass
208: Access to the client of choice
209: A modern browser to complete the OAuth 2.1 authorization flow, or API token credentials for headless authentication
210: If your organization admin has disabled authentication via API token, MCP clients can’t connect with a token and need to use OAuth 2.1 instead.
211: For IDEs or local clients (desktop setup)
212: An Atlassian Cloud site with one or more supported products
213: A supported IDE (for example, Claude Desktop, VS Code, or Cursor) or a custom MCP-compatible client
214: Node.js v18+ installed to run the local MCP proxy (mcp-remote)
215: A modern browser for completing OAuth login, or API token credentials for headless authentication
216: Data and security
217: The server enforces several security controls:
218: All traffic is encrypted in transit over HTTPS (TLS 1.2 or later), per Atlassian’s security practices.
219: OAuth 2.1 and API token authentication provide secure access control.
220: Data access respects user permissions across every connected Atlassian product, including Jira, Confluence, Jira Service Management, Bitbucket, Compass, and Loom.
221: If your organization uses IP allowlisting for Atlassian Cloud products, tool calls made through the Atlassian MCP Server also honor those IP rules.
222: For a deeper overview of the security model and admin controls, see:
223: Understand Atlassian MCP Server
224: Control Atlassian MCP Server settings
225: How it works
226: Architecture and communication
227: A supported client connects to the server endpoint. The recommended endpoint for all clients is:
228: https://mcp.atlassian.com/v2/mcp
229: The v1 endpoints (https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/mcp/authv2 and https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/mcp) remain supported, and existing v1 connections automatically start to expose and use v2 tools.
230: Depending on your setup, a secure browser-based OAuth 2.1 flow is triggered, or API token authentication is used.
231: Once authorized, the client streams contextual data and receives real-time responses from your connected Atlassian products.
232: [!WARNING]
233: After 30 June 2026, the legacy Server-Sent Events endpoint (https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/sse) will no longer be supported. Update any custom clients configured to use /sse so they point to /mcp — preferably https://mcp.atlassian.com/v2/mcp.
234: [!NOTE]
235: Clients that can’t complete authentication after the move to v2 tools may need to clear cached client IDs or .well-known credentials.
236: Permission management
237: Access is granted only to data that the user already has permission to view in Atlassian Cloud. All actions respect existing project or space-level roles. OAuth and API token authentication both honor configured scopes and Atlassian permissions.
238: API token authentication (headless)
239: API token authentication is available for headless, service-style, or non-interactive client setups (for example, backend systems or automations). It is also required for Jira Service Management tools.
240: Two mechanisms are supported:
241: Mechanism
242: Header
243: Personal API token (Basic auth)
244: Authorization: Basic <base64(email:api_token)>
245: Service account API key (Bearer token)
246: Authorization: Bearer <api_key>
247: Admin enablement required: An organization admin must enable API token authentication for the Atlassian MCP Server (Atlassian Administration → Rovo → Rovo MCP server → Authentication).
248: Scoped token required: Create a personal API token, or ask your admin for a service account API key, with the scopes required for the tools and data you need to access.
249: Configuration guide: Configure authentication via API token
250: Admin setting reference: Control Atlassian MCP Server settings: Configure authentication
251: Example workflows
252: Once connected, you can run tasks like these from your client.
253: Jira workflows
254: Search: “Find all open bugs in Project Alpha.”
255: Create/update: “Create a story titled ‘Redesign onboarding’.”
256: Bulk create: “Make five Jira issues from these notes.”
257: Confluence workflows
258: Summarize: “Summarize the Q2 planning page.”
259: Create: “Create a page titled ‘Team Goals Q3’.”
260: Navigate: “What spaces do I have access to?”
261: Compass workflows
262: Create: “Create a service component based on the current repository.”
263: Bulk create: “Import components and custom fields from this CSV/JSON.”
264: Query: “What depends on the api-gateway service?”
265: Loom workflows
266: Retrieve: “Find the Loom recording of last week’s design review.”
267: Summarize: “Summarize this Loom walkthrough and list the action items.”
268: Projects and Goals workflows
269: Status: “What’s the current status of the Checkout Revamp project?”
270: Roll up: “Which goals are at risk this quarter, and why?”
271: Combined tasks
272: Link content: “Link these three Jira work items to the ‘Release Plan’ page.”
273: Find documentation: “Fetch the Confluence documentation page linked to this Compass component.”
274: Move work forward: “Move PROJ-456 to ‘In Review’ and add a comment that the PR is up.”
275: [!NOTE]
276: Actual capabilities vary depending on your permission level and client platform.
277: Tips and tricks
278: Set default CloudId, Jira project, and Confluence space
279: Update your AGENTS.md with the Markdown below to reduce discovery tool calls, save time and tokens, and set maximum search results.
280: ## Atlassian MCP
281: When connected to atlassian-rovo-mcp:
282: - **MUST** use Jira project key = YOURPROJ
283: - **MUST** use Confluence spaceId = "123456"
284: - **MUST** use cloudId = "https://yoursite.atlassian.net" (do NOT call getAccessibleAtlassianResources)
285: - **MUST** use `maxResults: 10` or `limit: 10` for ALL Jira JQL and Confluence CQL search operations.
286: Use skills
287: If you’re using a desktop client like Claude, you can create or reuse skills for repeated tasks. See the default Atlassian MCP skills.
288: For Cursor, skills are part of the marketplace plugin.
289: Admin notes: managing access
290: If you’re an admin preparing your organization to use the Atlassian MCP Server, review the points below. For more detailed admin guidance, see:
291: Understand Atlassian MCP Server
292: Control Atlassian MCP Server settings
293: Manage Atlassian MCP Server
294: Monitor Atlassian MCP Server activity
295: Manage, monitor, and revoke access
296: Admin controls:
297: Site and organization admins can manage, review, or revoke the MCP app’s access from Manage your organization’s Marketplace and third-party apps.
298: Domain controls:
299: Use the Rovo MCP server settings page in Atlassian Administration to control which external AI tools and domains are allowed to connect. By default, Atlassian-supported domains are allowed; you can add trusted domains or block supported ones. Domain controls apply to OAuth 2.1 connections. For details, see Available Atlassian MCP server domains.
300: IP controls:
301: If your organization uses IP allowlisting for Atlassian Cloud apps, requests made through the Atlassian MCP Server must originate from an IP address allowed by your organization’s IP allowlist for the relevant app. For configuration details, see Specify IP addresses for product access.
302: Bitbucket Cloud IP restrictions are configured separately by workspace administrators under Workspace settings → Access controls. See Control access to private content in a workspace.
303: End-user controls:
304: Individual users can revoke their own app authorizations from their profile settings.
305: Audit logging:
306: Every time a tool is used through the Atlassian MCP Server, an event is recorded in your organization’s audit log. Admins can review these in Atlassian Administration under Insights → Audit log (filter for Rovo MCP User Actions or search MCP). For more information, see Monitor Atlassian MCP server activity.
307: Troubleshooting common issues
308: “You don’t have permission to connect from this IP address. Please ask your admin for access.”
309: This usually indicates that IP allowlisting is enabled and the request’s source IP address isn’t allowed to access the relevant app via the Atlassian MCP Server. Ask your site, organization, or Bitbucket workspace administrator to review the applicable IP allowlist.
310: Hosted AI clients can send requests from the AI provider’s outbound IP addresses rather than the user’s corporate network or VPN. Being on an allowed VPN may therefore be insufficient. Ask your administrator to review the provider’s published outbound IP ranges and approve the required access. For OpenAI-hosted connectors, see OpenAI’s IP egress guidance. Local MCP connections can use the local network’s outbound IP address. See how IP allowlisting works with Atlassian MCP.
311: OAuth sign-in succeeds, but tool calls return 403.
312: Successful sign-in does not guarantee that tool calls will pass IP restrictions. A 403 can also indicate insufficient scopes, app permissions, or another access policy. Confirm the denial reason before changing an IP allowlist.
313: Security
314: Model Context Protocol (MCP) lets AI agents connect to tools and Atlassian data using your account’s permissions, which creates powerful workflows but also structural risks. Any MCP client or server you enable (for example, IDE plugins, desktop apps, hosted MCP servers, or “one-click” integrations) can cause an AI agent to perform actions on your behalf.
315: Large language models (LLMs) are vulnerable to prompt injection and related attacks (such as indirect prompt injection and tool poisoning). These attacks can instruct the agent to exfiltrate data or make unintended changes without explicit requests.
316: To reduce risk, only use trusted MCP clients and servers, carefully review which tools and data each agent can access, and apply least privilege (scoped tokens, minimal project/workspace access). For any high-impact or destructive action, require human confirmation and monitor audit logs for unusual activity. We strongly recommend reviewing Atlassian’s guidance on MCP risks at MCP Clients: Understanding the potential security risks.
317: Support and feedback
318: We use your feedback to improve the Atlassian MCP Server. If you hit a bug or limitation, or have a suggestion:
319: Visit the Atlassian Support Portal to report issues and feature requests.
320: Share your experiences and questions on the Atlassian Community, and developer-related asks on the Atlassian Developer Community.
321: Go to our Ecosystem Developer Portal if you are building an app and found a bug or issue, or have suggestions.
322: Disclaimer
323: MCP clients can perform actions across Atlassian products with your existing permissions. Use least privilege, review high-impact changes before confirming, and monitor audit logs for unusual activity.
324: Learn more: MCP Clients: Understanding the potential security risks.
325: This site is open source. Improve this page.

To learn about developing for Atlassian Government Cloud, go to our Atlassian Government Cloud developer portal. 55: Ending Connect support 56: You can no longer publish Connect apps on the Atlassian Marketplace. All new extensibility features 57: will be delivered only on Forge. 58: Refer to this blog post for our timeline 59: to end Connect support. 60: Have an existing Connect app? You can incrementally migrate it to Forge. 61: Getting started with Connect 62: Connect is a development framework for extending Atlassian cloud products. Connect gives you control over the tech stack, infrastructure, and integration with Atlassian Cloud products. You determine your security implementation and authentication with external cloud providers, such as AWS, Google Cloud, or Heroku. 63: It handles discovery, installation, authentication, and seamless integration into the user interface. 64: In this tutorial, you'll learn how to use Connect to develop apps for Jira Cloud products, including: 65: Jira Cloud platform 66: Jira Software Cloud 67: Jira Service Management. 68: This includes getting an Atlassian cloud development instance, setting up your local development environment, 69: and validating your setup by building and deploying a Hello World app. 70: Before you begin 71: To complete this tutorial, you need the following: 72: Your favorite IDE or text editor 73: A basic knowledge of JavaScript and web development 74: A basic understanding of Jira 75: Node.js (version 12.1.0 or later). You also need npm, which is 76: included with Node.js 77: A tool to tunnel your local development environment to the internet. We recommend 78: ngrok, which is free and easy to use 79: Set up your development environment 80: You need the following things to develop for Jira Cloud: 81: A developer instance of Atlassian Cloud for testing and validating apps 82: A local development environment for creating apps 83: Step 1: Prepare for tunneling 84: In this tutorial, the app server will run on your local development machine. A tunnel tunnel is necessary to allow Jira or Confluence Cloud to send requests to the server running on your machine and install the app. ACE creates tunnels using the ngrok Node.js module, which can be used free of charge after creating an ngrok account. In order to use ngrok in ACE, an auth token is all that's required. Follow this process to obtain one: 85: Create a new ngrok account 86: Obtain an authtoken 87: Copy your personal token value (you'll need this later) 88: Step 2. Get a cloud development site 89: The Cloud Developer Bundle provides a free Atlassian cloud development site for building and testing 90: apps. To create your site: 91: Go to go.atlassian.com/cloud-dev and sign up. It may take 92: several minutes to provision your site. 93: Once your site is ready, sign in, and complete the setup wizard. 94: Your cloud development site has Confluence and all the Jira products installed. Note that 95: Atlassian cloud development sites have limits on the number of users. 96: If necessary, use the app switcher to navigate to Jira. Select the app switcher icon, and then 97: choose Jira. 98: Step 3. Enable development mode in your site 99: With development mode you can install app descriptors in your development site from any public URL. 100: This means you don't need to list an app in the Atlassian Marketplace before installing it. 101: In the top navigation bar, click Apps then Manage your apps. If Apps isn't visible, 102: click More first. 103: Under User-installed apps, click Settings. 104: Select Enable development mode, and then click Apply. 105: After the page refreshes, you see the Upload app link. This link enables you to install apps 106: during development. 107: Step 4. Set up your local development environment 108: If you install an Atlassian Connect app in an Atlassian cloud instance, it's usually hosted elsewhere 109: (for example, a cloud platform service like Heroku). However, it's easiest to develop an app on your 110: local machine and make it available over the internet by tunneling (using HTTPS). This enables you to 111: work locally and test against your Atlassian cloud instance. 112: On your command line, run: 113: 1 114: 2 115: npm install -g ngrok 116: Identify to ngrok using your auth token (from the step "Prepare for tunneling") 117: 1 118: 2 119: ngrok authtoken 120: Start ngrok by running the following command: 121: 1 122: 2 123: ngrok http 8000 124: We're assuming that you have a working web application listening on http://localhost:8000. If your app is listening on a different URL, change the above command to match. 125: You should see something similar to the following console UI in your terminal. 126: 1 127: 2 128: 3 129: Forwarding https://84c5df439d74.ngrok-free.dev -> http://localhost:8000 130: Confirm new tunnel 131: Important: for any recently created ngrok account there will be a warning page displayed that needs to be confirmed once before the tunnel can be used. To do this, look for the message Forwarding https://.ngrok-free.app/ and open that URL in your browser. You'll see a page like this: 132: Confirm by clicking on the button labeled "Visit Site". Your tunnel is now fully operational, but this step needs to be repeated every time a new tunnel is opened. 133: Making your app available to the internet using ngrok is covered later in this tutorial. 134: Build a basic app 135: This part of the tutorial gives you a hands-on introduction to Atlassian Connect by building a simple 136: Atlassian Connect app. It also validates that your development environment is set up correctly. The 137: app uses a generalPages module and adds a link titled Greeting to the Jira sidebar. 138: Step 1. Define the app descriptor 139: The fundamental building block of an app is the app descriptor file, usually named atlassian-connect.json. The 140: descriptor file describes your app to the Atlassian application (in this case, Jira Cloud), including the key, 141: name, permissions needed to operate, and modules it uses for integration. 142: First, create a project directory and define your app descriptor. 143: Create a project directory for your app's source files. 144: In the project directory, create a new file named atlassian-connect.json with this content: 145: 1 146: 2 147: 3 148: 4 149: 5 150: 6 151: 7 152: 8 153: 9 154: 10 155: 11 156: 12 157: 13 158: 14 159: 15 160: 16 161: 17 162: 18 163: 19 164: 20 165: 21 166: 22 167: 23 168: 24 169: 25 170: 26 171: 27 172: { 173: "name": "Hello World", 174: "description": "Atlassian Connect app", 175: "key": "com.example.myapp", 176: "baseUrl": "https://", 177: "vendor": { 178: "name": "Example, Inc.", 179: "url": "http://example.com" 180: }, 181: "authentication": { 182: "type": "none" 183: }, 184: "apiVersion": 1, 185: "modules": { 186: "generalPages": [ 187: { 188: "url": "/helloworld.html", 189: "key": "hello-world", 190: "location": "system.top.navigation.bar", 191: "name": { 192: "value": "Greeting" 193: } 194: } 195: ] 196: } 197: } 198: Note, you must specify the correct baseUrl value instead of placeholder-url. 199: Save the descriptor file. 200: (optional) Validate your descriptor using the JSON schema validator. 201: This handy tool shows you any errors in your app descriptor, such as missing properties or syntax errors. 202: You don't need to change the placeholder used for baseUrl now. You update it later in this tutorial, 203: when you deploy your app. 204: Step 2. Create the user interface 205: Now, create the user interface using a simple static HTML page. An app consisting of an app descriptor 206: and an HTML page is the most basic Atlassian Connect app. Such apps are not typical. However, when you 207: understand how the example works, it only takes a few more steps to turn it into a fully-functional app. 208: For production environments, we recommend bundling CSS and JS files with your site, rather than relying on a third-party CDN. 209: In your project directory, create a new file named helloworld.html with this content: 210: 1 211: 2 212: 3 213: 4 214: 5 215: 6 216: 7 217: 8 218: 9 219: 10 220: 11 221: 12 222: 13 223: 224: 225: 226: 227: 228: 229: 230:
231:

Hello World

232:
233: 234: 235: Note that the app descriptor file, atlassian-connect.json, references this file in the generalPages element: url: /helloworld.html 236: Save the file. 237: That's all the coding you need to do. Now take a closer look at the contents of the helloworld.html file: 238: Styling: The helloworld.html page uses CSS from Atlaskit. Atlaskit is a library 239: of reusable front-end UI components. This app uses the CSS styling to render the h1 element using the Atlassian font stack. 240: script tag: This script tag includes the all.js file, the client library for the Atlassian Connect JavaScript API. 241: It simplifies client interactions with the Atlassian application, such as making an XMLHttpRequest. 242: ac-content class: This class wraps the contents of your app and dynamically resizes the iframe 243: in Jira. This class keeps your app content visible without scrollbars. 244: Deploy and install your app 245: Use ngrok to make the local app available to the internet, and then tell your Jira instance how to find the 246: descriptor. 247: Step 1: Host the app on a local web server 248: You need a simple web server to serve the directory containing your atlassian-connect.json and 249: helloworld.html files. There are several tools you can use to do this, this tutorial uses 250: http-server (available via npm). 251: Open your project directory at the command line 252: Install http-server by running: 253: 1 254: 2 255: npm install http-server -g 256: Start the server on port 8000 by running: 257: 1 258: 2 259: http-server -p 8000 260: A message on your command line indicates that the server is serving HTTP at an address and port. It will look 261: something like this: 262: 1 263: 2 264: Starting up http-server, serving ./ on: http://0.0.0.0:8000/ 265: Confirm that the files you created in steps 1 and 2 are being served by visiting the following URLs: 266: http://localhost:8000/atlassian-connect.json 267: http://localhost:8000/helloworld.html 268: The public hosting of files for download is not enough. The files must be hosted by 269: a web server. 270: The descriptor file can only be fetched from web server ports 80, 443, or 8080. 271: Step 2: Make the app files available to the internet 272: Now that your app is hosted on a local web server, use ngrok to make it available over the internet. 273: In a new command line window, run this command to expose your web server to the internet. If your app is not 274: running on port 8000, change the command to use your app's port number. 275: 1 276: 2 277: ngrok http 8000 278: You see a status page on the command line that shows the tunnel's public URL and other information about 279: connections made over the tunnel. If your app is not running when you try to start ngrok, you see a 280: "Failed to complete tunnel connection" message. 281: Get the HTTPS URL from the ngrok status page. 282: Edit the app descriptor file, and set the baseUrl property to the ngrok HTTPS URL. For example: 283: 1 284: 2 285: "baseUrl": "https://bb5a163ef415.ngrok.io" 286: Confirm that the descriptor is available by opening the atlassian-connect.json file in your browser 287: at the ngrok HTTPS URL. For example: 288: 1 289: 2 290: https://bb5a163ef415.ngrok.io/atlassian-connect.json 291: This is the URL you use in the next section to install your app. 292: Step 3: Install and test your app 293: The final step in deploying your app is to install it in your Atlassian cloud instance. You do 294: this by adding a link to your app's descriptor file in your Atlassian cloud instance. This enables Jira to install your app. 295: Navigate to Jira in your Atlassian Cloud instance, then choose Jira settings (cog icon) > Apps > Manage apps. 296: Click Upload app. 297: In the From this URL field, provide a link to your app descriptor. This URL is the same as the hosted location of your atlassian-connect.json descriptor file. The example uses the following URL: 298: 1 299: 2 300: https://bb5a163ef415.ngrok.io/atlassian-connect.json 301: Click Upload. Jira displays the Installed and ready to go message when the installation is complete. 302: Click Close. 303: Verify that your app appears in the User installed apps list. For example, if you used Hello World for your app name, 304: then Hello World appears in the list. 305: In the top navigation bar, click Apps then Greeting. If Apps isn't visible, 306: click More first. 307: The Hello World message displays. 308: You've now set up a development environment and built your first app. 309: Next steps 310: You now know enough to start developing apps with Atlassian Connect. To continue learning about app development 311: for Jira Cloud: 312: Work through some more involved tutorials for building apps for Jira Software, 313: Jira Service Desk tutorials, or Jira platform 314: Check out the REST API to see what is possible 315: Rate this page: 316: Unusable 317: Poor 318: Okay 319: Good 320: Excellent 321: ChangelogSystem statusPrivacyNotice at CollectionDeveloper TermsTrademarkCookie preferences© 2026 Atlassian

89: Build an app with Asana
90: Learn the basics of Asana's developer platform
91: What is an Asana app?
92: An Asana app makes it possible to extend or enhance what’s possible with Asana. Many people build Asana apps to integrate with other tools, add or extract data about the Work Graph, or automate workflows.
93: Apps can be built and then shared with other Asana users or they can be built just for your organization. Apps can be built for individual users, for example Google Drive which attaches Google files to tasks. Apps can also be built to run org-level processes. For example like onboarding users from Okta or running custom scripts.
94: Build an app and publish to the App Directory
95: If you are building an integration with a 3rd party tool and intend for any Asana user to discover it, apps can be published to the Asana App Directory. The app directory is a great place for users to discover new apps that help them get the most out of Asana. We recommend visiting the app directory and try using an app to learn more about what’s possible to build with Asana.
96: Build an app for just one organization
97: If your app is not meant to be used by any Asana user, apps can also be created and then shared with only organizations of your choice. By default, all apps start out private to the developer. You can change the sharing permissions of your app in the Manage distribution tab inside the developer console.
98: Asana apps use features like our rest API, app components, and webhooks. Learn more about how these features are used to power our most common use cases.
99: What do I need to know before I build an app with Asana?
100: While no two apps are exactly the same. We have a general set of best practices that will help you build a successful app with Asana.
101: Here’s an overview of the steps you will need to follow to build an app.
102: Plan your app
103: Before you get started building your Asana app, we recommend you familiarize yourself with the Work Graph, meaning the core Asana objects and their relationships. Check out this quick guide on understanding objects.
104: Next, we recommend planning your app. This step helps you define the exact problem your app is meant to solve and become familiar with features in the Asana platform that will help you build the right solution. Check out our library of use cases, example apps, and other apps in the directory for inspiration.
105: Get started with the API
106: The next step is to try using the API to test how it works. The primary feature of Asana’s platform is our rest API, so we recommend getting familiar with how our API works.
107: Here’s a brief overview of how to get started:
108: Choose your test workspace. You can test in any of your existing workspaces, create a free account, or request a developer sandbox. The developer sandbox will allow you to test premium features not included in a free account.
109: Choose your authentication method. Your app may ultimately use OAuth, but most developers test our API by creating a Personal Access Token (PAT) to make their first API calls.
110: Create your token or app in the developer console.
111: Use your token to make an API call. Visit the API Reference and learn about the different types of APIs that are available. Our embedded API explorer lets you try using the API from the reference. Build your request on the documentation page, press “Try it” and see a response in seconds. If you’d like a step-by-step guide for making your first API call, check out our quick start guide.
112: Build and share your app with its intended audience
113: Once you have your app planned, and have moved beyond testing the API, you’re ready to build your app. If you are building with a PAT or Service Account token, your app can only be used in your organization. If you are building an app for any user to discover, we recommend creating an app and using OAuth. All OAuth apps are created privately by default. You will need to change the app distribution setting to either share the app with just a specific organization or to anyone with the OAuth redirect URL.
114: Learn more about the different features you might want to consider like webhooks for reacting to changes in Asana or app components for embedding apps directly into Asana.
115: Use the API reference to determine what types of API calls will best serve your use case.
116: Set-up your authentication method (OAuth recommended). Learn more about authentication options.
117: Write your app code. If you would like to start from an example, you can check out our Github repository of example apps.
118: Deploy your app.
119: Locally - For a simple script, creating a launchd job (or Windows task scheduler) may be sufficient, whereas more complex apps or those using features like webhooks or app components will have more sophisticated hosting, security, and uptime requirements.
120: Hosted - Some developers choose to use their company’s on-prem solution, many use hosting providers. If your company doesn’t already have a hosting provider that you can use, here are some common choices: Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud, Heroku, Microsoft Azure, IBM Cloud, SAP, Vercel
121: Share your app (optional). When your app is ready to use, we recommend checking your distribution settings. In the Developer Console > Manage distribution. There you can share your app with more workspaces or choose to share your app with “any workspace”, meaning any user with the OAuth Redirect URL can authorize the app. If you are using a PAT or Service Account token, sharing your app will not be necessary as those tokens can only be used in workspaces where you are a user.
122: Publish your app (optional). If you would like your app to be published in the Asana App Directory. Set your distribution to “any workspace”, then follow the instructions on the Developer Console > Submit for Review page.

89: Personal access token
90: Overview
91: A personal access token (PAT) contains your security credentials for the Asana platform. Much like an API key, generating a PAT allows you to access (i.e., make requests to) the Asana REST API upon successful authentication.
92: A user can create many, but not unlimited, personal access tokens. When creating a token, you must give it a description to help you remember what you created the token for.
93: 📘
94: PAT or OAuth?
95: If you build an app, and the app needs to perform actions on behalf of users (e.g., getting data from Asana or making changes within Asana), you should use OAuth.
96: Generating a PAT
97: You can generate a personal access token from the Asana developer console.
98: 📘
99: API explorer
100: Your PAT also gives you access to the API explorer, where you can make API requests (and view responses) directly in your browser window. For more information, see API explorer.
101: Example
102: Personal access tokens should be used similarly to OAuth access tokens when accessing the API (i.e., passing them in the Authorization header).
103: Below is an example of a cURL request authenticating with a PAT:
104: Shell
105: curl https://app.asana.com/api/1.0/users/me \
106: -H "Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN"
107: In the above snippet, replace ACCESS_TOKEN with your PAT.
108: ⚠️
109: Note on token format
110: Asana API tokens should be treated as opaque. Token formats may change without notice. Validating a token’s format on the client side could result in unexpected breakages. This applies to any Asana API tokens, including: personal access tokens, service account tokens, and both OAuth refresh tokens and access tokens.
111: PAT security
112: For security, you should regularly review the list of personal access tokens you have created and deauthorize those that you no longer need.
113: 📘
114: Advanced admin controls
115: Personal access tokens are persistent by default. Enterprise+ tiers include admin controls—such as those in the Manage apps panel—that influence how PATs are handled. See this Help Center article for additional information.
116: Remember to keep your tokens secret and treat them just like passwords. Your tokens act on your behalf when interacting with the API. As such, do not hardcode them into your programs.
117: Especially as your application grows, it's recommended to use a robust secrets management solution (e.g., HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, or Azure Key Vault) to prevent potential security risks. These solutions provide secure storage, encryption, access control, and auditing capabilities. In containerized environments, tools like Kubernetes Secrets or Docker Secrets with encryption enabled can further enhance security. Additionally, you should pull secrets into memory at runtime, ensuring they are never exposed in logs or code repositories.
118: By implementing these practices, you ensure your tokens remain safe and your application stays secure as it scales.

Portfolio to CSV export 83: Script action examples 84: Triage bot 85: Using bots 86: Postman Collection 87: Changelog 88: Powered by 89: OAuth 90: At its core, OAuth ("Open Authorization") is a mechanism for applications to access the Asana API on behalf of a user, all without the application having access to the user's username and password. Instead, the application gets a token, which can be used in subsequent API calls through the addition of an Authorization header: 91: Shell 92: -H "Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN" 93: In the above example,ACCESS_TOKEN should be replaced by the actual token received during the token exchange. 94: Most of the time, OAuth is the preferred method of authentication for developers, users, and Asana as a platform. If you are building a custom app, you should consider building a secure OAuth flow to authenticate users of your app. 95: 📘 96: Quick reference 97: If you are already using an OAuth library and/or have a deep understanding of OAuth, you may wish to skip ahead to the quick reference below: 98: Asana supports the authorization code grant flow 99: Applications can be created from the developer console (i.e., "My apps") 100: The endpoint for user authorization is GET https://app.asana.com/-/oauth_authorize 101: The endpoint for token exchange is POST https://app.asana.com/-/oauth_token 102: The endpoint for revoking a token is POST https://app.asana.com/-/oauth_revoke 103: Once an access token (i.e., bearer token) has been obtained, your application can make API requests on behalf of the user 104: 📘 105: Open source examples 106: You can access an open source examples for OAuth servers, provided in the following languages: 107: Node.js (Express.js) 108: Python (Flask) 109: Feel free to follow the comments in the server files as you inspect the overall OAuth flow. Note: These OAuth servers should only be used for testing and learning purposes. 110: In addition to learning about how to use OAuth on the Asana platform (i.e., through this guide), feel free to review the official OAuth 2.0 specification. 111: Overview of the OAuth process 112: This section describes the overall OAuth process (i.e., with the authorization code grant flow, which is the most common). 113: 📘 114: OAuth libraries 115: We recommend using a library (available in your language of choice) to handle the details of OAuth. Along with expediting development time, using a library can help mitigate the risk of security vulnerabilities due to inexperience or oversight. 116: As a prerequisite, ensure that you have registered an application with Asana. Take note of the application's client ID and the client secret (which should be protected as a password). Then, to begin: 117: A user arrives at your application and clicks a button that says Authenticate with Asana (or Connect with Asana, etc.) 118: The user is taken to the user authorization endpoint, which displays a page that asks the user if they would like to grant access to your third-party application 119: If the user clicks Allow, they are redirected back to your application, bringing along a special code in the query string 120: The application makes a request to the token exchange endpoint to exchange that code, along with the application's client secret, for two tokens: 121: An access token (i.e., a bearer token, which lasts an hour) 122: A refresh token (which can be used to fetch a new access token when the current one expires) 123: Using this access token, the application can now make requests against the Asana API for the next hour 124: Once the access token expires, the application can use the token exchange endpoint again (i.e., without user intervention) to exchange the refresh token for a new access token. This can be repeated for as long as the user has authorized the application 125: 📘 126: Authorization code grant 127: For additional details and a diagram of the authorization code grant flow, see Authorization Code Grant in the OAuth 2.0 specification. 128: Register an application 129: You must first register your application with Asana to receive a client ID and client secret. To do so, first visit the developer console and select Create new app, as shown below: 130: To build a proper OAuth flow, you must supply your new application with three key details: 131: App name - The name for your application. Users will see this name when your application requests permission to access their account as well as when they review the list of apps they have authorized. 132: The app name can be changed at any time in the Basic information tab in the sidebar of the developer console 133: Redirect URL - Otherwise known as the callback URL, this is where the user will be redirected upon successful or failed authentication. Native or command line applications should use the special redirect URL urn:ietf:wg:oauth:2.0:oob. For security reasons, non-native applications must supply a "https" URL (more on this below). 134: ❗️ 135: Client secret 136: Your client secret is a secret, and it should never be shared with anyone or added into source code that others could gain access to. If you need to reset your client secret: 137: Select your app in the developer console 138: Navigate to the OAuth tab in the sidebar 139: Select Reset next to your client secret 140: (OAuth) Permission scopes: You'll need to specify which OAuth scopes your app can request during this registration step. Only these pre-approved scopes will be accepted later during user authorization. 141: You can always update the list of scopes later in the developer console (under OAuth > Permission scopes). Below is an example of what it looks like in the developer console. Note that you can either toggle Full permissions (which grants access to all endpoints) or manually choose a specific set of OAuth scopes for your app: 142: In the above example, the following OAuth scopes were chosen (we'll review OAuth scopes in more detail shortly in this guide): 143: projects:read 144: tasks:read 145: tasks:write 146: tasks:delete 147: Along with all the app registration information above, you can also upload an icon, a description, and other basic information about your application. All of these attributes can also be changed later as well. 148: Once you have created an app, the OAuth tab in the sidebar will include a client ID (needed to uniquely identify your app to the Asana API) as well as a client secret. 149: User authorization endpoint 150: During the user authorization step, the user is prompted by the application to either grant or deny the application to access to their account. 151: The API endpoint for user authorization is: GET https://app.asana.com/-/oauth_authorize 152: ❗️ 153: App distribution settings 154: In order for a user to be able to authorize the OAuth application via this user authorization endpoint, the application must be available in the user's workspace. 155: If you have not yet configured your application's distribution settings, visit the manage distribution documentation before moving forward. 156: Request 157: Here is an example of basic link that sends a user to https://app.asana.com/-/oauth_authorize: 158: Example 159: 169: Authenticate with Asana 170: 171: This example usesscopes chosen during the app registration example above. The scope parameter is space-separated but must be URL-encoded in practice (i.e., spaces become %20). 172: By clicking on Authenticate with Asana link in the above example, the application redirects the user to https://app.asana.com/-/oauth_authorize, passing query parameters along as a standard query string: 173: Query parameterDescription 174: client_id (required)The client ID uniquely identifies the application making the request 175: redirect_uri (required)The URI to redirect to on success or error. This must match the redirect URL specified in the application settings 176: response_type (required)Must be either code or id_token, or the space-delimited combination: code id_token 177: state (required)Encodes state of the app, which will be returned verbatim in the response and can be used to match the response up to a given request 178: code_challenge_method (conditional)PKCE The hash method used to generate the challenge. This is typically S256 179: code_challenge (conditional)PKCE. The code challenge used for PKCE 180: scopeA space-delimited set of one or more scopes to get the user's permission to access. If no scopes are specified, the default OAuth scope will be used—provided the app was originally registered with Full permissions. 181: The resulting authentication screen will look something like this to the end-user: 182: OAuth scopes 183: Asana uses OAuth 2.0 for secure user authorization. Scopes allow your app to request only the access it needs, following the principle of least privilege. That is, OAuth scopes define which parts of the Asana API your app can access. This helps users trust your app and ensures their data is protected. 184: 📘 185: Register for scopes before requesting them 186: If you request a scope that is not in your app's approved (i.e., registered) list, the user will see a forbidden_scopes error on the authorization page. 187: You can update the scopes your app is allowed to request by editing your app's settings in the developer console. Visit the developer console, navigate to OAuth in the sidebar, then select your preferred scopes under Permission scopes. 188: 📘 189: What scopes are available? 190: To view all scopes currently available view its documentation. 191: Full permissions: Opting out of scopes 192: Using scopes is strongly recommended, however, scopes are not yet available for every Asana API endpoint. If you need to use an endpoint which does not yet have scopes associated with it, you can toggle on Full permissions in the Developer Console under OAuth > Permission Scopes. A full list of scopes is available here. 193: Scope structure 194: Each scope follows the format: : 195: Where: 196: refers to an object (e.g.,tasks, projects, users) 197: is one of: read, write, or delete 198: Note: these do not imply inheritance (e.g., write does not grant read access) 199: For example: 200: tasks:read – View basic task information like name and assignee 201: projects:write – Create or modify projects 202: users:read – Access user information like email and profile picture 203: Related object fields in responses 204: Asana’s data model is graph-based, so many endpoints include nested related objects (e.g., a task object may include the assignee, which is a user object). By default, only the following fields are available for these related objects without additional scopes: 205: gid 206: name or title 207: resource_type 208: resource_subtype 209: Fields which are not in this list will be omitted. If you request any additional fields (using the opt_fields query parameter), your app must request the corresponding scope. For example: 210: Example 211: GET /tasks/123?opt_fields=assignee.email 212: This request requires the users:read scope. Without it, you’ll receive a 403 Forbidden error. 213: Request a subset of scopes 214: Apps with registered scopes must specify scopes at the authorization endpoint using the scope query parameter. Previously, this was optional. 215: You may request a subset of the scopes you registered for. This is useful if you do not need all scopes initially (for example, if the user is only using a subset of the features your app offers) and you would like to progressively ask for additional access as needed. 216: To request additional scopes, you can send the user back to the authorization endpoint. Subsequent requests will not be additive. You must specify the full set of scopes needed. 217: To check which scopes are authorized for a given access token or refresh token, you may use the token introspection endpoint. 218: For example, in the scenario above, we showed an app registered with these scopes: projects:read, tasks:read, tasks:write, and tasks:delete. However, this app may request only the project:readscope when requesting authorization: 219: Example 220: 230: Connect with Asana 231: 232: Response 233: If either the client_id or redirect_uri do not match, the user will simply see a plain-text error. Otherwise, 234: all errors will be sent back to the redirect_uri specified. 235: The user then sees a screen giving them the opportunity to accept or reject the request for authorization. In either case, the user will be redirected back to the redirect_uri. 236: Below is an example URL through which a user is redirected to the redirect_uri: 237: https://my.app.com?code=325797325&state=thisIsARandomString 238: Query parameterDescription 239: codeIf value of response_type is code in the authorizing request, this is the code your app can exchange for a token 240: stateThe state parameter that was sent with the authorizing request 241: 🚧 242: Preventing CSRF attacks 243: The state parameter is necessary to prevent CSRF attacks. As such, you must check that thestate is the same in this response as it was in the request. If the state parameter is not used, or not tied to the user's session, then attackers can initiate an OAuth flow themselves before tricking a user's browser into completing it. That is, users can unknowingly bind their accounts to an attacker account. 244: In terms of requirements, the state parameter must contain an unguessable value tied to the user's session, which can be the hash of something tied to their session when the OAuth flow is first initiated (e.g., their session cookie). This value is then passed back and forth between the client application and the OAuth service as a form of CSRF token for the client application. 245: For additional security resources, see: 246: OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice 247: Prevent Attacks and Redirect Users with OAuth 2.0 State Parameters 248: Token exchange endpoint 249: The token exchange endpoint is used to exchange a code or refresh token for an access token. 250: The API endpoint for token exchange is: POST https://app.asana.com/-/oauth_token 251: Request 252: When your app receives a code from the authorization endpoint, it can now be exchanged for a proper token. At this point, your app should make a POST request to https://app.asana.com/-/oauth_token, passing the parameters as part of a standard form-encoded POST body (i.e., passing in the data into a request with header 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded') 253: Below is an example request body in a POST request to https://app.asana.com/-/oauth_token and an example cURL call: 254: JSONcURL 255: { 256: "grant_type": "authorization_code", 257: "client_id": "753482910", 258: "client_secret": "6572195638271537892521", 259: "redirect_uri": "https://my.app.com", 260: "code": "325797325", 261: "code_verifier": "fdsuiafhjbkewbfnmdxzvbuicxlhkvnemwavx" 262: } 263: curl --location 'https://app.asana.com/-/oauth_token' \ 264: --header 'Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded' \ 265: --data-urlencode 'grant_type=refresh_token' \ 266: --data-urlencode 'refresh_token=' \ 267: --data-urlencode 'client_id=' \ 268: --data-urlencode 'client_secret=' 269: 🚧 270: Sending the client_secret 271: If you have a client_secret, this request should be sent from your secure server. The browser should not see your client_secret (i.e., the client_secret should never be exposed in client-side code). 272: Details of each parameter are described below: 273: ParameterDescription 274: grant_type (required)One of authorization_code or refresh_token (see below for more details) 275: client_id (required)The client ID uniquely identifies the application making the request 276: client_secret (required)The client secret belonging to the app, found in the Basic information tab of the developer console 277: redirect_uri (required)Must match the redirect_uri specified in the original request 278: code (required)This is the code you are exchanging for an authorization token 279: refresh_token (conditional)If the value of grant_type is refresh_token, this is the refresh token you are using to be granted a new access token 280: code_verifierThis is the string previously used to generate the code_challenge. 281: Response 282: In the response to the request above, you will receive a JSON object similar to the example below: 283: JSON 284: { 285: "access_token": "f6ds7fdsa69ags7ag9sd5a", 286: "expires_in": 3600, 287: "token_type": "bearer", 288: "data": { 289: "id": 4673218951, 290: "gid": "4673218951", 291: "name": "Greg Sanchez", 292: "email": "[email protected]" 293: }, 294: "refresh_token": "hjkl325hjkl4325hj4kl32fjds" 295: } 296: Details of each property are described below: 297: PropertyDescription 298: access_tokenThe token to use in future requests against the API. This token is only valid for the scopes requested during user authorization. To gain additional permissions, the user must reauthorize the app with an updated set of scopes. 299: expires_inThe number of seconds that the token is valid, typically 3600 (one hour) 300: token_typeThe type of token (in our case, bearer) 301: refresh_tokenIf exchanging a code, this is a long-lived token that can be used to get new access tokens when older ones expire 302: dataAn object encoding a few key fields about the logged-in user. Currently, this is the user's id, gid, name, and email 303: Token expiration 304: When an access (bearer) token has expired, you'll see the following error when using such a token in an API request: 305: The bearer token has expired. If you have a refresh token, please use it to request a new bearer token, otherwise allow the user to re-authenticate. 306: You can get a new access token by having your application make a POST request back to the token exchange endpoint using a grant type of "refresh_token". In the same request you must also pass in your long-lived refresh_token from the original token exchange request. 307: 🚧 308: Note on token format 309: Asana API tokens should be treated as opaque. Token formats may change without notice. Validating a token’s format on the client side could result in unexpected breakages. This applies to any Asana API tokens, including: personal access tokens, service account tokens, and both OAuth refresh tokens and access tokens. 310: Token deauthorization endpoint 311: An authorization token can be deauthorized or invalidated (i.e., revoked) by making a request to Asana's API. 312: The endpoint for revoking a token is: POST https://app.asana.com/-/oauth_revoke 313: Request 314: Your app should make a POST request to https://app.asana.com/-/oauth_revoke, passing the following parameters as part of a standard form-encoded POST body: 315: ParameterDescription 316: client_id (required)The client ID uniquely identifies the application making the request. 317: client_secret (required)The client secret belonging to the app, found in the details pane of the developer console 318: token (required)The refresh token that should be deauthorized. Access tokens (i.e., bearer tokens) will be rejected 319: The body should include a valid refresh token, which will cause the refresh token and any associated bearer tokens to be deauthorized. Bearer tokens are not accepted in the request body since a new bearer token can always be obtained by reusing an authorized refresh token. 320: Response 321: A successful response with a 200 status code indicates that the token was deauthorized or not found. An unsuccessful response with a 400 status code will be returned if the request was malformed due to missing any required fields or due to an invalid token (such as a bearer token). 322: Token introspection endpoint 323: The token introspection endpoint provides information about an Asana API token: 324: The API endpoint for token introspection is: POST https://app.asana.com/-/token_info 325: Request 326: POST https://app.asana.com/-/token_info with standard form-encoded request body: 327: Request Body ParameterDescription 328: token (required)Token string for an OAuth access or refresh token, personal access token, or service account token 329: Response 330: The response is similar to the token exchange endpoint: 331: JSON 332: { 333: "token_type": "bearer", 334: "expires_in": 315359969, 335: "exp": 2069346816, 336: "scope": "tasks:read tasks:write projects:read projects:write openid email profile", 337: "active": true 338: } 339: Details of each property: 340: PropertyDescription 341: token_typeThe type of tokenbearer (OAuth access token, personal access token, or service account) or refresh (OAuth refresh token) 342: expires_inThe number of seconds that the token is valid. OAuth access tokens expire in 1 hour (3600 seconds) 343: expThe unix timestamp (integer timestamp, number of seconds since January 1, 1970 UTC) indicating when this token will expire. 344: scopeA JSON string containing a space-separated list of scopes associated with this token. 345: activeBoolean indicating whether or not the token is still valid. false if the token has expired or been revoked / deauthorized. 346: client_idAssociated OAuth app / client id. This is returned only for OAuth access tokens and OAuth refresh tokens 347: Security considerations 348: PKCE OAuth extension 349: PKCE (proof key for code exchange) proves the app that started the authorization flow is the same app that finishes the flow. You can read more about it here: Protecting Apps with PKCE. 350: In short, the process is as follows: 351: Whenever a user wants to OAuth with Asana, your app server should generate a random string called the code_verifier. This string should be saved to the user, since every code_verifier should be unique per user. This should stay in the app server and only be sent to the token exchange endpoint. 352: Your app server will hash the code_verifier with SHA256 to get a string called the code_challenge. Your server will give the browser only the code_challenge & code_challenge_method. The code_challenge_method should be the string "S256" to tell Asana we hashed with SHA256. More specifically, code_challenge = BASE64URL-ENCODE(SHA256(ASCII(code_verifier))). 353: The browser includes code_challenge & code_challenge_method when redirecting to the user authorization endpoint: 354: { 355: ... 356: "code_challenge": "671608a33392cee13585063953a86d396dffd15222d83ef958f43a2804ac7fb2", 357: "code_challenge_method": "S256" 358: } 359: The app server should include the code_verifier in its request to the token exchange endpoint. 360: Asana confirms that hashing the code_verifier with the code_challenge_method results in the code_challenge. This proves to Asana the app that hit the user authorization endpoint is the same app that hit the token exchange endpoint: 361: { 362: ... 363: "code_verifier": "fdsuiafhjbkewbfnmdxzvbuicxlhkvnemwavx" 364: } 365: ⚠️ 366: PKCE is required for localhost redirect URLs 367: OAuth flows that use a localhost, 127.0.0.1, or native URN redirect URI must use PKCE (S256). Include a code_challenge in the authorization request and the matching code_verifier in the token exchange. Requests without these parameters will be rejected. 368: Secure redirect endpoint 369: As the redirect from the authorization endpoint in either grant procedure contains a code that is secret between Asana's authorization servers and your application, this response should not occur in plaintext over an unencrypted http connection. Because of this, we enforce the use of https redirect endpoints for application registrations. 370: For non-production or personal use, you may wish to check out stunnel, which can act as a proxy to receive an encrypted connection, decrypt it, and forward it on to your application. For development work, you may wish to create a self-signed SSL/TLS certificate for use with your web server; for production work we recommend purchasing a certificate from a certificate authority. You may review a short summary of the steps for each of these processes here. 371: Your application will need to be configured to accept SSL/TLS connections for your redirect endpoint when users become authenticated. For many apps, this will simply require a configuration update of your application server. Instructions for Apache and Nginx can be found on their respective websites, and most popular application servers will contain documentation on how to proceed. 372: Troubleshooting 373: Forbidden scopes: Full permissions 374: Error:forbidden_scopes: Your app is not allowed to request user authorization for default identity scopes 375: Your app is requesting Full permissions (the default scope), but is not registered for Full permissions in the developer console. 376: If you would like to request Full permissions: toggle on Full Permissions under OAuth > Permission Scopes in the developer console. 377: If you would like to use scopes to limit access: 378: Select your desired scopes under OAuth > Permissions in the developer console and save. 379: Specify scopes in the scope query parameter at the https://app.asana.com/-/oauth_authorize page. More on this here. 380: Forbidden scopes despite full permissions 381: Example error: forbidden_scopes: Your app is not allowed to request user authorization for 'attachments:read' scopes. 382: Your app has Full permissions enabled in the developer console, but you are specifying individual scopes in the authorization URL. When Full permissions is enabled, you cannot request specific scopes. 383: If you would like to keep Full permissions: Remove the scope query parameter from your authorization URL, or use scope=default. 384: If you would like to use specific scopes: 385: Disable Full permissions in the developer console under OAuth > Permission scopes. 386: Select only the required scopes and save your changes. 387: Specify your chosen scopes in the scope query parameter at the authorization endpoint. Note that you may request a subset of your registered scopes. 388: Updated about 1 month ago 389: Personal access token 390: OAuth Code Samples / Libraries 391: Did this page help you? 392: Yes 393: No 394: Copy Page 395: Overview of the OAuth process 396: Register an application 397: User authorization endpoint 398: Request 399: OAuth scopes 400: Response 401: Token exchange endpoint 402: Request 403: Response 404: Token expiration 405: Token deauthorization endpoint 406: Request 407: Response 408: Token introspection endpoint 409: Request 410: Response 411: Security considerations 412: PKCE OAuth extension 413: Secure redirect endpoint 414: Troubleshooting 415: Forbidden scopes: Full permissions 416: Forbidden scopes despite full permissions
