90: Learn how to request a developer sandbox
91: Before moving forward with making sample API requests or building apps that leverage that Asana API, we recommend first getting an Asana developer sandbox. A developer sandbox is a temporary Asana domain with limited users.
92: Developer sandboxes are intended for:
93: Developers building or maintaining a third-party integration with Asana (i.e., submitting your completed integration to get listed in our app directory)
94: Existing Asana Starter customers or higher tiers who require a separate environment to perform risk-free testing on the API
95: Sandboxes can include Enterprise, Advanced, and Starter features upon request, and are valid for a maximum of one year. Extensions requested after one year will go through Legal review. Approval is not guaranteed, though you may be eligible to request a new sandbox.
96: To see the feature differences between the Asana plans, please visit our pricing page.
97: ➡ To request a developer sandbox, please complete and submit this form.
98: 📘
99: Processing time
100: Please note that at this time, it may take up to one (1) week to process and provision your developer sandbox.

89: Integrating with Asana's MCP Server
90: This guide walks you through connecting your MCP client to the official Asana MCP server. You'll create an OAuth app in the Asana developer console and use it to authenticate your MCP client.
91: Overview
92: The Asana V2 MCP server is generally available and uses OAuth for authorization. You'll pre-register your MCP app in the developer console, where you can create both standard API apps and MCP apps.
93: The same registration steps apply to Asana's Command MCP server. Each user needs a Command license. For client-specific setup, see Using Asana's Command MCP Server.
94: 🚧
95: V1 Beta Deprecation Notice
96: The V1 Beta MCP server https://mcp.asana.com/sse is deprecated and will shut down on Wed 5 Aug 2026.(extended from the previous date 11 May 2026). Learn more and get migration steps in this changelog post
97: Important: Tokens issued for MCP apps only work with the MCP server. This separation follows MCP security best practices—if a token is compromised, the blast radius is contained. If you need to make standard Asana API requests, create a separate API app and obtain tokens through the standard OAuth or PAT flow.
98: Create your OAuth app
99: Start by creating an OAuth app in the Asana developer console. This app will handle authentication for your MCP client.
100: Step 1: Create your app
101: Go to the developer console and sign in
102: Click "Create new app"
103: Enter your app name (e.g., "My MCP Client")
104: Select "MCP app" as the app type
105: Click "Create app"
106: You'll see your app's Client ID and Client secret. Keep these handy—you'll need them for authentication.
107: ❗️
108: Client secret
109: Your client secret is a secret, and it should never be shared with anyone or added into source code that others could gain access to. If you need to reset your client secret:
110: Select your app in the developer console
111: Navigate to the OAuth tab in the sidebar
112: Select Reset next to your client secret
113: Step 2: Configure OAuth settings
114: In the left sidebar, click "OAuth"
115: Add your Redirect URL—the callback URL where Asana will send authorization codes
116: Step 3: Configure workspace access
117: Configure which workspaces can use your app:
118: In the left sidebar, click "Manage distribution"
119: Under "Distribution method," choose one of the following:
120: Specific workspaces: Select individual workspaces where you want the MCP integration to be usable
121: Any workspace: Allow the app to be used in any workspace
122: If you selected "Specific workspaces," add the workspace(s) where you want to test
123: Click "Save changes"
124: Important: If you choose "Specific workspaces" but don't select any workspaces, users will see an error saying "This app is not available to your Asana workspace or organization." Make sure to select at least one workspace before testing.
125: Connect your MCP client
126: With your OAuth app created, you're ready to connect your MCP client to Asana.
127: Authorization flow
128: The MCP authorization flow follows the same process as our existing OAuth authorization flow, with one key difference: the optional resource parameter.
129: When directing users to the authorization endpoint, you can include the resource parameter to specify the MCP server:
130: https://app.asana.com/-/oauth_authorize
131: ?client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID
132: &redirect_uri=YOUR_REDIRECT_URL
133: &response_type=code
134: &resource=https://mcp.asana.com/v2
135: &state=RANDOM_STRING
136: &code_challenge={SHA256_CHALLENGE}
137: &code_challenge_method=S256
138: Parameters:
139: resource (optional): Use https://mcp.asana.com/v2 for the Asana MCP server, or https://mcp.asana.com/v2/command/mcp for the Command MCP server.
140: scope (optional): Use default or omit this parameter—MCP apps don't require specific scopes
141: All other OAuth parameters and steps remain the same as documented in our OAuth guide.
142: Use the token with MCP
143: Once you have an access token, configure your MCP client to use it with the server you want to connect to:
144: Asana MCP server: https://mcp.asana.com/v2/mcp
145: Command MCP server: https://mcp.asana.com/v2/command/mcp
146: Include the access token in the Authorization header of your MCP requests:
147: Authorization: Bearer YOUR_ACCESS_TOKEN
148: Refresh tokens
149: Access tokens expire after one hour. Use the refresh token to get a new access token without requiring the user to re-authorize. See our OAuth documentation for details on the refresh token flow.
150: Discovery endpoint
151: MCP provides an OAuth protected resource metadata document at:
152: https://mcp.asana.com/v2/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
153: For the Command MCP server, use:
154: https://mcp.asana.com/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/v2/command/mcp
155: This document:
156: Identifies the MCP server URL and supported bearer methods
157: Points to Asana's authorization server metadata at https://app.asana.com/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server
158: The authorization server metadata includes OAuth endpoints for authorization, token exchange, revocation, and supported grant types. Although these documents can be used to dynamically discover endpoints, clients must still pre-register to get a client id and client secret as described above. Dynamic client registration is not supported with Asana’s V2 MCP Server.
159: Available MCP tools
160: The Asana and Command MCP servers expose different tool sets.
161: To view all available tools and their current parameters, use the tools/list MCP command. This ensures your client always has the most up-to-date list of supported tools and their schemas.
162: 📘
163: Note
164: The tool set may evolve over time based on usage patterns and feedback. Tools may be added, updated, or deprecated. To ensure your client always has the most up-to-date list of supported tools and their schemas, use the tools/list MCP command and subscribe to our developer changelog for updates.
165: Security and permissions
166: Token security
167: Tokens issued for MCP apps only work with the Asana MCP server—you can't use them with the standard Asana API. Keep your tokens secure:
168: Store client secrets and all refresh/access tokens securely (never commit them to version control)
169: Use HTTPS for all requests
170: Implement proper token refresh logic
171: Revoke tokens when they're no longer needed
172: For additional security resources, see:
173: OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice
174: Prevent Attacks and Redirect Users with OAuth 2.0 State Parameters
175: Scopes / permissions
176: Asana MCP access is currently user-based. All actions taken over MCP will appear as the user who authorized them.
177: All authorizations may access any available MCP tool (at the time of authorization or any tools added in the future). Access is determined by the authenticated user's Asana permissions. The MCP token doesn't grant any permissions beyond what the user already has in Asana, they can only access workspaces, projects, and tasks they already have access to.
178: Common issues
179: "This app is not available to your workspace"
180: This happens when the users's workspace isn't added to your app's distribution settings. Fix it by:
181: Going to your app in the developer console
182: Navigating to "Manage distribution"
183: Selecting "Specific workspaces" and adding the workspace where you want to use the integration, or selecting "Any workspace" to enable it to be used in all workspaces
184: "Invalid scope(s) requested"
185: This error appears if you include a scope parameter in your authorization request. MCP apps don't require scopes—remove the scope parameter entirely from your authorization URL.
186: Authentication failures
187: If authentication fails:
188: Verify your redirect URL matches exactly in both your app settings and authorization request
189: Ensure your client ID and client secret are correct
190: Check that your app is properly configured in "Manage distribution"
191: Make sure you're using the correct authorization and token endpoints
192: Connection issues
193: If your MCP client can't connect:
194: Verify the MCP server URL is https://mcp.asana.com/v2/mcp for Asana or https://mcp.asana.com/v2/command/mcp for Command.
195: Check that you're including the access token in your requests
196: Verify the access token hasn't expired (they last one hour)

357: Required scope: tasks:read
358: Returns the compact task records for some filtered set of tasks. Use one or more of the parameters provided to filter the tasks returned. You must specify a project or tag if you do not specify assignee and workspace.
359: For more complex task retrieval, use workspaces/{workspace_gid}/tasks/search.
360: 📘
361: Customizing the response
362: Requests to this endpoint return "compact" task objects (schema) by default. To include more fields in the response, see input/output options.
363: Query Params
364: limit
365: integer
366: 1 to 100
367: Results per page.
368: The number of objects to return per page. The value must be between 1 and 100.
369: offset
370: string
371: Offset token.
372: An offset to the next page returned by the API. A pagination request will return an offset token, which can be used as an input parameter to the next request. If an offset is not passed in, the API will return the first page of results.
373: Note: You can only pass in an offset that was returned to you via a previously paginated request.
374: assignee
375: string
376: The assignee to filter tasks on. If searching for unassigned tasks, assignee.any = null can be specified.
377: Note: If you specify assignee, you must also specify the workspace to filter on.
378: project
379: string
380: The project to filter tasks on.
381: section
382: string
383: The section to filter tasks on.
384: workspace
385: string
386: The workspace to filter tasks on.
387: Note: If you specify workspace, you must also specify the assignee to filter on.
388: completed_since
389: date-time
390: Only return tasks that are either incomplete or that have been completed since this time.
391: modified_since
392: date-time
393: Only return tasks that have been modified since the given time.
394: Note: A task is considered “modified” if any of its properties
395: change, or associations between it and other objects are modified
396: (e.g. a task being added to a project). A task is not considered
397: modified just because another object it is associated with (e.g. a
398: subtask) is modified. Actions that count as modifying the task
399: include assigning, renaming, completing, and adding stories.
400: custom_type
401: string
402: Filter results by custom type. Provide a custom type GID to return only objects of that custom type (an unknown GID returns 400). Provide an empty string to return only objects with no custom type assigned. If this parameter is omitted, results are not filtered by custom type.
403: opt_fields
404: array of strings
405: This endpoint returns a resource which excludes some properties by default. To include those optional properties, set this query parameter to a comma-separated list of the properties you wish to include. Properties can include nested fields. To learn more, see the input/output options guide.
406: opt_fields
407: Show 117 enum values
408: ADD string
409: opt_pretty
410: boolean
411: Provides “pretty” output.
412: Provides the response in a “pretty” format. In the case of JSON this means doing proper line breaking and indentation to make it readable. This will take extra time and increase the response size so it is advisable only to use this during debugging.
413: truetruefalse

415: 200
416: Successfully retrieved requested tasks.
417: 400
418: This usually occurs because of a missing or malformed parameter. Check the documentation and the syntax of your request and try again.
419: 401
420: A valid authentication token was not provided with the request, so the API could not associate a user with the request.
421: 403
422: The authentication and request syntax was valid but the server is refusing to complete the request. This can happen if you try to read or write to objects or properties that the user does not have access to.
423: 404
424: Either the request method and path supplied do not specify a known action in the API, or the object specified by the request does not exist.
425: 500
426: There was a problem on Asana’s end. In the event of a server error the response body should contain an error phrase. These phrases can be used by Asana support to quickly look up the incident that caused the server error. Some errors are due to server load, and will not supply an error phrase.

151: GraphQL overview
152: The monday.com API is built with GraphQL, a flexible query language that allows you to return as much or as little data as you need. It's important to know that GraphQL is an application layer that parses the query you send it and returns (or changes) data accordingly.
153: Unlike REST APIs, where multiple endpoints return different data, GraphQL always exposes one endpoint and allows you to determine the structure of the returned data. Our API uses the following endpoint: https://api.monday.com/v2.
154: This document will walk through the GraphQL operations and object types to help you understand the essential components of a request. We will also discuss the GraphQL visual interface that enables you to test your queries and mutations, and finally, we cover where you can access the monday.com schema. Let's get started!
155: 👍
156: Pro tip
157: Check out this introduction to GraphQL to understand what all you can do with GraphQL!
158: Operations
159: There are two possible operations in GraphQL: queries and mutations.
160: Query
161: Queries perform the READ operation and do not change or alter any data. The result of each query will be formatted in the same way as the query itself. The following example retrieves the ID, title, and type of each column on board 1234567890.
162: Sample query
163: GraphQL
164: query {
165: boards {
166: columns {
167: id
168: title
169: type
170: }
171: }
172: }
173: Sample response
174: JSON
175: {
176: "columns": [
177: {
178: "id": "name",
179: "title": "Name",
180: "type": "name"
181: },
182: {
183: "id": "subitems",
184: "title": "Subitems",
185: "type": "subtasks"
186: },
187: {
188: "id": "person",
189: "title": "Person",
190: "type": "people"
191: },
192: {
193: "id": "status",
194: "title": "Status",
195: "type": "status"
196: }
197: ]
198: }
199: Mutation
200: Mutations are special queries that perform the CUD (Create, Update, Delete) operations to modify your data. Mutations return an instance of the object you just modified, so you can query the data you changed. The following example creates a new item on board 1234567890 and returns the ID and name of the new item.
201: Sample mutation
202: GraphQL
203: mutation{
204: create_item (board_id: 1234567890, item_name: "New Item"){
205: id
206: name
207: }
208: }
209: Sample response
210: JSON
211: {
212: "data": {
213: "create_item": {
214: "id": "9876543210",
215: "name": "New Item"
216: }
217: },
218: "account_id": 12345678
219: }
220: Multiple operations in one request
221: You can also send multiple queries in one request, and they will be executed one after the other. The following query returns the ID and name for boards 1234567890 and 9876543210. The mutation creates a new item and retrieves the item's ID and name on both boards 1234567890 and 9876543210.
222: Sample query
223: GraphQL
224: query {
225: checkBoard1: boards (ids:1234567890) {
226: id
227: name
228: }
229: checkBoard2: boards (ids:9876543210) {
230: id
231: name
232: }
233: }
234: Sample response
235: JSON
236: {
237: "data": {
238: "checkBoard1": [
239: {
240: "id": "1234567890",
241: "name": "Test Board 1"
242: }
243: ],
244: "checkBoard2": [
245: {
246: "id": "9876543210",
247: "name": "Test Board 2"
248: }
249: ]
250: },
251: "account_id": 12345678
252: }
253: Sample mutation
254: GraphQL
255: mutation{
256: createItem1: create_item (board_id: 1234567890, item_name:"Test Item 1") {
257: id
258: name
259: }
260: createItem2: create_item(board_id: 9876543210, item_name:"Test Item 2") {
261: id
262: name
263: }
264: }
265: Sample response
266: JSON
267: {
268: "data": {
269: "createItem1": {
270: "id": "11223344",
271: "name": "Test Item 1"
272: },
273: "createItem2": {
274: "id": "44332211",
275: "name": "Test Item 2"
276: }
277: },
278: "account_id": 12345678
279: }
280: Object Types
281: Object types are a collection of fields used to describe the set of possible data you can query using the API. They can also have arguments on the fields to pass parameters when querying data.
282: Fields
283: Fields specify properties or attributes of objects to help define what information to retrieve from a query. Every object in the schema contains fields that can be queried by name to retrieve specific properties of the object.
284: Take the boards object, for example. You can query these fields to return specific information about your board(s). The following example returns the boards' ID and name and the ID, title, and type of each column on the boards.
285: GraphQL
286: query {
287: boards {
288: id
289: name
290: columns {
291: id
292: title
293: type
294: }
295: }
296: }
297: Arguments
298: You can pass arguments in a query to specify what data to return (i.e., filter the search results) and narrow down the results to only the specific ones you’re after.
299: Building on the boards example above, you can also use these arguments to reduce the number of results returned in your query. The following example returns the ID and name only for boards 1234567890 and 9876543210 and the ID, title, and type of each column on those boards.
300: GraphQL
301: query {
302: boards (ids: [1234567890, 9876543210]) {
303: id
304: name
305: columns {
306: id
307: title
308: type
309: }
310: }
311: }
312: Variables
313: You can use variables to pass dynamic values to your arguments. They are written outside of the query string itself in the variables section and passed to the arguments.
314: When we start working with variables, we need to do three things:
315: Replace the static value in the query with $variableName
316: Declare $variableName as one of the variables accepted by the query
317: Pass variableName: value in the separate, transport-specific (usually JSON) variables dictionary
318: GraphQL
319: mutation change_column_value($value: JSON!) {
320: change_column_value (board_id: 157244624,item_id: 9539475, column_id: "status", value: $value) {
321: id
322: }
323: }
324: query variables:
325: {
326: "value": "{\"index\": 1}"
327: }
328: monday.com schema
329: Our GraphQL schema defines the structure of the available API data and contains all of the available queries and mutations. It is a valuable resource for verifying API responses and extracting useful information from the metadata.
330: We expose our schema here. By default, it is in introspection JSON format for the Current API version. You can request a different version using the optional version=<API-Version> parameter with the version name.
331: For example: https://api.monday.com/v2/get_schema?version=2024-04
332: You can also retrieve the schema definition language (SDL) version using the optional format=sdl parameter.
333: For example: https://api.monday.com/v2/get_schema?format=sdl
334: 📘
335: Join our developer community!
336: We've created a community specifically for our devs where you can search through previous topics to find solutions, ask new questions, hear about new features and updates, and learn tips and tricks from other devs. Come join in on the fun! 😎

151: Authentication
152: Learn about monday platform API token permissions, how to access tokens, and how to authenticate requests
153: The monday.com platform API utilizes personal V2 API tokens to authenticate requests and identify the user making the call. These tokens are unique to each user and have no explicit length.
154: Personal tokens allow you to interact with the API using your own user account. Their permissions mirror what you can do in the monday.com UI, ensuring that API access is consistent with your platform-level permissions.
155: If you don't have a monday.com account yet, create a free developer account to get an API token and start testing.
156: Token permissions
157: Personal tokens mirror all permission levels set in the monday.com UI, including board, column, item, or account access.
158: For example: If you don't have permission to access a certain workspace via the UI, you won't have permission using your personal API token either.
159: App tokens have an additional set of permission scopes that specify which queries and mutations it can access, while personal tokens have all permission scopes.
160: Accessing your token
161: You can access your API token in two ways, depending on your user type.
162: In the Developer Center (all users)
163: All users with API access can follow these steps to access their API token:
164: In your monday.com account, click on your profile picture in the top right corner.
165: Select Developers. This will open the Developer Center in another tab.
166: Click API token > Show.
167: Copy your personal token.
168: In the Administration tab (account admins only)
169: Account admins can use the Developer Center steps above or access their token via the Administration tab:
170: In your monday.com account, click on your profile picture in the top right corner.
171: Select Administration > Connections > Personal API token.
172: Copy your personal token.
173: Making requests with your token
174: Once you have your token, you can make requests with the API by passing the token in the Authorization header.
175: cURL
176: curl -X POST https://api.monday.com/v2 \
177: -H "Authorization: xxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxxx" \
178: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
179: -d '{"query": "query { me { id name } }"}'
180: Regenerating a token

151: Developer Sandbox Account
152: Sign up for a free monday.com developer account to build and test apps and API integrations in a sandbox separate from your production data.
153: A developer account (also called a sandbox account) is a free monday.com account designed for building and testing monday apps and API integrations. It runs in an environment separate from your production or work data, so you can experiment without affecting live workflows.
154: You can use any monday.com account to explore the apps framework and API. A developer account is the recommended option when you need higher limits and Pro/Enterprise capabilities for thorough testing.
155: Sign up for a developer account
156: Create a free developer account and start building right away:
157: Sign up for a free developer account
158: After sign-up, open the Developer Center from your profile menu (Developers) to manage apps, API tokens, and usage.
159: Other account options
160: OptionWhen to use it
161: Existing monday.com accountYou already have an account and only need light testing.
162: Trial accountYou want to evaluate monday.com beyond development. Sign up for a trial.
163: Trial extensionYour trial is ending but you need more time. Contact support to request an extension.
164: What's included
165: Developer accounts include everything in the Free plan, plus higher limits and advanced capabilities tailored for app development. They also include select Pro and Enterprise features commonly needed for building and testing apps.
166: FeatureLimit
167: monday.com productsAccess to all products (Work Management, CRM, Service, Dev, and more)
168: SeatsUp to 10
169: ItemsUp to 1,000 items per product
170: Boards, dashboards, and workdocsUnlimited
171: Automations25,000 actions/month
172: Integrations25,000 actions/month
173: API complexity10M
174: PermissionsAccount-, column-, and item-level permissions
175: Column typesAccess to all column types
176: BoardsPrivate and shareable boards
177: ViewsItem and board views
178: Activity logTracking and filtering
179: TemplatesIncluded
180: ThemeHacker theme
181: 📘
182: Existing developer accounts were upgraded automatically with full product access and higher limits. See the developer account upgrades changelog for details.
183: Account terms and intended use
184: Developer accounts are for development and testing only. They are not intended for running production business workflows or serving end customers.
185: Keep these guidelines in mind:
186: Separate from production data — Use your developer account to build and test apps and API integrations without touching live account data.
187: Invite teammates for realistic testing — You can add up to 10 users to simulate collaboration, permissions, and multi-user app flows.
188: Respect account limits — Item, automation, integration, and API complexity limits apply. Plan load tests and large-scale scenarios accordingly.
189: Request more capacity when needed — If your app requires limits beyond the defaults, submit a request (see below). The team reviews requests within five business days.
190: Request additional testing capacity
191: If your app needs higher limits—for example, more items, automation actions, or API complexity—submit a request through the marketplace partner extensions form. The monday.com team reviews requests within five business days.

175: OAuth and Permissions
176: Authenticating monday apps with OAuth2 and defining permission scopes.
177: OAuth 2.0 is a protocol that lets your app request authorization to read or modify data in a user's monday account. At the end of the OAuth process, your app gets an access token that belongs to the user and grants access to specified permission scopes.
178: You can set up OAuth for your app in just two steps: configuring your app and going through the standard OAuth flow.
179: 🚧
180: A new OAuth 2.1 flow is available
181: monday.com now supports an improved OAuth 2.1 flow with expiring access tokens, refresh tokens, and token revocation. This page describes the current (legacy) flow. If you are building a new integration or want to upgrade your existing app, see Migrating to the new OAuth 2.1 flow.
182: Configure your scopes and redirect URLs
183: To start, you must first configure your app's scopes and redirect URLs. If you don't have an app, follow these steps to create an app in the monday UI and locate your client_id and client_secret.
184: Once your app has been created, set the scopes and redirect URLs in the OAuth tab in the Developer Center.
185: Permission scopes
186: OAuth scopes define what your app can and cannot do. Each endpoint in the monday API requires a certain permission scope, which can be found in our API reference.
187: When you ask a monday user to grant access to your app, you have to specify which of the following supported scopes you're requesting access to:
188: ScopeDescription
189: account:readRead general information about the account
190: assets:readRead data from assets the user has access to
191: boards:readRead a user's board data
192: boards:writeModify a user's board data
193: departments:readRead the account's department data
194: departments:writeModify the account's departments
195: docs:readRead a user's docs
196: docs:writeModify a user's docs
197: me:readRead a user's profile information
198: notifications:writeSend notifications on behalf of the user
199: tags:readRead the account's tags
200: teams:readRead information about the account's teams
201: teams:writeModify the account's teams
202: updates:readRead updates and replies the user can see
203: updates:writePost or edit updates on behalf of the user
204: users:readRead profile information of the account's users
205: users:writeModify profile information of the account's users
206: webhooks:readRead existing webhooks configuration
207: webhooks:writeCreate and modify webhooks
208: workspaces:readRead a user's workspaces data
209: workspaces:writeModify a user's workspaces data
210: Redirect URLs
211: After a monday user approves or denies your app’s authorization request, they will be redirected back to your app's specified redirect_uri. You can use multiple URLs if you want to route users to different pages based on their context.
212: The OAuth flow
213: Once you've created and configured your monday app, you're ready to go through the standard OAuth flow. A successful OAuth authorization between your app, the user, and the monday OAuth server occurs in the following order:
214: Make an authorization request and redirect the user to the monday OAuth URL with the client ID: https://auth.monday.com/oauth2/authorize
215: The user sees the permission scopes your app is requesting and approves the request.
216: The user is redirected to a defined URL (redirect URL) with a temporary authorization code in the query params after approval.
217: Your app's backend sends a POST to the token request endpoint with this code. The token endpoint will respond with an access token. The access token gives your app access to the monday API on behalf of the user and will be valid until the user uninstalls your app.
218: Authorization request
219: The first step in the OAuth flow is making an authorization request and redirecting a user to the monday OAuth page. The OAuth request URL is: https://auth.monday.com/oauth2/authorize.
220: Example: GET https:/auth.monday.com/oauth2/authorize?client_id=1111
221: ParameterDescriptionDefault valueRequired
222: client_idYour app's identifier. Located in the Basic Information tab.Yes
223: redirect_uriURL to redirect back on approval/denial. Must match one of the redirect URLs added to your app.If you've only configured one redirect_uri, it will be used.Yes, if more than one redirect_uri is configured
224: scopeA space-separated list of OAuth scopes indicating the permissions your app is requesting. All requested scopes must match the list you configured in your app.The full scope list configured in your appNo
225: stateAn arbitrary value that will be passed to your app on approval or denial. Use a unique state parameter to avoid forgery attacks and check the value at every step of the OAuth flow.No
226: app_version_idThe app version's unique identifier. Enables app collaborators to go through the OAuth flow for the requested app version (live or draft). You can get it from your app's URL, after app_versions. This will not work for deprecated versions and non-app collaborators.The live version's callback URL defined in the Developer Center. If there is no live version, the latest version created on the app will be used.No
227: force_install_if_neededEnables a seamless OAuth flow by automatically redirecting users to the app installation page if the app is not installed. Once an admin installs the app, they are redirected back to the OAuth page to complete the authentication process.No
228: Redirect
229: After the user grants permission to your app in step 2, they will be redirected to your app using the provided redirect_uri as part of step 3. We will add the authorization code, scope, and state to query parameters:
230: ParameterDescription
231: codeThe generated authorization code. Valid for 10 minutes.
232: stateThe state parameter supplied in the previous step.
233: Token request and response
234: Once you have obtained an authorization code from the authorization endpoint, you can exchange it for an access token to make calls to monday’s API. The authorization code is only valid for 10 minutes, after which you will have to make another request to get another code.
235: Request structure
236: The HTTP verb in your request should be POST, and the token URL is https://auth.monday.com/oauth2/token.
237: ParameterDescription
238: client_idYour app's unique identifier. Located in the Basic Information tab.
239: client_secretYour app's secret. Located in the Basic Information tab.
240: redirect_uriThis parameter is used for validation only - there is no redirection. The value must match the value supplied in the Authorization Request step.
241: codeThe authorization code from the previous step.
242: Response structure
243: On success, the response contains the status 200 OK in the header and the following JSON data in the body:
244: KeyDescription
245: access_tokenThe access token used to make API calls. Tokens do not expire and are valid until the user uninstalls your app. Our OAuth flow does not support refresh tokens.
246: token_typeAll monday OAuth tokens are bearer tokens.
247: scopeA comma-separated list of scopes that have been granted for this access token.
248: The JSON body of the response will look like the following:
249: JSON
250: {
251: "access_token": "NgeFeX...FEmEka",
252: "token_type": "Bearer",
253: "scope": "boards:write boards:read"
254: }
255: OAuth flow for users with multiple accounts
256: Some monday.com users will be part of multiple accounts, so your app may want to specify which account to authorize the user for. In the standard OAuth flow, the user can select the monday.com account where they'd like to authorize using a dropdown menu.
257: If you want to ensure the user authorizes a specific account, you can change the Authorization URL based on their account URL.
258: There are two methods to do this using the account slug: constructing the URL or adding a query parameter.
259: Constructing the URL
260: This method involves constructing the URL with the slug/subdomain of the account, or the first part of the URL that comes before .monday.com. Users can still change the account using the dropdown, but the slug you specify will be the default. You can easily access an account's slug by querying the account through monday API.
261: Let's say we queried the account and the slug is awesomeapp. The OAuth flow URL would look like this:
262: https://awesomeapp.monday.com/oauth2/authorize?client_id=<CLIENT_ID>&redirect_uri=<YOUR_URL>
263: Adding a query parameter
264: Instead of constructing the URL, you can add the subdomain=<ACCOUNT_SLUG> query parameter to the URL to create the link using their account slug. Unlike the previous option, users can't change the account using the dropdown since they are forced to use this specific slug.
265: Using the example above, the URL would look like this:
266: https://auth.monday.com/oauth2/authorize?client_id=<CLIENT_ID>&redirect_uri=<YOUR_URL>&subdomain=awesomeapp
267: Error codes
268: On an error of any kind, the user will be redirected back to the specified redirect_uri. The possible errors you can get are:
269: Error codeDescription
270: 400invalid_request
271: 403unauthorized_client
272: 403access_denied
273: 403invalid_scope
274: 500server_error
275: 500temporary_unavailable
276: 📘
277: Join our developer community!
278: We've created a community specifically for our devs where you can search through previous topics to find solutions, ask new questions, hear about new features and updates, and learn tips and tricks from other devs. Come join in on the fun! 😎

151: Authenticate with an API token
152: Connect to the monday.com hosted MCP server with a personal API token for personal use, prototyping, and testing
153: If you're using one of the compatible MCP clients, you don't need a token — add the server URL and authenticate via OAuth when prompted. Use a personal API token when your client isn't a compatible MCP client or doesn't support the MCP OAuth flow — for example, custom scripts, homegrown agents, or tools that only support static Bearer tokens.
154: For personal use, prototyping, and testing, this is the fastest way to connect. No app or registration is needed.
155: Get your token
156: Log in to your monday.com account
157: Click your profile picture in the top-right corner and select Developers
158: Click My access tokens in the left menu
159: Copy your personal access token
160: Configure your MCP client
161: Pass the token as a Bearer token in the Authorization header of your MCP requests:
162: Authorization: Bearer YOUR_API_TOKEN
163: For MCP clients that support custom headers, the configuration looks like this:
164: JSON
165: {
166: "mcpServers": {
167: "monday-mcp": {
168: "url": "https://mcp.monday.com/mcp",
169: "headers": {
170: "Authorization": "Bearer YOUR_API_TOKEN"
171: }
172: }
173: }
174: }
175: Personal tokens mirror your UI permissions, so the MCP server can access everything your user can — and nothing more. This is ideal for individual development, but not for integrations used by other people.
176: ⚠️
177: Warning
178: Never share your API token or commit it to version control. Rotate tokens regularly, and revoke them when they're no longer needed.

109: 2 min read
110: monday MCP is the hosted server that gives AI tools secure access to your monday.com workspace. It connects your account directly to AI assistants like Claude, Cursor, and Copilot Studio through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard for AI integrations.
111: Prerequisites
112: An active monday.com account with appropriate permissions
113: MCP is preinstalled on all monday.com accounts.
114: If you can't connect, ask your admin to check Admin → Permissions → AI Connectors. See Managing AI Connectors & MCP Access for more information.
115: Supported AI client
116: OAuth consent for monday MCP when prompted by your client
117: What can you do with monday MCP?
118: Project reporting – generate sprint summaries, team performance reports, and deadline tracking from your boards (including monday dev sprints)
119: Smart task management – convert meeting notes into structured items, assign tasks, and update statuses through natural language
120: Cross-team visibility – ask for rollups like “What’s blocking the launch?” across Product, Marketing, and RevOps boards
121: Operational workflows – create and triage incidents, support requests, and ops checklists (with clear owners, priority, and due dates)
122: CRM workflows – create leads and deals, update pipeline stages, and log next steps from call notes
123: Docs + knowledge workflows – create specs, SOPs, and retros as monday docs (in a workspace or attached to an item)
124: Dashboards & insights – build dashboards and widgets, and answer questions using board insights (such as status distribution, workload, and throughput)
125: Workspace discovery – quickly find the right board, doc, form, or folder, even in large workspaces
126: Key use cases
127: Quick data retrieval – ask for board status, find items, or summarize what changed this week
128: Task creation and cleanup – turn a meeting transcript into tasks with owners, priority, and due dates
129: Updating existing work – update status, people, or date fields when plans change, with human review before applying changes
130: Cross-board analysis – ask questions like “What’s overdue across all launch boards?” or “Which team has the most blockers?”
131: Executive reporting – create weekly rollups such as shipped vs. planned, scope changes, and risk summaries
132: Support and Service operations – intake requests, link relevant context, and keep stakeholders updated through item updates
133: Documentation workflows – generate a spec in monday docs and attach it to the relevant initiative item
134: Automation-style chains – run multi-step flows like “Create a bug, assign it, set severity, and notify the team in an update”
135: Note: Other tools that support the Model Context Protocol should also be compatible, though individual setup steps may vary
136: Available tools
137: Please check out the Available tools article for a full list.
138: FAQs
139: Pricing and availability
140: Is MCP included in my monday.com plan?
141: Yes. MCP is available on all monday.com plans at no additional cost.
142: Are there usage limits?
143: Standard API limits apply.
144: Security and privacy
145: What permissions does MCP have?
146: Each user individually authorizes MCP via OAuth. MCP only has access to the data that you, as an individual user, can access in monday.com. The specific permissions depend on the OAuth scopes you grant during setup.
147: Is my data secure?
148: Yes. MCP uses industry-standard OAuth for authentication and TLS encryption for all data transfers. MCP respects your monday.com permissions, meaning you can only access or modify data you’re authorized to change. Because MCP can perform actions on your behalf, we recommend reviewing AI-suggested changes before confirming actions that modify your workspace.
149: Who can see my data?
150: Only you and your AI assistant can see the data exchanged through MCP. monday.com does not review or access the content of your conversations.
151: If you have any questions, please reach out to our team right here. We’re available 24/7 and happy to help.

56: Authenticate to the ClickUp API using a personal token or OAuth.
57: Authentication
58: To use the ClickUp API, you must authenticate every request.
59: For personal use, authenticate with your personal API token.
60: For apps or integrations that other people use, use the OAuth flow, allowing users to authorize Workspaces for your app.
61: Include the token in the Authorization header of your requests.
62: Both methods ensure that you and your users only have access to the information permitted by ClickUp.
63: 👍
64: View the OAuth endpoints.
65: Personal Token
66: Use a personal API token for individual or testing purposes. Personal tokens begin with pk_.
67: Add the token to the header: Authorization: {personal_token}. This is also needed to use the Try-It feature in the API docs.
68: Generate or regenerate a Personal API Token
69: Log in to ClickUp.
70: In the upper-right corner, click your avatar.
71: Select Settings.
72: In the sidebar, click Apps. Or click here to go directly to your settings.
73: Under API Token, click Generate or Regenerate.
74: 👀
75: Note
76: You'll need to sign in to your ClickUp account in order to generate or regenerate a token.
77: Click Copy to copy the personal token to your clipboard. Personal tokens never expire.
78: Build Apps for others - OAuth Flow
79: To allow others to use your app, implement the OAuth2 flow so each user has their own token for accessing their ClickUp resources.
80: OAuth resources and specs:
81: Authentication: OAuth 2.0
82: Grant Type: Authorization Code. Learn more.
83: Authorization URL: https://app.clickup.com/api
84: Access Token URL: https://api.clickup.com/api/v2/oauth/token
85: 👀
86: Note
87: ClickUp uses the authorization code grant type.
88: Use your personal API key to use the Try-It feature in the API docs.
89: Step 1: Create an OAuth app
90: Only Workspace owners or admins can create OAuth apps.
91: Log in to ClickUp.
92: In the upper-right corner, click your avatar.
93: Select Settings.
94: In the sidebar, click Apps.
95: Click Create new app.
96: Name the app and add a redirect URL.
97: You'll receive a client_id and secret.
98: Step 2: Retrieve an Authorization Code
99: Send users to this URL to connect their ClickUp account:
100: https://app.clickup.com/api?client_id={client_id}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}
101: You can also add a state parameter:
102: https://app.clickup.com/api?client_id={client_id}&redirect_uri={redirect_uri}&state={state}
103: 👀
104: Note
105: Non-SSL redirect URIs may not be supported in the future.
106: Users will be redirected back to the redirect_uri with the authorization code after logging in.
107: Select Workspaces
108: Users can authorize one or more Workspaces. Use the Get Authorized Teams (Workspaces) endpoint to see which Workspaces are authorized. Redirect users to the authorization URL to modify Workspace permissions.
109: Step 3: Request a Token
110: Use the Get Access Token endpoint with client_id, client_secret, and code to get the access token. This token is used in the Authorization: Bearer {access_token} header for all API requests made on behalf of the user.
111: The access token currently does not expire. This is subject to change.
112: Learn more about OAuth:

114: OAuth Simplified
115: Digital Ocean Intro to OAuth 2.0

56: Use these supported tools with ClickUp's MCP Server.
57: The ClickUp MCP exposes many of the capabilities available in our API. The real magic happens when your AI assistant combines several tools to complete a larger request.
58: Note: Your AI assistant will only be able to perform actions in ClickUp that you have permission to do.
59: Search
60: ToolDefinitionExample usage (for an AI assistant)
61: Search WorkspaceSearches for items across the entire ClickUp Workspace, including tasks, Docs, dashboards, attachments, whiteboards, Chats, and forms."Find all tasks related to the 'Q4 Marketing Launch'."
62: Search tasks by tagRetrieves tasks filtered by tags."Show me the tasks with the 'UX-quality' tag."
63: Task management
64: ToolDefinitionExample usage (for an AI assistant)
65: Create TaskCreates a new task in a specific List. You can specify details like the task name, description, assignees, due date, and priority."Create a task to 'Draft blog post' in the 'Content Pipeline' List, assign it to me, and set the due date for this Friday."
66: Get TaskRetrieves the full details of a single task using its unique task ID."What are the details for task 'Design-123'?"
67: Update TaskModifies the properties of an existing task. This can include changing the task's name, description, status, assignees, or due date."Change the status of task 'Draft blog post' to 'In Progress' and add 'Review' as a subtask."
68: Set Custom FieldsSet Custom Fields on tasks.
69: Note: Your AI assistant understands the Custom Fields, options, and supported values that are available on tasks."Set the 'release number' to '4.07'."
70: Get Custom FieldsRetrieves the Custom Fields available on a List, Folder, Space, or Workspace."What Custom Fields does the 'Bugs' List have?"
71: Delete taskDeletes a task or subtask.
72: Note: Your AI assistant may confirm the correct task is selected before deleting the task."Delete the "testing use only" task."
73: Merge tasksMerges one or more tasks into a target task, combining their comments, attachments, subtasks, and tracked time."Merge the duplicate 'Login bug' tasks into the original one."
74: Manage tasks in bulk
75: Bulk actions run through the Execute Operator tool (see Generic operations).
76: ToolDefinitionExample usage (for an AI assistant)
77: Create tasks in bulk (clickup_execute_operator, task.create_many)Creates multiple tasks in a specified List with a single call."Add these items as new tasks in the 'Onboarding' List: 'Send welcome email', 'Schedule orientation', and 'Set up hardware'."
78: Update tasks in bulk (clickup_execute_operator, task.update_many)Applies the same change to multiple tasks at once. This is useful for changing the status, assignee, or due date for a group of tasks simultaneously."Move all tasks in the 'Sprint 3' List with the 'Ready for Review' status to 'In Review'."
79: Task attachments
80: ToolDefinitionExample usage (for an AI assistant)
81: Attach File to TaskUploads and attaches a file (like a document, image, or ZIP file) to a specific task."Attach this document [file_upload] to the 'Submit Final Report' task."
82: Request Attachment UploadGets a short-lived upload link for adding a large file (up to 1 GB) to a task or Chat."Upload this recording to the 'Customer Interview' task."
83: Download Task AttachmentRetrieves a file attached to a task."Open the spec PDF attached to task 'Design-123'."
84: Task comments
85: ToolDefinitionExample usage (for an AI assistant)
86: Get Task CommentsRetrieves all comments from a specific task."What's the latest update on the 'Develop new feature' task?"
87: Get Threaded RepliesRetrieves threaded replies under a parent task comment."Summarize this comment thread and tell me my action items."
88: Create Task CommentAdds a new comment to a task. This can be used to ask questions, provide updates, or @mention other team members."Add a comment to task 'Design-123' saying: '@Mark, can you please provide the latest mockups?'"
89: Create CommentAdds a comment to a task, List, or view, or replies to an existing comment."Reply to Mark's comment and say the mockups are attached."
90: Update CommentEdits, resolves, or reassigns an existing comment."Resolve my comment on the 'Design-123' task."
91: Delete CommentDeletes a comment."Delete my last comment on the 'Design-123' task."
92: Task tags
93: ToolDefinitionExample usage (for an AI assistant)
94: Create Space TagCreates a new tag that every task in a Space can use."Create an 'Urgent' tag in the 'Engineering' Space."
95: Add Tag to TaskApplies an existing tag (label) to a task for categorization."Add the 'Urgent' tag to task 'Fix login bug'."
96: Remove Tag from TaskRemoves a specific tag from a task."Remove the 'Backend' tag from task 'Update button color'."
97: Task relationships
98: ToolDefinitionExample usage (for an AI assistant)
99: Add task linkRelate two tasks by linking them."Link feature 123 with design for feature 123."
100: Remove task linkRemove links between tasks."Remove the link between feature 123 and scope designs for feature 123."
101: Add dependencyCreate a dependency relationship between tasks."This task is blocked by its subtask called 'support Google authentication'."
102: Remove dependencyRemove a dependency relationship between tasks."Remove the dependency between feature 123 and support Google authentication."
103: Move and add tasks to other Lists
104: ToolDefinitionExample usage (for an AI assistant)
105: Move task to a new ListMove a task to a new home List."Move the feature 123 task from the Backlog List to 'Sprint 3'."
106: Add task to another ListAdd a task to another List."Add the feature 123 task to 'Sprint 3'."
107: Remove task from a ListRemove a task from an additional List. The task stays in its home List."Take the feature 123 task out of 'Sprint 3'."
108: Time tracking
109: ToolDefinitionExample usage (for an AI assistant)
110: Get Task Time EntriesRetrieves all time log entries for a specific task."How much time has been logged for the 'Client Research' task?"
111: Get time entries for multiple tasksRetrieves time entries and totals across tasks, filtered by date range, assignee, or billable status."How much time did I log last week?"
112: Start Time TrackingStarts a timer for a specific task for the current user."Start tracking time for the 'Code Review' task."
113: Stop Time TrackingStops the currently active timer for the user."Stop the timer."
114: Add Time EntryManually adds a block of time (a time entry) to a task, including a start and end time or a duration."Log 2 hours of work on the 'Database optimization' task for yesterday."
115: Get Current Time EntryChecks if the user has a timer currently running and, if so, returns the details of that time entry."What am I currently tracking time for?"
116: Workspace Hierarchy
117: ToolDefinitionExample usage (for an AI assistant)
118: Get Workspace HierarchyRetrieves the full structure of the Workspace, including all Spaces, Folders, and Lists."Show me all the Lists in the 'Engineering' Space."
119: Create ListCreates a new List within a specific Space. To create a List inside a Folder, use Create List in Folder."Create a new List named 'Sprint 4 Planning' in the 'Product' Space."
120: Create List in FolderCreates a new List specifically inside a designated Folder."Inside the 'Marketing Campaigns' Folder, create a new List called 'Social Media Content'."
121: Get ListRetrieves the details and settings for a single List."What are the custom statuses for the 'Bugs' List?"
122: Update ListModifies the settings of an existing List, such as changing its name, description, or status."Rename the 'New Ideas' List to 'Approved Ideas'."
123: Get FolderRetrieves the details for a single Folder, such as its ID, name, and the Space it belongs to."Which Space is the 'Client Projects' Folder in?"
124: Create FolderCreates a new Folder within a specific Space."Create a new Folder named 'Q1 Projects' in the 'Operations' Space."
125: Update FolderModifies the settings of an existing Folder, such as changing its name."Rename the 'Design' Folder to 'Design Team'."
126: Members and assignees
127: ToolDefinitionExample usage (for an AI assistant)
128: Get Workspace MembersRetrieves a list of all members and guests in the Workspace."Who are all the members of this Workspace?"
129: Find Member by NameSearches for a Workspace member using their name or email."What is David Smith's user ID?"

131: Get UserRetrieves the signed-in user, their timezone, and the current time."What time is it for me right now?"
132: Chat
133: ToolDefinitionExample usage (for an AI assistant)
134: Get Chat ChannelsRetrieves a list of all Chat channels (views) in the Workspace."List all available Chat channels."
135: Send Chat MessageSends a message to a specific Chat channel."Post a message in the 'General' channel: 'Team lunch at 1 PM today.'"
136: Get Channel MessagesRetrieves recent messages from a Chat channel."What did I miss in the 'General' channel today?"
137: Get Message RepliesRetrieves the replies in a message thread."Summarize the replies to the launch announcement."

141: ToolDefinitionExample usage (for an AI assistant)
142: Create DocumentCreates a new Doc within the Workspace, usually in a specific location (like a Space or Folder) or in the private Docs area."Create a new document named 'Project Kickoff Notes' in the 'Project Phoenix' Space."
143: List Document PagesRetrieves the structure or table of contents of a Doc, listing all its pages."What are the pages in the 'Employee Handbook' Doc?"
144: Get Document PagesRetrieves the content of one or more pages from a specific Doc."Show me the content of the 'Onboarding' page from the 'Team Wiki' Doc."
145: Create Document PageAdds a new page (or sub-page) to an existing Doc."Add a new page titled 'Security Protocols' to the 'Company Policies' Doc."
146: Update Document PageEdits the content of an existing page within a Doc."On the 'Security Protocols' page, add a new section for 'Password Management'."
147: List Page AttachmentsLists the files attached to a Doc page."What files are attached to the 'Onboarding' page?"
148: Download Page AttachmentRetrieves a file attached to a Doc page."Open the org chart attached to the 'Onboarding' page."

164: To connect a client and sign in, see MCP Server Setup Instructions. Tool names below are the exact names your MCP client sees.
165: Every tool acts as the signed-in user, with that user's ClickUp permissions, exactly as in the app. The server adds no access of its own. In ChatGPT Team, Enterprise and Edu workspaces, only owners and admins can configure MCP servers. Every tool also accepts an optional workspace_id (required when the user belongs to more than one workspace; if it's missing, the server lists the choices).
166: Columns: Type is Read or Write. Sensitive marks tools that delete or irreversibly overwrite data, post content as the user, or move files. Side effects covers what changes in ClickUp and who is notified.

250: Generic operations (Unified API)
251: ToolTypeSensitiveInputsReturnsSide effects / permissions
252: clickup_get_operatorsReadNoOptional filterAllowed operations and their inputsNone
253: clickup_get_schemaReadNoOptional filterHow ClickUp objects relateNone
254: clickup_execute_operatorWriteYesmodel, operator. Optional: parameters, body, queryThe operation's resultRuns one allowed operation as the user. Don't retry a timeout; the operation may have completed.
255: Allowed operations: Tasks: read many by ID, create many (task.create_many), update many (task.update_many, one shared change applied to every named task), archive, unarchive. Lists and statuses: update a List; read statuses of a List, Space or Folder; add, rename or remove a Space's statuses. Custom fields: create, list. Views: create, update, read, list. Forms: create, update, read, list. None of these delete anything; archive is reversible. Bulk update and archive must name task IDs.
256: Status handling
257: Success: a normal result. Writes return success: true plus the IDs of what changed.
258: Failure: a result with isError: true and a JSON body {"error": "..."} (see Errors).
259: No pending states: every tool completes in a single request; there is nothing to poll.
260: Paging: pass next_cursor back as cursor. Cursor-paged read tools also return has_more.
261: Partial results: some writes return warnings naming parts of the request that weren't applied (e.g. an unresolvable watcher) while the rest succeeded.
262: Task statuses: statuses are defined per List. Use clickup_get_list or clickup_get_task (with expand_statuses) to find a List's valid statuses before setting one.
263: Errors
264: ErrorMeaningRetry?
265: HTTP 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer ... error="invalid_token"Sign-in missing or invalidSign in again
266: HTTP 400x-workspace-id header isn't a numberFix the header
267: HTTP 429 with Retry-After: 60Too many requests to the serverWait, then retry
268: JSON-RPC -32602 Unknown tool: <name>Tool doesn't exist or is switched offNo
269: Tool result isError: true, {"error":"Failed to <action>: <reason>"}The operation failedSee below
270: Tool result errorCode: RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED, retryAfter: <seconds>Daily or per-plan limit reachedRetry after retryAfter seconds
271: Bad input, permission or "not found" errors: don't retry; change the request.
272: "Request timed out" or "ClickUp server error" on a read: safe to retry.
273: Same errors on a write: check whether it happened first. Creates, sends, comments and time entries make a second copy if repeated.
274: Rate limits
275: Server: 1,000 requests per minute per connection.
276: File uploads: 20 per 15 minutes per user, up to 1 GB per file.
277: Daily MCP call limits by plan: see ClickUp's MCP Server.

218: https://api.clickup.com/api/v2/list/{list_id}/task
219: View the tasks in a List. Responses are limited to 100 tasks per page. You can only view task information of tasks you can access.
220: This endpoint only includes tasks where the specified list_id is their home List. Tasks added to the list_id with a different home List are not included in the response by default. To include tasks that exist in multiple lists, use the include_timl parameter.
221: The time_spent field displays time tracked in milliseconds, and is only included in the response for tasks with time entries.
222: Each task's custom_fields array only includes Custom Fields applicable to that task's custom_item_id.

92: Superhuman Docs API (1.7.0)
93: Developer Support: care@superhuman.com URL: https://superhuman.com/developers License: Superhuman Developer Terms Terms of Service
94: Introduction
95: The Superhuman Docs API is a RESTful API that lets you programmatically interact with data in Superhuman Docs (formerly Coda):
96: List and search documents
97: Create new docs and copy existing ones
98: Share and publish docs
99: Discover pages, tables, formulas, and controls
100: Read, insert, upsert, update, and delete rows
101: If you plan to integrate Superhuman Docs with an AI tool, you may also want to consider using the
102: Superhuman Docs MCP server. It's optimized for LLM usage
103: patterns and often exposes more granular methods for accessing and modifying data.
104: Getting Started
105: Our Getting Started Guide helps you learn the
106: basic of working with the API and shows a few ways you can use it. Check it out, and learn how to:
107: Read data from tables and write back to them
108: Build a one-way sync from one document to another
109: Automate reminders
110: Sync your Google Calendar to Superhuman Docs
111: Changes to the API
112: As we update and release newer versions of the API, we reserve the right to remove
113: older APIs and functionality with a 3-month deprecation notice. We will post about such changes as well as announce
114: new features in the Developers Central section of our Community,
115: and update the API updates doc.
116: Using the API
117: The Superhuman Docs REST API is designed to be straightforward to use. You can use the language and platform of your choice to
118: make requests. To get a feel for the API, you can also use a tool like Postman or
119: Insomnia.
120: API Endpoint
121: This API uses a base path of https://coda.io/apis/v1.
122: Resource IDs and Links
123: Each resource instance retrieved via the API has the following fields:
124: id: The resource's immutable ID, which can be used to refer to it within its context
125: type: The type of resource, useful for identifying it in a heterogenous collection of results
126: href: A fully qualified URI that can be used to refer to and get the latest details on the resource
127: Most resources can be queried by their name or ID. We recommend sticking with IDs where possible, as names are
128: fragile and prone to being changed by your doc's users.
129: List Endpoints
130: Endpoints supporting listing of resources have the following fields:
131: items: An array containing the listed resources, limited by the limit or pageToken query parameters
132: nextPageLink: If more results are available, an API link to the next page of results
133: nextPageToken: If more results are available, a page token that can be passed into the pageToken query parameter
134: The maximum page size may change at any time, and may be different for different endpoints. Please do not rely on it
135: for any behavior of your application. If you pass a limit parameter that is larger than our maximum allowed limit,
136: we will only return as many results as our maximum limit. You should look for the presence of the nextPageToken on the
137: response to see if there are more results available, rather than relying on a result set that matches your provided limit.
138: To fetch a subsequent page of results, pass the pageToken parameter. Set this parameter to the value given to you as the nextPageToken
139: in a page response. If no value is provided, there are no more results available. You only need to pass the pageToken to get
140: the next page of results, you don't need to pass any of the parameters from your original request, as they are all
141: implied by the pageToken. Any other parameters provided alongside a pageToken will be ignored.
142: Doc IDs
143: While most object IDs will have to be discovered via the API, you may find yourself frequently wanting to get the
144: ID of a specific document.
145: Here's a handy tool that will extract it for you. (See if you can find the pattern!)
146: Doc ID Extractor
147: Your doc ID is:
148: Rate Limiting
149: The Superhuman Docs API sets a reasonable limit on the number of requests that can be made per minute. Once this limit is
150: reached, calls to the API will start returning errors with an HTTP status code of 429.
151: These are the current rate limits. They are subject to change at any time without notice. For robustness,
152: all API scripts should check for HTTP 429 Too Many Requests errors and back off and retry the request.
153: Limits apply per-user across all endpoints that share the same limit and across all docs.
154: Reading data (with the exceptions below): 100 requests per 6 seconds
155: Writing data (POST/PUT/PATCH): 10 requests per 6 seconds
156: Writing doc content data (POST/PUT/PATCH): 5 requests per 10 seconds
157: Listing docs: 4 requests per 6 seconds
158: Reading analytics: 100 requests per 6 seconds
159: Consistency
160: While edits made in Superhuman Docs are shared with other collaborators in real-time, it can take a few seconds for them to
161: become available via the API. You may also notice that changes made via the API, such as updating a row, are not
162: immediate. These endpoints all return an HTTP 202 status code, instead of a standard 200, indicating that the
163: edit has been accepted and queued for processing. This generally takes a few seconds, and the edit may fail if
164: invalid. Each such edit will return a requestId in the response, and you can pass this requestId to the
165: #getMutationStatus endpoint to find out if it has been applied.
166: Similarly, when you get doc data from the API (rows, pages, columns, etc), the data you receive comes from
167: the most recent "snapshot" of the doc, which might be slightly stale relative to the data you observe in
168: your browser. If you want to ensure that the data you receive is up to date and are ok getting an error if not,
169: you can pass this header in your request: X-Coda-Doc-Version: latest. If the API's view of the doc is
170: not up to date, the API will return an HTTP 400 response.
171: Volatile Formulas
172: Superhuman Docs exposes a number of "volatile" formulas, as as Today(), Now(), and User(). When used in a live
173: document, these formulas affect what's visible in realtime, tailored to the current user.
174: Such formulas behave differently with the API. Time-based values may only be current to the last edit made to the
175: doc. User-based values may be blank or invalid.
176: Free and Paid Workspaces
177: We make the Superhuman Docs API available to all of our users free of charge, in both free and paid workspaces. However, API
178: usage is subject to the role of the user associated with the API token in the workspace applicable to each API
179: request. What this means is:
180: For the #createDoc endpoint specifically, the owner of the API token must be a Doc
181: Maker (or Admin) in the workspace. If the "Any member can create docs" option in enabled in the workspace
182: settings, they can be an Editor and will get auto-promoted to Doc Maker upon using this endpoint. Lastly, if in
183: addition, the API key owner matches the "Auto-join email domains" setting, they will be auto-added to the
184: workspace and promoted to Doc Maker upon using this endpoint
185: This behavior applies to the API as well as any integrations that may use it, such as Zapier.
186: Examples
187: To help you get started, this documentation provides code examples in Python, Unix shell, and Google Apps Script.
188: Python examples
189: These examples use Python 3.6+. If you don't already have the requests module, use pip or easy_install to
190: get it.
191: Shell examples
192: The shell examples are intended to be run in a Unix shell. If you're on Windows, you will need to install
193: WSL.
194: These examples use the standard cURL utility to pull from the API, and then process it with jq to extract and
195: format example output. If you don't already have it, you can either install it
196: or run the command without it to see the raw JSON output.
197: Google Apps Script examples
198: Google Apps Script makes it easy to write code in a JavaScript-like syntax and
199: easily access many Google products with built-in libraries. You can set up your scripts to run periodically,
200: which makes it a good environment for writing tools without maintaining your own server.
201: Superhuman Docs provides a library for Google Apps Script. To use it, go into Resources -> Libraries... and enter the
202: following library ID: 15IQuWOk8MqT50FDWomh57UqWGH23gjsWVWYFms3ton6L-UHmefYHS9Vl. If you want to see the
203: library's source code, it's available
204: here.
205: Google provides autocomplete for API functions as well as generated docs. You can access these docs via the
206: Libraries dialog by clicking on the library name. Required parameters that would be included in the URL path are
207: positional arguments in each of these functions, followed by the request body, if applicable. All remaining
208: parameters can be specified in the options object.
209: OpenAPI/Swagger Spec
210: In an effort to standardize our API and make it accessible, we offer an OpenAPI 3.0 specification:
211: OpenAPI 3.0 spec - YAML
212: OpenAPI 3.0 spec - JSON
213: Postman collection
214: To get started with prototyping the API quickly in Postman, you can use one of links above to import the Superhuman Docs API
215: into a collection. You'll then need to set the appropriate header and environment
216: variables.
217: Client libraries
218: We do not currently support client libraries apart from Google Apps Script. To work with the Superhuman Docs API, you can
219: either use standard network libraries for your language, or use the appropriate Swagger Generator tool to
220: auto-generate Superhuman Docs API client libraries for your language of choice. We do not provide any guarantees that these
221: autogenerated libraries are compatible with our API (e.g., some libraries may not work with Bearer
222: authentication).
223: OpenAPI 3.0
224: Swagger Generator 3 (that link takes you to the docs for the generator API) can
225: generate client libraries for these languages. It's relatively new
226: and thus only has support for a limited set of languages at this time.
227: Third-party client libraries
228: Some members of our amazing community have written libraries to work with our API. These aren't officially
229: supported by Superhuman, but are listed here for convenience. (Please let us know if you've written a library and would
230: like to have it included here.)
231: PHP by Daniel Stieber
232: Node-RED by Mori Sugimoto
233: NodeJS by Parker McMullin
234: Ruby by Carlos Muñoz at Getro
235: Python by Mikhail Beliansky
236: Go by Artur Safin

3611: Rows
3612: You'll likely use this part of the API the most. These endpoints let you retrieve row data from tables in Superhuman Docs as well as create, upsert, update, and delete them. Most of these endpoints work for both base tables and views, but for inserting/upsering rows, you must use a base table.
3613: List table rows
3614: Returns a list of rows in a table.
3615: Value results
3616: The valueFormat parameter dictates in what format the API should return values for individual cells.
3617: simple (default): Returns cell values as the following JSON values: string, number, or boolean. Array values (like multiselects) are returned as comma-delimited strings.
3618: simpleWithArrays: Singleton values are returned as simple. Array values are returned as JSON arrays and the values within are simple values (including nested arrays).
3619: rich: If applicable, returns many values with further encoding, allowing API users to have lossless access to data in Superhuman Docs.
3620: For text values, returns data in Markdown syntax. If the text field is simple text (e.g. has no formatting),
3621: the field will be fully escaped with triple-ticks. E.g
3622: `
3623: This is plain text
3624: `
3625: For currency, lookup, image, person and hyperlink values, the value will be encoded in JSON-LD format.
3626: // Currency
3627: {
3628: "@context": "http://schema.org",
3629: "@type": "MonetaryAmount",
3630: "currency": "USD",
3631: "amount": 42.42
3632: }

65: The Smartsheet API enables you to programmatically access and manage your organization's Smartsheet resources. The API Reference includes object schemas, operation specifications, and code snippets for Sheets, Folders, Users, and more.
66: Required plan: Business, Enterprise, or Advanced Work Management
67: Developer Agreement: The Developer Agreement governs the use of the Smartsheet API and Smartsheet software development kits (SDKs)
68: 🚀 What's new!
69: Smartsheet MCP server: Connect Smartsheet to AI clients like Claude, Cursor, and Codex, and use 30+ tools to manage your sheets, rows, columns, and more through natural-language prompts. Get the details here.
70: Report CRUD endpoints: Manage the entire lifecycle of a report with the new endpoints. Explore creating a row report here.
71: Asset path endpoints: Get locations of sheets, reports, dashboards, and folders, for context and to explore related assets. Learn more here.
72: Try the API
73: You can call operations from within the site via our Try it request editor.
74: It's just that easy to start using the API!
75: Go to the Get started article (next) for a quickstart video and guidance on making your first API call.
76: Base URL
77: Smartsheet: https://api.smartsheet.com/2.0
78: Important: Smartsheet Gov and Smartsheet Regions Europe use the respective base URLs:
79: Smartsheet Gov: https://api.smartsheetgov.com/2.0
80: Smartsheet Regions Europe: https://api.smartsheet.eu/2.0
81: Smartsheet Regions Australia: https://api.smartsheet.au/2.0
82: Client SDKs
83: Smartsheet provides client libraries that make it easy to call the API from your preferred language. The SDKs handle authentication, request formatting, and response parsing so you can focus on building your integration. You'll find SDK code examples alongside REST snippets throughout the API documentation.

99: The API authenticates using access tokens (API keys). You can generate access tokens in the Smartsheet UI.
100: Important: Smartsheet Gov and Smartsheet Regions Europe use separate tokens from Smartsheet.com.
101: Each API request requires passing in an access token as the Bearer value in your authorization header. For example,
102: Authorization: Bearer JKlMNOpQ12RStUVwxYZAbcde3F5g6hijklM789
103: This article provides best practices to consider when working with the Smartsheet API and any access tokens (API keys), or other sensitive information.
104: Authentication Approaches
105: When choosing an authentication method, it is important to consider your integration scenario. Is the integration machine-to-machine without user interaction, or do you want user consent and interaction?
106: If your scenario involves user consent and interaction, it's typically best to use OAuth with Smartsheet. Note that the Smartsheet implementation of OAuth 2.0 is a 3-legged process, which requires human intervention. See OAuth Walkthrough for details.
107: If your scenario is strictly machine-to-machine, execute raw token requests over HTTPS. It's a straightforward, secure way to authenticate. See Access Token Best Practices for details.
108: Each scenario requires an HTTP authorization header containing an access token.
109: Note: In applications and for routine requests, it is best to use a shared account, such as ticket-processor@example.com, rather than your individual work account.
110: Warning: If an unauthorized user gets a copy of this token, they will be able to access all Smartsheet data that you have access to, both to read and modify on your behalf. You should keep your tokens secure and do not share them with anyone.
111: Access Token Best Practices
112: You can generate access tokens in the Smartsheet UI.
113: Never commit access tokens (API keys) to accessible version control systems like GitHub or BitBucket. Instead, use one of the following recommended storage options.
114: Recommended Storage Options
115: Use an app configuration tool suitable for deploying secrets to your app, or
116: Use a config file outside of source control, or
117: Use environment variables set outside of source control.
118: If you have mistakenly deployed API keys to a publicly accessible location such as GitHub, then you should immediately revoke those API keys, revise your application to use a preferred method of key deployment, and then generate new keys.
119: Storing in a database
120: If you need to store API keys in a database, consider the following protections:
121: Restrict access so API keys are only readable by the owner of the object
122: Restrict read privileges to the database table
123: Make sure your database or the disk the database is on is set to encrypt data at rest
124: Note: When using any Smartsheet SDK, you can use the environment variable of SMARTSHEET_ACCESS_TOKEN. If the access token is null on input to the client builder, the SDK will automatically pick up the value of that environment variable.
125: Revoking and Regenerating Tokens
126: If you've committed code to a repository before implementing these security best practices, here are some steps to secure your API keys.
127: For requests with raw tokens:
128: Revoke the token
129: Create a new token
130: For OAuth with Smartsheet: Work through the OAuth Walkthrough to regenerate client secrets, auth codes, and tokens.
