89: OAuth 2.0 (OAuth) provides a way for your app users to grant limited access to their Smartsheet resources. Here, we demonstrate registering apps to use OAuth and implementing an OAuth flow with your apps.
90: Note: The Smartsheet SDKs also support OAuth 2.0.
91: Register for Developer Tools
92: Developer Tools is a Smartsheet user interface for registering client applications that use OAuth to access Smartsheet user resources with the user's consent. Here's how to register for Developer Tools.
93: Designate a Smartsheet account for using OAuth with your apps.
94: Tip: A best practice is to use an additional Smartsheet account (a service account) that you don't personally use in the Smartsheet application.
95: Go to the Developer Tools Registration page.
96: In the Developer Tools Registration page, enter the email address of a user account to associate with your apps.
97: Read the Smartsheet Developer Agreement. If you agree and are ready to register your user, click Register User Account.
98: A developer tools registration confirmation message appears.
99: Upon accepting your request, Smartsheet activates the Developer Tools user interface for the user account.
100: Note: If Smartsheet denies your request, consult with your Customer Success Manager.
101: Create your developer profile
102: A developer profile is a prerequisite for registering apps. Here's how to create one:
103: In the Smartsheet application, select your Account icon in the lower-left corner
104: and then select Developer Tools.... The Developer Tools window appears.
105: Click Create Developer Profile. The Developer Profile form appears.
106: In the Developer Profile form, name your profile. Optionally, you can also enter a website URL and an email address to associate with your profile.
107: Save your profile.
108: Now, you have a developer profile with which to register apps that use OAuth.
109: Register an app
110: Here's how you register an app to access Smartsheet via OAuth.
111: Go to the Developer Tools, if you're not already there.
112: Click Create New App. The Create New App form appears.
113: In the Create New App form, enter the following information:
114: App name: A name to identify your app to the user
115: App description: A brief description of your app
116: App URL: The URL that launches your app, or the landing page if not a web app
117: App contact/support: Support information
118: App redirect URL: Also known as a callback URL. The URL within your application that receives OAuth 2.0 credentials.
119: Publish App?: If selected, Smartsheet makes your app's profile page publicly available for anyone to learn more about your applications.
120: Note: When you save the app registration, Smartsheet generates a profile page for it. You can access the App profile page URL if you view the app details in Developer Tools.
121: Logo: An image to associate with your app.
122: Click Save to register your app. A window appears, confirming your newly created app registration and the App client ID and App secret.
123: Note: You'll use the client ID and secret in the OAuth flow steps. You can note them now or look them up again in the Developer Tools pages.
124: You're ready to implement an OAuth flow for your newly registered app.
125: Implement an OAuth flow for your app
126: Your app must implement an OAuth flow to retrieve an access token it can use to access Smartsheet data on behalf of an end user. Here,
127: The following diagram provides an overview of the OAuth flow:
128: Note: OAuth flow require HTTPS.
129: Access scopes
130: Access scopes specify the types of resources your app needs to access and the types of actions to perform on those resources. Your app will present these access scopes to the user and request the user's consent to operate on the applicable resources on the user's behalf.
131: You must determine the access scopes your app needs.
132: Note: Access scopes don't override existing access-level restrictions (that is, sharing permissions).
133: For example, having the access scope of WRITE_SHEETS doesn't allow your app to update a sheet on which the user has only VIEWER access level permissions.
134: Here are the access scopes:
135: Access ScopeDescription
136: ADMIN_SHEETSModify sheet structure, including column definition, publish state, and more.
137: ADMIN_SIGHTSModify Sight/dashboard structure.
138: ADMIN_USERSAdd and remove users from your Smartsheet organization account; create groups and manage seat types.
139: ADMIN_WEBHOOKSCreate, delete, and update webhooks; get all webhooks; reset shared secrets.
140: ADMIN_WORKSPACESCreate and manage workspaces and folders, and their shares.
141: CREATE_SHEETSCreate new sheets.
142: CREATE_SIGHTSCreate new Sights/dashboards.
143: DELETE_SHEETSDelete sheets.
144: DELETE_SIGHTSDelete Sights/dashboards.
145: READ_CONTACTSRetrieve contacts.
146: READ_EVENTSRetrieve events.
147: READ_SHEETSRead all sheet data, including attachments, discussions, and cell data.
148: READ_SIGHTSRead all Sight/dashboard data.
149: READ_USERSRetrieve users and groups for your Smartsheet organization account.
150: SHARE_SHEETSShare sheets, including sending sheets as attachments.
151: SHARE_SIGHTSShare Sights/dashboards.
152: WRITE_SHEETSInsert and modify sheet data, including attachments, discussions, and cell data.
153: You'll specify the access scopes in an authorization request (covered next).
154: Important: Your authorization code request must specify all the access scopes your app needs.
155: You must request at least one access scope for your app, but should only request necessary ones.
156: Note: Regardless of the access scopes you specify, your app will be able to call the Get current user operation using a valid access token that you obtain using the authorization code you request next.
157: Request an authorization code
158: In your app, you must send a request for an authorization code by redirecting the end user's browser to Smartsheet's authorization endpoint. You can do this by executing the following operation.
159: Operation:
160: GET https://app.smartsheet.com/b/authorize
161: Here are the operation parameters:
162: ParameterDescription
163: client_idRequired. The client ID you obtained when you registered your app.
164: response_typeRequired. Indicates whether the endpoint returns an authorization code. Set this to "code".
165: scopeRequired. Space-delimited list of access scopes to which you are asking the user to grant access.
166: For example, in scope=READ_SHEETS%20WRITE_SHEETS.
167: Important: %20 is the URL encoding for a space character between the two access scopes.
168: Note: If you simply need to validate that the user has a Smartsheet account, you don't need to specify the scope query parameter in your request.
169: stateOptional. An arbitrary string of your choosing that is returned to your app; a successful round-trip of this string helps ensure that your app initiated the request.
170: For example,
171: https://app.smartsheet.com/b/authorize?response_type=code&client_id=dheu3dmkd32fhxme&scope=READ_SHEETS%20WRITE_SHEETS&state=MY_STATE
172: Smartsheet generates the consent page based on a combination of the information you registered for your app and the parameters you send with the authorization request.
173: Note: If the user isn't signed in to Smartsheet, the redirect first takes the user to a sign in page. After the user signs in, Smartsheet displays the consent page.
174: At this point, the user can allow or deny your app access their Smartsheet account.
175: If the user clicks Allow
176: If the user clicks Allow, Smartsheet redirects the user's browser to your redirect URL and includes the following parameters:
177: ParametersDescription
178: codeAuthorization code required to obtain access token. For example, sample6p9qisx6a.
179: expires_inNumber of milliseconds the code remains valid once issued; this is currently 599135 milliseconds, or approximately 10 minutes--you must obtain an access token within that time.
180: stateThe same value for state that you sent when you requested the authorization code. Your app can verify that the state value matches what you sent to the user when you requested the authorization code.
181: Note: The state value helps you determine that the response came from the user and not a malicious script. If the values don't match, you should reject the response.
182: For error conditions, see the list of OAuth Error Types.
183: If you want to start making requests on behalf of the user, you can skip ahead to get an access token. Otherwise, read on to learn what happens if the user denies authorization.
184: If the user clicks Deny
185: If the user clicks Deny, Smartsheet redirects the user's browser to the redirect URL with the following parameters:
186: AttributeDescription
187: error"access_denied"
188: stateThe same value for state that you sent when you requested the authorization code.
189: Get an access token to call the API
190: When the user grants you authorization, you can exchange the authorization code that you received in the callback URL for an access token.
191: Important: The authorization code expires after 599135 milliseconds.
192: You can request an access token by calling POST /token with grant_type=authorization_code".
193: Here's an example of an unencrypted request:
194: curl https://api.smartsheet.com/2.0/token \
195: -d 'grant_type=authorization_code&code=YOUR_AUTHORIZATION_CODE&client_id=YOUR_CLIENT_ID&client_secret=YOUR_CLIENT_SECRET' \
196: -X POST
197: ParameterDescription
198: grant_type"authorization_code" declares that you're requesting an access token via the authorization code flow.
199: codeYOUR_AUTHORIZATION_CODE is a placeholder for the authorization code you received in the callback URL.
200: client_idYOUR_CLIENT_ID is a placeholder for your app's client ID.
201: client_secretYOUR_CLIENT_SECRET is a placeholder for your app's client secret.
202: Important: Instead of submitting the code and client_secret parameters in plain text, you can encrypt them in the hash parameter. See the POST /token reference page for details.
203: If the access code is valid, the operation responds with an access_token value that you can use to access resources on behalf of the user.
204: Otherwise, if the code has expired, the operation returns a 401 code.
205: Note: Access tokens expire after 604799 seconds, which is approximately 7 days.
206: If the access token expired, you can call POST /token with grant_type=refresh_token" to get a new access token and refresh token.
207: Make API calls
208: Here's a typical workflow for using the access tokens in API calls:
209: Acquire an access and refresh token pair through the OAuth flow (POST /token + grant_type=authorization_code).
210: Execute requests to the API using the access token.
211: In time, the access token expires and API requests fail with authorization errors.
212: Acquire a NEW access and refresh token pair via the refresh token (POST /token + grant_type=refresh_token + refresh_token=YOUR_REFRESH_TOKEN, replacing YOUR_REFRESH_TOKEN with the refresh token received in step 1).
213: Go back to step 2.
214: You're operating on the Smartsheet resources on behalf of the user.
215: Note: For operation details, see the POST /token reference page.
216: OAuth error types
217: For reference, here are some OAuth-related error types:
218: ValueDescription
219: invalid_clientThe client information is invalid. Ensure your client id is correct.
220: invalid_grantThe authorization code or refresh token is invalid or expired or the hash value does not match the app secret and/or code.
221: invalid_requestThe request parameters are invalid or missing.
222: invalid_scopeOne or more of the requested access scopes is invalid. Please check the list of access scopes.
223: unsupported_grant_typegrant_type must equal authorization_code or refresh_token.
224: unsupported_response_typeresponse_type must be set to code.

31: The Smartsheet Model Context Protocol (MCP) server provides a way to leverage Smartsheet’s public API via AI clients, allowing you to interact with your data using natural language. The MCP server's underlying tools (operations) interact with your Smartsheet data (with your permission) to respond to your prompts. The following sections describe the key tools available to your AI client once connected to the Smartsheet MCP server.
32: Required plan: Business, Enterprise, or Advanced Work Management
33: To execute any tool, your AI client requires specific OAuth access scopes. Each tool lists its Access scopes below its name.
34: For starters, explore the discovery and navigation tools.
35: Tokens are the basic units that AI language models use to process text. They're chunks of text that can be individual words, parts of words, or even punctuation marks. Both your input and the AI's responses are measured in tokens. This matters because:
36: Models have maximum token limits (context windows)
37: Processing speed decreases with increasing token count
38: The tools are subject to Smartsheet API rate limiting and standard limitations.
39: Discovery and navigation
40: search
41: Access scopes: READ_SHEETS
42: The search tool is a discovery tool that lets you search across all accessible Smartsheet assets to find resources by name or content.
43: This tool is particularly useful as a starting point when you need to find an asset ID before using other Smartsheet tools like browse_workspace, browse_folder, or get_sheet_summary.
44: Basic Parameters
45: query (required): The search term to look for. Use specific terms like "Q4 Budget" for better results. You can use double-quotes for exact matches (e.g., "Q4 Budget 2024").
46: scopes (optional): Narrow your search to specific asset types. Available scopes include:
47: sheetNames — Search in sheet names
48: reportNames — Search in report names
49: sightNames — Search in dashboard names
50: folderNames — Search in folder names
51: workspaceNames — Search in workspace names
52: cellData — Search within cell contents
53: comments — Search in comments
54: attachments — Search in file attachments
55: summaryFields — Search in summary fields
56: templateNames — Search in template names
57: modified_since (optional): Filter results by modification date using ISO 8601 timestamp format to find resources changed after a specific date.
58: Key Features
59: Fuzzy Matching: Supports approximate matching, so you don't need exact names.
60: Results Context: Returns asset names, types, parent folder/workspace context, match excerpts, and favorite indicators.
61: Maximum Results: Returns up to 100 results (no pagination available).
62: Wide Coverage: Can search across sheets, reports, dashboards, folders, workspaces, and more in one call.
63: Limitations
64: Eventually consistent (new items may take a few minutes to appear in search results).
65: First-time API users may experience a 24-hour data provisioning delay.
66: Returns maximum 100 results with no pagination options.
67: Use Cases
68: Discover assets: Find sheets, reports, or dashboards when you don't know exact IDs or locations.
69: Locate by content: Search for specific text within sheets or comments.
70: Browse by modification date: Find recently updated assets.
71: Find attachments: Locate files attached to sheets or discussions.
72: Workspaces and folders
73: browse_workspace
74: Access scopes: READ_SHEETS
75: The browse_workspace tool lets you explore all the contents of a workspace, discovering the top-level sheets, reports, dashboards, and folders it contains. Here's the breakdown:
76: Basic Parameters
77: workspace_id (required): The ID of the workspace to browse. Obtain this from list_workspaces or the search tool.
78: asset_types (optional): Filter results by specific resource types:
79: folders — Nested folders
80: sheets — Individual sheets
81: reports — Reports
82: sights — Dashboards
83: templates - Templates
84: If not specified, returns all asset types.
85: max_item (optional): Control page size (1–1000 items per page; defaults to 100).
86: last_key (optional): Token for pagination. Use the last_key from a previous response to fetch the next page of results.
87: Key Features
88: Top-Level Only: Returns direct children of the workspace (not recursively nested contents within folders).
89: Token-Based Pagination: Supports pagination via last_key for workspaces with more than 100 items.
90: Server-Side Filtering: Filter by asset type during the request, not after retrieving results.
91: Asset Information: Returns names, IDs, types, creation/modification dates, and favorite status for each asset.
92: Limitations
93: Returns only top-level workspace contents (doesn't drill into nested folder structures).
94: Maximum 1000 items per page.
95: Requires a valid workspace ID.
96: Use Cases
97: Discover workspace structure: See all sheets, reports, and dashboards at the workspace root level.
98: Find assets by type: List only sheets or only dashboards in a workspace.
99: Navigate hierarchically: Get folder IDs to use with browse_folder for deeper exploration.
100: Inventory assets: Audit what's in a workspace without searching.
101: browse_folder
102: Access scopes: READ_SHEETS
103: The browse_folder tool navigates and explores the contents of a specific folder within Smartsheet. It retrieves all direct children of a folder—including nested folders, sheets, reports, and dashboards—making it essential for hierarchical folder navigation. This tool helps users discover and access assets organized within folder structures without needing to know exact resource IDs in advance.
104: Basic Parameters
105: folder_id - The unique identifier of the folder to browse (positive integer; obtain from search results, browse_workspace results, or parent folder responses).
106: asset_types - (Optional) Filter results by resource type; acceptable values are "folders", "sheets", "reports", "sights" (dashboards) or "templates". Pass as an array to filter for multiple types, or omit to return all asset types.
107: last_key - (Optional) Pagination token from a previous response used to fetch the next page of results; leave empty for the first page.
108: max_item - (Optional) Number of items to return per page, ranging from 1 to 1000; defaults to 100.
109: Key Features
110: Hierarchical Navigation - Returns only direct children of the specified folder, allowing step-by-step exploration of nested folder structures.
111: Asset Type Filtering - Efficiently narrow results to specific resource types (folders, sheets, reports, dashboards) to surface only the resources you need.
112: Pagination Support - Handles large folder contents through token-based pagination; use the last_key parameter to retrieve subsequent pages when more than 100 items exist.
113: Complete Asset Details - Provides metadata for each child resource, including IDs, names, permalinks, and ownership information needed for downstream operations.
114: Limitations
115: Returns only direct children, not a recursive tree of all nested contents.
116: Maximum of 1000 items returned per page; folders with more than 100 children require pagination.
117: Does not include folder content counts or summary statistics for performance reasons.
118: Use Cases
119: Folder Content Exploration - Browse the contents of a folder to discover sheets, reports, dashboards, and subfolders without knowing their exact IDs.
120: Asset Filtering - Filter results to show only sheets or only reports within a folder for focused navigation.
121: Hierarchical Traversal - Use folder_id values returned from browse_folder results to navigate deeper into nested folder structures.
122: Pagination Through Large Folders - Systematically retrieve all contents of folders with more than 100 items using token-based pagination.
123: Asset Inventory - Build a complete map of folder structure and contents for administrative or archival purposes.
124: list_workspaces
125: Access scopes: READ_SHEETS
126: Retrieves a list of workspaces from Smartsheet with pagination support. This tool is essential for discovering and managing all workspaces within a Smartsheet account, allowing you to browse the organization's workspace structure without nested content exploration.
127: Best Practices
128: Use pagination parameters (last_key and max_item) when working with large numbers of workspaces to avoid overwhelming API responses.
129: Store workspace IDs after retrieval for use in subsequent operations like creating sheets, folders, or browsing workspace contents.
130: Cache workspace lists locally if you perform frequent lookups to reduce API calls.

310: The find_in_sheet tool searches for text within a specific Smartsheet sheet. It returns matching cells with row and column IDs, display values, and character offsets for each match. It supports case-sensitive search, column-scoped filtering, formula-based filtering, sorting, and pagination.
311: Best Practices
312: Restrict the search to specific columns using the columns parameter when you know where the target data lives, to improve performance and reduce noise.
313: Use the filter parameter with a formula (for example, =OR([Status]@row = "Active")) to pre-filter rows before the search term is applied, narrowing results to relevant data.
314: Use pagination (limit and offset) when working with large sheets to manage result set size.

317: request.term — The search term to look for, between 1 and 250 characters.
318: request.caseSensitive — Boolean flag indicating whether the search is case-sensitive. It defaults to false.
319: request.columns — An optional array of column IDs that restricts the search to only those columns.
320: request.filter — An optional formula string (must begin with =) applied to filter rows before searching.
321: request.sort — An optional array of up to three sort criteria, each specifying a column name and sort direction (ASC or DESC).

328: Case sensitivity control — Toggles case-sensitive matching on or off to suit the precision requirements of the search.
329: Multi-column sorting — Sorts the result set by up to three columns, each with an independent direction.
330: Pagination support — Supports high-volume result sets with configurable page size (up to 20,000 results) and offset-based paging.

335: create_sheet
336: The create_sheet tool creates a new sheet within a specified Smartsheet folder or workspace.
337: The tool supports two creation modes:
338: Building a blank sheet from scratch with fully custom column definitions
339: Instantiating a sheet from an existing template
340: The create_sheet tool serves as the primary entry point for adding new structured data grids to an organization's Smartsheet environment.
341: Access scopes: CREATE_SHEETS
342: Best Practices
343: The following items are best practices for using the create_sheet tool:
344: Always designate exactly one column as the primary column (using primary: true) when creating a blank sheet, and ensure that column is of type TEXT_NUMBER.
345: When creating from a template, use the include parameter to selectively copy only the elements you need (such as data, attachments, or rules) to avoid unnecessary duplication.
346: Verify the target container ID and type before calling this tool, using the browse_folder or browse_workspace tool to confirm the destination exists and that you have edit permissions on it.
347: Choose column types carefully at creation time, as restructuring columns after rows have been added is more disruptive.
348: Basic Parameters
349: The create_sheet tool has the following parameters:
350: container_id — The integer ID of the folder or workspace in which to create the sheet.
351: container_type — The type of container, either FOLDER or WORKSPACE.
352: sheet — The sheet definition object. Pass a CreateSheet object (with a name and columns array) for a blank sheet, or a CreateSheetFromTemplate object (with a name and fromId) when creating from a template.
353: include — An optional list of elements to copy from the template when using CreateSheetFromTemplate. Valid values are attachments, cellLinks, data, discussions, filters, forms, ruleRecipients, and rules. This parameter is ignored when creating a blank sheet.
354: Key Features
355: The create_sheet tool has the following key features:
356: Blank sheet creation — Accepts a fully custom column schema, allowing you to define column titles, types, options, formulas, formatting, and system column types (such as AUTO_NUMBER, CREATED_DATE, or MODIFIED_BY) at creation time.
357: Template-based creation — Creates a new sheet pre-populated with the structure (and optionally the content) of any accessible template by referencing its ID via fromId.
358: Selective template element copying — When creating from a template, the include parameter lets you choose exactly which elements (data, attachments, discussions, filters, forms, rules, etc.) to copy into the new sheet.
359: Flexible container targeting — Supports placing the new sheet in either a folder or a workspace by specifying the container_type and container_id.
360: Project and Gantt configuration — Accepts optional ganttEnabled, dependenciesEnabled, resourceManagementEnabled, and projectSettings fields to configure the sheet as a project sheet at creation time.
361: Rich column typing — Supports a full range of column types including TEXT_NUMBER, DATE, DATETIME, CHECKBOX, CONTACT_LIST, MULTI_CONTACT_LIST, PICKLIST, MULTI_PICKLIST, PREDECESSOR, DURATION, and ABSTRACT_DATETIME.
362: Limitations
363: The create_sheet tool has the following limitations:
364: The sheet name must be unique within the target container; duplicate names in the same folder or workspace are not allowed.
365: The user must have edit permissions on the parent container (folder or workspace).
366: When creating from a template, the template must be accessible to the authenticated user.
367: Exactly one column must be designated as the primary column when creating a blank sheet, and it must be of type TEXT_NUMBER.
368: Column titles must remain unique within the sheet; duplicates cause the operation to fail.
369: Column titles are limited to 50 characters.
370: Use cases
371: The following items describe use cases for the create_sheet tool:
372: Standardized project intake — Create a new project tracking sheet from a pre-approved template, copying filters and rules so every project sheet starts with consistent structure and automation.
373: Dynamic report scaffolding — Programmatically generate a blank sheet with a specific set of columns to serve as a data destination for an automated reporting workflow.

376: Audit trail sheets — Create a sheet that includes CREATED_BY, CREATED_DATE, MODIFIED_BY, and MODIFIED_DATE system columns to automatically capture row-level audit information.

666: attach_url
667: The attach_url tool attaches a URL to a Smartsheet sheet, row, or comment, linking to external resources such as Google Drive files, Box documents, Dropbox links, OneDrive files, or any generic web URL.
668: Access scopes: WRITE_SHEETS
669: Best Practices
670: The following items are best practices for using the attach_url tool:
671: Use the most specific attachmentType value that matches the source service rather than defaulting to LINK, as this allows Smartsheet to render the attachment with the appropriate service icon and metadata.
672: When attaching Google Drive items, also supply the attachmentSubType parameter to indicate whether the item is a document, spreadsheet, presentation, PDF, drawing, or folder, so Smartsheet can display the correct file-type context.
673: Use the attach_url tool in conjunction with the get_sheet_summary tool to verify the attachment was created as expected.
674: Basic Parameters
675: The attach_url tool has the following parameters:
676: sheet_id — The integer ID of the sheet to which the attachment belongs. This is required for all target types.
677: target_type — The type of object receiving the attachment. Valid values are SHEET, ROW, or COMMENT.
678: target_id — The integer ID of the row or comment receiving the attachment. This parameter is required when target_type is ROW or COMMENT, and is omitted when target_type is SHEET.
679: attachment.url — The URL string to attach, such as a Google Drive link, Dropbox link, or any generic web URL.
680: attachment.attachmentType — The service category of the URL. Valid values are LINK, GOOGLE_DRIVE, BOX_COM, DROPBOX, EVERNOTE, EGNYTE, and ONEDRIVE. Note that Dropbox, Egnyte, and Evernote are not supported for Smartsheet.gov accounts.
681: attachment.attachmentSubType — An optional sub-classification of the attachment, used only with GOOGLE_DRIVE or EGNYTE attachment types. Valid values are DOCUMENT, SPREADSHEET, PRESENTATION, PDF, DRAWING, and FOLDER. The FOLDER sub-type applies only to EGNYTE; all other sub-types apply to GOOGLE_DRIVE. The attachment.attachmentSubType parameter defaults to null.
682: Key Features
683: The attach_url tool has the following key features:
684: Multi-target support — A URL can be attached to a sheet, a specific row, or a specific comment, providing flexible linking at different levels of granularity.
685: Cloud service integration — Explicit attachment types for Google Drive, Box, Dropbox, OneDrive, Egnyte, and Evernote allow Smartsheet to render service-appropriate icons and metadata alongside the link.
686: Google Drive sub-type classification — An optional attachmentSubType parameter enables further classification of Google Drive items by file type (document, spreadsheet, presentation, PDF, drawing) or folder type for Egnyte.
687: Generic URL support — The LINK attachment type accommodates any web URL that does not belong to a supported cloud storage service.
688: Limitations
689: The attach_url tool has the following limitations:
690: Attachments cannot be moved between targets after creation; if the wrong target is specified, the attachment must be deleted and re-created.
691: Dropbox, Egnyte, and Evernote attachment types are not supported on Smartsheet.gov accounts.
692: There is no built-in validation of the URL itself; the tool accepts any string passed as the URL without confirming the link is reachable or valid.
693: Use Cases
694: The following items describe use cases for the attach_url tool:
695: Linking supporting documents — Attach a Google Drive document or OneDrive file to a sheet row so that team members can access reference materials directly from the relevant row in context.
696: Connecting cloud storage folders — Attach an Egnyte or Google Drive folder link at the sheet level to give collaborators quick access to a shared file repository related to the entire project.
697: Adding external references to comments — Attach a URL to a specific comment to provide a direct source or citation alongside a discussion point on a row.
698: Surfacing generic web resources — Use the LINK attachment type to associate any public web page, dashboard, or web application URL with a sheet, row, or comment.

914: Use Cases
915: Data analysis: Extract report data for analysis, dashboards, or business intelligence purposes.
916: Reporting workflows: Retrieve aggregated metrics or KPIs from Smartsheet reports for integration into external systems.
917: Audit and compliance: Pull report snapshots for record-keeping or compliance documentation.
918: Dashboard integration: Feed report data into custom dashboards or visualizations.
919: create_report
920: The create_report tool creates a new Smartsheet report that aggregates data from one or more source sheets or from all of the sheets in one or more workspaces. The create_report tool supports custom column definitions, filters, grouping, sorting, and summarizing criteria, and can produce either a row report or a sheet summary report.
921: Access scopes: READ_SHEETS
922: Best Practices
923: The following items are best practices for using the create_report tool:
924: Verify that all column title values exactly match the corresponding column titles in the source sheets, as matching is case-sensitive and must be precise.
925: Ensure all column index values are unique and zero-based across the full column definition list.
926: For row reports, designate exactly one column with primary=true using type=TEXT_NUMBER.
927: For sheet summary reports, designate exactly one column with sheetNameColumn=true using type=TEXT_NUMBER.
928: When grouping criteria are defined, be aware that the primary column moves to index 0 on first render in the app, which may affect expected column ordering.
929: Use the the get_report tool after creation to confirm the report structure and data before sharing or embedding the report in dashboards.
930: Basic Parameters
931: The create_report tool has the following parameters:
932: name — The report name, between 1 and 50 characters.
933: destination — The destination folder or workspace where the report is created, specified as an object with a destinationId (the numeric folder or workspace ID) and a destinationType (either "folder" or "workspace").
934: scope — A list of 1 to 100 source sheets or workspaces to aggregate, each specified with an assetId and an assetType of either "sheet" or "workspace".
935: columns — A list of 1 to 400 column definitions, each with a zero-based index, a type, and additional identifying fields depending on the column kind (regular, system, primary, or sheet name column). Optional per-column fields include hidden, width, primary, sheetNameColumn, systemColumnType, and title.
936: is_summary_report — A boolean that controls whether the report is a sheet summary report (true) or a row report (false). The is_summary_report parameter defaults to false.
937: report_definition — An optional object containing filters, groupingCriteria, sortingCriteria, and summarizingCriteria to shape the report's data presentation.
938: Refer to the POST /2.0/reports API operation documentation for details on creating a report and specifying the report definition.
939: Key Features
940: The create_report tool has the following key features:
941: Row and summary report types — Supports both row reports, which aggregate individual rows from source sheets, and sheet summary reports, which aggregate sheet summary fields.
942: Multi-source scoping — Accepts up to 100 source sheets (specified explicitly or as part of workspaces) as input, enabling cross-sheet and cross-workspace data aggregation in a single report.
943: Flexible column definitions — Supports regular columns (matched by type and title), system columns (matched by type and system column type), primary columns, and sheet name columns, with optional hidden and width settings.
944: Filter expressions — Supports nested filter expressions up to 3 levels deep using AND/OR operators and a wide range of filter operators covering equality, comparisons, date ranges, blank checks, and multi-value matching.
945: Grouping criteria — Allows columns to be used as grouping criteria with configurable sort direction and expand/collapse state.
946: Sorting criteria — Supports multi-column sorting with ASCENDING or DESCENDING direction per column.
947: Summarizing criteria — Supports column-level aggregations using SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX, COUNT, FIRST, and LAST.
948: Limitations
949: The create_report tool has the following limitations:
950: Report names are limited to 50 characters.
951: A maximum of 400 columns may be defined per report.
952: The scope is limited to 100 sheets.
953: Filter expressions support a maximum nesting depth of 3 levels.
954: Use Cases
955: The following items describe use cases for the create_report tool:
956: Cross-sheet status rollup — Aggregate task status columns from multiple project sheets into a single report to give stakeholders a unified view of progress across all projects.
957: Department-wide resource tracking — Scope a report to an entire workspace to consolidate resource allocation rows from every sheet in a department's workspace.
958: Filtered executive summary — Create a row report with filter criteria that surfaces only high-priority or overdue items from across dozens of source sheets.
959: Grouped pipeline view — Define grouping criteria on a status or owner column to organize aggregated rows into collapsible sections for easier review.
960: Summarized financial rollup — Use summarizing criteria with SUM or AVG aggregations on numeric columns to produce totals and averages across source sheets.
961: Sheet summary dashboard feed — Create a sheet summary report (is_summary_report=true) to pull sheet-level summary fields together, useful for high-level KPI dashboards.
962: Sorted delivery schedule — Apply sorting criteria on a date column so that aggregated rows from multiple sheets appear in chronological order across the full report.

986: create_workflow
987: Access scopes: WRITE_SHEETS
988: Toolset: automations
989: create_workflow creates a new workflow on a sheet using human-readable names for columns, recipients, and other references. The workflow is defined as a typed tree specifying a trigger and a chain of actions or conditions.
990: Best Practices
991: The following items are best practices for using the create_workflow tool:
992: Use the get_workflows tool on an existing sheet to study the tree structure before composing a new workflow from scratch.
993: Verify that all referenced column titles, recipient emails, and document mapping names exist on the sheet before calling — unknown names are rejected by the API without creating anything.
994: Use {} for notificationCustomizationJson on EMAIL_RECIPIENT, UPDATE_REQUEST, and APPROVAL actions unless explicit customization is needed.
995: Basic Parameters
996: The create_workflow tool has the following parameters:
997: sheet_id (required): The ID of the sheet the workflow attaches to.
998: name (required): Display name for the workflow (up to 255 characters).
999: root_node (required): The workflow definition as a typed tree. The root has type: "ROOT_NODE" and contains a trigger and a childNode. All type discriminants are UPPER_SNAKE_CASE. Columns are referenced by title (columnTitle); people are referenced by email address. The ID field in recipient objects is always a string.
1000: frequency (optional): How often the workflow runs once triggered. The frequency parameter defaults to RIGHT_AWAY (run immediately when the trigger fires).
1001: enabled (optional): Whether the workflow is active immediately after creation. The enabled parameter defaults to true.
1002: Key Features
1003: The create_workflow tool has the following key features:
1004: Human-readable references: Columns, recipients, and document mappings are specified by name rather than numeric ID, making workflows easier to compose and read.
1005: Schema-validated tree: The root_node structure is validated before the API call; errors report the exact field path and permitted values for precise correction.
1006: Immediate activation: Workflows are enabled by default upon creation; set enabled: false to create a workflow in a disabled state.
1007: Limitations
1008: The create_workflow tool has the following limitations:
1009: All referenced column titles and email addresses must already exist on the sheet — the tool does not create missing resources.
1010: Recipient emails must belong to Smartsheet users; assign-people emails must have an existing contact record.
1011: Column title matching is case-sensitive.
1012: Use Cases
1013: The following items describe use cases for the create_workflow tool:
1014: Automated notifications: Create a workflow that sends an email alert when a row's status column changes to a specific value.
1015: Approval routing: Build an approval workflow triggered when a new row is added, sending an update request to a designated reviewer.
1016: Scheduled reminders: Set up a time-based workflow that sends reminders at a defined frequency when a due-date condition is met.
1017: Row automation: Automatically move or copy rows to another sheet when specific criteria are satisfied.
1018: update_workflow
1019: Access scopes: WRITE_SHEETS
1020: Toolset: automations
1021: The update_workflow tool updates a Smartsheet workflow by ID, fully replacing its definition using human-readable names. It overwrites the stored workflow tree with exactly the tree sent — anything omitted from root_node is removed from the workflow. Updating a workflow also invalidates any in-flight approval actions: pending approval emails stop being actionable.
1022: (⚠️ destructive, irreversible)
1023: Best Practices
1024: The following items are best practices for using the update_workflow tool:
1025: Call the get_workflows tool first to read the current definition, then modify it and send the COMPLETE tree back — never send a partial tree.
1026: Omit enabled to preserve the workflow's current enabled/disabled state; only pass it to deliberately toggle that state.
1027: Pass expected_version (from a previous update_workflow, enable_workflow, or disable_workflow response) to guard against concurrent edits; on a 409 conflict, re-read the workflow and retry with the fresh definition.
1028: Reference columns by title and people by email; use UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for all type discriminants, exactly as in the create_workflow tool.
1029: Do not include node id fields in root_node — the tree schema rejects them; node identity is regenerated on every edit.
1030: Basic Parameters
1031: The update_workflow tool has the following parameters:
1032: workflow_id (required, string) — The ID of the workflow to update, as shown in Smartsheet.
1033: sheet_id (required, integer) — The current sheet ID of the workflow. Must match the sheet the workflow already lives on — workflows cannot be moved to another sheet.
1034: name (required, string) — The workflow display name to store. Up to 255 characters; may be empty.
1035: root_node (required) — The complete replacement workflow tree using the by-names contract: {type: 'ROOT_NODE', trigger: {type: <TRIGGER_TYPE>, ...}, childNode: {type: <NODE_TYPE>, ...}}. Uses the same schema as the create_workflow tool. The stored definition becomes exactly this tree.
1036: frequency (required) — How often the workflow runs once triggered. Must always be supplied on update; there is no default.
1037: enabled (boolean, optional) — Whether the workflow is enabled. Omit to keep the current enabled/disabled state; pass true or false only to deliberately change it.
1038: expected_version (integer, optional) — Optimistic-concurrency guard. The version from a previous update_workflow, enable_workflow, or disable_workflow response. If the workflow was edited by someone else since that version, the update fails with 409 and makes no changes. Omit for an unconditional update.
1039: Key Features
1040: The update_workflow tool has the following key features:
1041: Full replacement semantics — The stored workflow definition becomes exactly the root_node tree sent; any node omitted is removed, making this a complete overwrite rather than a patch.
1042: Human-readable names — Columns are referenced by title and recipients by email address, avoiding the need to look up internal IDs.
1043: Optimistic concurrency control — The optional expected_version parameter detects concurrent edits and fails safely with 409, enabling read-modify-write patterns without data loss.
1044: Enabled/disabled state preservation — Omitting enabled keeps the workflow's current state; an edit alone never inadvertently re-enables a disabled workflow.
1045: Pre-flight tree validation — Tree-structure violations (invalid condition counts, missing child nodes, etc.) are caught and the offending path is reported before anything is sent to the backend.
1046: Limitations
1047: The update_workflow tool has the following limitations:
1048: Full replace, not a patch: the workflow becomes exactly what is sent; any node omitted from root_node is removed.
1049: sheet_id must be the workflow's current sheet — workflows cannot be moved to another sheet via update.
1050: Updating a workflow invalidates its in-flight approval actions: pending approval emails stop being actionable.
1051: The caller must have permission to edit the workflow's sheet.
1052: Condition nodes must carry 1–20 conditions AND a childNode; IF_ELSE nodes require at least one condition branch; ELSE nodes require a childNode — violations are rejected with the offending path.
1053: Node id fields must not be included in root_node — the schema rejects them.
1054: Use Cases
1055: The following items describe use cases for the update_workflow tool:
1056: Modifying trigger or action configuration — Read the current workflow, adjust a trigger type or notification recipient, and write the full updated tree back.
1057: Restructuring a workflow tree — Add, remove, or reorder condition branches and action nodes by sending a revised complete tree.
1058: Renaming a workflow — Update the name field while passing the rest of the definition unchanged.

1228: Exploratory data analysis — Use the tool when first working with an unfamiliar sheet to discover what charts and metrics the data is best suited for.

1232: create_chart_from_prompt generates charts and metrics from a natural language description by starting or continuing a conversation against a sheet's data. 1233: Best Practices
1234: The following items are best practices for using the create_chart_from_prompt tool:
1235: Use the get_chart_suggestions tool before this tool to surface relevant chart and metric ideas based on the sheet's data.

1244: Key Features
1245: The create_chart_from_prompt tool has the following key features:
1246: Natural language input: Accepts a plain-language prompt describing the desired chart or metric, so no chart configuration syntax is required.
1247: Multi-output responses: A single call can return multiple charts and metrics together in the messages array.
1248: Conversation continuity: Supports multi-turn conversations by accepting a conversation_id and previous_message_id to refine or extend a prior result.
1249: Rich result data: Each message in the response includes the chart type, labels, and datasets needed to render the visualization.
