2254: Limitations
2255: The delete_shadow_sheet_rows tool has the following limitations:
2256: Deletion is permanent within the scenario and cannot be automatically undone.
2257: The sheet_id must identify a scenario sheet, not a regular sheet.
2258: Requires at least Editor permissions on the workspace and all associated project sheets.
2259: Use Cases
2260: The following items describe use cases for the delete_shadow_sheet_rows tool:
2261: Scenario simplification — Remove tasks or milestones from a scenario sheet that are not relevant to a particular "what-if" scenario being modeled.
2262: Hierarchy pruning — Delete parent rows along with all their children to eliminate entire work packages from a scenario in a single operation.
2263: Scenario cleanup — Remove incorrectly added rows from a scenario sheet before using the get_scenario_diffs tool or the apply_scenario tool.
2264: User plans
2265: The following sections describe Smartsheet MCP server tools for managing users plans and seats.
2266: get_plan_id
2267: Access scopes: Not applicable
2268: Toolset: users
2269: Important: The get_plan_id is available to system admins only.
2270: The get_plan_id tool retrieves the list of plans that the authenticated user is a member of. It is primarily used to discover a planId when it is required by other plan-based operations, such as retrieving seat requests or managing plan members. The user's identity is resolved automatically from the authenticated session, so no user ID input is required.
2271: Best Practices
2272: The following items are best practices for using the get_plan_id tool:
2273: Call this tool first whenever a plan-based tool requires a planId and the user has not provided one.
2274: If only one plan is returned, use that planId directly without asking the user.
2275: If multiple plans are returned, present the list to the user using plan_name to identify each plan, with seat_type and is_internal as additional context, and ask them to confirm which planId to use.
2276: If last_key is present in the response, fetch the next page before presenting the full list to the user.
2277: Basic Parameters
2278: The get_plan_id tool has the following parameters:
2279: last_key — an opaque pagination token for fetching the next page of results. The last_key parameter defaults to an empty string.
2280: max_items — the maximum number of items to return per page (1–100). The max_items parameter defaults to 100.
2281: Key Features
2282: The get_plan_id tool has the following key features:
2283: Session-based identity resolution: The authenticated user's ID is resolved automatically from the session — no user ID input is required.
2284: Pagination support: Supports keyset pagination via last_key to iterate through plans when the user belongs to many.
2285: Plan context fields: Returns plan_name, seat_type, and is_internal to help identify and select the correct plan when multiple are present.
2286: Limitations
2287: The get_plan_id tool has the following limitations:
2288: Returns plan memberships for the authenticated user only — cannot look up plans for other users.
2289: plan_name may be absent for plans whose organization cannot be resolved; fall back to the raw planId when presenting such a plan.
2290: Admin status is not surfaced by this endpoint — it exists at the org layer and cannot be inferred from plan membership data.
2291: Use Cases
2292: The following items describe use cases for the get_plan_id tool:
2293: Plan ID discovery: Resolves the planId required before calling tools such as the get_seat_requests tool or the get_seat_usage tool.
2294: Multi-plan selection: Presents users who belong to multiple plans with a labeled list so they can confirm which plan to target.
2295: get_seat_usage
2296: Access scopes: ADMIN_USERS
2297: Toolset: users
2298: The get_seat_usage tool retrieves per-user seat usage detail and activity scores for a plan as a flat, paginated list. Plan administrators use it to review who holds seats, how users are billed, and how active each user is.
2299: This tool is unavailable for the Microsoft 365 Copilot Connector (the Copilot Studio connector for Copilot Chat)
2300: Best Practices
2301: The following items are best practices for using the get_seat_usage tool:
2302: Paginate through all pages by passing the last_key from each previous response into the next call until no last_key is returned.
2303: Use the activity_window parameter to match the lookback period to your review cycle — longer windows produce more stable scores for infrequent but legitimate users.
2304: Combine min_activity_score/max_activity_score with billing_states to identify paid seats held by inactive users before making licensing decisions.
2305: Basic Parameters
2306: The get_seat_usage tool has the following parameters:
2307: plan_id — the ID of the plan to query. Required.
2308: seat_types — filters results to one or more seat types: MEMBER, PROVISIONAL_MEMBER, GUEST, or CONTRIBUTOR.
2309: billing_states — filters results to one or more billing states: PAID, CONVERT_THIS_CYCLE, CONVERT_NEXT_CYCLE, or FREE.
2310: departments — filters results to one or more department names.
2311: user_ids — filters results to one or more specific user IDs.
2312: min_activity_score — lower bound (inclusive) on the activity score filter (0–100).
2313: max_activity_score — upper bound (inclusive) on the activity score filter (0–100).
2314: activity_window — the lookback period used to compute each user's activity score. The activity_window parameter defaults to NINETY_DAYS. Other values are ONE_HUNDRED_EIGHTY_DAYS, TWO_HUNDRED_SEVENTY_DAYS, and THREE_HUNDRED_SIXTY_FIVE_DAYS.
2315: max_items — the maximum number of users returned per page. The max_items parameter defaults to 25.
2316: last_key — the pagination token used to fetch the next page of results. The last_key parameter defaults to an empty string (first page).
2317: sort_order — the sort direction (ASC or DESC) applied to the activity score column. The sort_order parameter defaults to DESC.
2318: Key Features
2319: The get_seat_usage tool has the following key features:
2320: Activity scoring — computes a 0–100 activity score per user based on the configured activity_window, along with component-level detail supporting nuanced engagement analysis.
2321: Flexible filtering — supports simultaneous filtering by seat type, billing state, department, user ID, and activity score range.
2322: Limitations
2323: The get_seat_usage tool has the following limitations:
2324: The caller must be an administrator of the plan.
2325: The maximum page size is 100 users per page; larger result sets require multiple paginated calls.
2326: Use Cases
2327: The following items describe use cases for the get_seat_usage tool:
2328: License reclamation — identify paid seats with low activity scores to reclaim unused licenses and reduce costs.
2329: Inactive user review — filter by min_activity_score/max_activity_score to generate a list of users who have not engaged with the plan recently.
2330: Billing audit — combine billing_states and seat_types filters to audit which users are in a conversion or paid state ahead of a billing cycle.
2331: Department-level reporting — filter by departments to produce per-department seat usage and activity summaries for team managers.
2332: get_license_inventory
2333: Access scopes: ADMIN_USERS
2334: Toolset: users
2335: get_license_inventory retrieves a point-in-time license usage snapshot for a Smartsheet plan. System administrators use it to check available licenses, track usage against plan limits, and monitor reconciliation period activity.
2336: This tool is unavailable for the Microsoft 365 Copilot Connector (the Copilot Studio connector for Copilot Chat)
2337: Best Practices
2338: The following items are best practices for using the get_license_inventory tool:
2339: Use the get_plan_id tool to look up a plan ID if you don't already have one.
2340: Pass period=RECON when you need usage counts scoped to the current reconciliation window rather than the full plan period.
2341: Basic Parameters
2342: The get_license_inventory tool has the following parameters:
2343: plan_id — ID of the plan to retrieve license inventory for. This parameter is required.
2344: period — Reporting period for the counts: ALL or RECON. This parameter is optional. The period parameter defaults to ALL, which reports counts across the full plan period.
2345: Key Features
2346: The get_license_inventory tool has the following key features:
2347: License counts and limits. Reports the number of member licenses in use and the total allowed under the plan.
2348: Provisional and guest/contributor counts. Includes counts for provisional members and guest or contributor users separately from licensed members.
2349: Pending purchase tracking. Reports how many additional licenses still need to be purchased to cover current membership.
2350: Reconciliation window scoping. Supports a RECON period option to isolate counts to the current reconciliation window.
2351: Date visibility. Returns plan usage period dates and the current reconciliation period dates alongside the counts.
2352: Limitations
2353: The get_license_inventory tool has the following limitations:
2354: Requires the caller to be an administrator of the plan.
2355: Use Cases
2356: The following items describe use cases for the get_license_inventory tool:
2357: Available license check. Answer "how many licenses are left on my plan?" before provisioning new members.
2358: Reconciliation review. Determine usage within the current reconciliation window to anticipate billing adjustments before the period closes.
2359: Capacity planning. Compare current license consumption against plan limits to decide whether to purchase additional seats.
2360: Pending purchase audit. Identify how many licenses need to be purchased to bring the plan into compliance with current membership counts.
2361: Get more tool and capability details
2362: The Smartsheet MCP server is fully self-describing, providing built-in tool definitions, detailed parameter schemas, and pre-defined prompt templates. Once your AI client is connected to the Smartsheet MCP server, your client's chat interface is a great way to learn more about the MCP server tools and capabilities.
2363: Here are some example prompts:
2364: Learn the MCP server's capabilities:
2365: Prompt:
2366: What can I do with the Smartsheet MCP server?
2367: List underlying tools:
2368: Prompt:
2369: List all available Smartsheet tools.
2370: Get tool examples:
2371: Prompt:
2372: Give me examples of using create_sheet_in_workspace.
2373: Surface underlying endpoints:
2374: Prompt:
2375: Which API endpoints does add_rows use?
2376: Tip: If you've connected your AI client to multiple MCP servers that share similar tool names, use the Smartsheet: prefix to avoid ambiguity.
2377: For example, Describe Smartsheet:list_workspaces
2378: Now you know the details and best practices regarding the Smartsheet MCP server tools.

124: 5 steps for getting started with the Smartsheet API
125: TK
126: Taylor Krusen
127: January 24, 2019
128: (updated August 21, 2025)
129: Innovative IT teams that use the Smartsheet API see benefits as soon as their integration is up and running. The API is a powerful tool for developers that helps ensure a combination of secure data management, automation through webhooks, and the ability to scale Smartsheet throughout your company.
130: So, do you want to build an integration using the Smartsheet API, but aren’t sure where to start? Follow these five steps, which we’ve detailed below:
131: Step 1: Explore Developer Resources
132: Step 2: Complete 'Developer Registration' (optional)
133: Step 3: Generate an Access Token
134: Step 4: Start Building Your Integration
135: Step 5: Ask Smartsheet for Support
136: 1. Explore developer resources
137: The Smartsheet Developer Portal is the “home base” for all developer resources. There you’ll find API documentation, information about Smartsheet SDKs, answers to your specific API questions from our user community, and more.
138: As tempting as it may be to dive right into building your integration, investing the time up front to review these resources will pay dividends down the road.
139: Where to find API documentation
140: After you’ve watched the video, visit our API Documentation page. Whether you’re planning to build an integration that calls the Smartsheet API directly, or one that uses a Smartsheet SDK, the API documents contain lots of useful information. Start off by familiarizing yourself with the following sections:
141: Overview: A high-level context for working with the Smartsheet API
142: Getting Started: Information that you’ll need to lay the groundwork for your integration
143: Troubleshooting: Make a plan to work through issues when you get stuck
144: Smartsheet SDKs
145: Smartsheet software development kits (SDKs) provide a means of accessing the Smartsheet API using the programming language of your choice without having to write all the code from scratch. In addition to the pre-built methods, each SDK also includes retry logic (for rate limit errors) and logging systems.
146: Each respective SDK (C#, Java, Node, Python) has documentation and a sample read/write sheet available for reference.
147: 2. Complete 'developer registration' (optional)
148: After you spend some time exploring our Smartsheet Developer Resources, you should be ready to lay the groundwork for creating your integration.
149: Create a developer account
150: If you’re planning to build a third-party application or if you want to create a sandbox Smartsheet account that you can use for development and testing purposes (without affecting data in your production Smartsheet account), you’ll need to complete the Developer Registration process.
151: 3. Generate an access token
152: Next, to authenticate API requests via Direct API Access, you’ll need an API access token that is owned by the Smartsheet account that you want to access. Access tokens can be generated by the Smartsheet UI: simply login to your Smartsheet account, then follow the instructions here to generate a token.
153: If you’re building a third-party application that will implement the OAuth2 Flow to retrieve an access token that can be used to access Smartsheet data on behalf of an end user, then you won’t need to manually generate an access token as described above. Instead, consult the API docs for information about third-party app development.
154: If you’re building a third-party application meant for other users, then you’ll need to implement an OAuth2 Flow to retrieve an access token. Automatically(rather than manually) generating an access token ensures that the user has their own respective token in order to access their Smartsheet data. We recommend consulting the API docs section on third-party app development.
155: 4. Start building your integration
156: The process of building your integration will vary depending on whether or not you choose to use an SDK. Both approaches are detailed below:
157: Using an SDK
158: To use an SDK as the basis for your integration, install the SDK of your choice by following instructions provided for that respective SDK. Then, leverage the API Documentation for code samples and follow these steps:
159: Using the code sample panel on the right side of the page, select the tab for the language that you’re interested in.
160: Review your respective SDKs readme and read/write sample. All links are available on the Smartsheet Developer Portal.
161: Navigate to any API Reference section to see a code sample that demonstrates how to execute the operation using the SDK.
162: Not using an SDK
163: While you can benefit from using an SDK, it’s by no means mandatory. If you choose to forgo using an SDK in favor of building a custom integration from scratch, leverage the API Documentation as your primary resource. If you get stuck, please don’t hesitate to ask questions on StackOverflow using the smartsheet-api tag. Your question could help someone in the future.
164: 5. Ask Smartsheet for support
165: You might encounter an API or SDK issue that you can’t resolve using our API Troubleshooting guidance, or have a question that’s not addressed by the API docs. Please post your issue or question to StackOverflow, where we (along with thousands of developers worldwide) are standing by, ready to assist you.
166: Have feedback about the API or want to suggest new API features? Please reach us at DevRel@smartsheet.com.
167: Discover more resources
168: There’s a learning curve when using a new API for the first time, but the proper resources and processes can make all the difference.
169: We encourage you to make the most of the Smartsheet Developer Portal for resources and guidance to help you accelerate the time it takes for you to get comfortable using the Smartsheet API and help you confidently deploy your solution.
170: Subscribe to the Smartsheet IT Newsletter for tips, strategies, and ideas focused on helping IT professionals increase their impact on their business.

95: Link your Smartsheet account to Claude to generate natural-language summaries and take action on individual sheets.
96: Who can use this?
97: Plans:
98: Business
99: Enterprise
100: Advanced Work Management
101: USM Content
102: This Connector uses the Model Context Protocol (MCP), a secure standard that allows Claude to access your Smartsheet data with your permission, understand your work in context, and act on your behalf.
103: Claude securely accesses live sheet data—such as task progress, overdue items, and key risks—and presents a concise summary directly in the Claude interface. You can also update statuses, dates, and risks using natural-language prompts, making it easy to understand project status and keep work moving without navigating multiple sheets.
104: The Smartsheet MCP prompt library shows you how to prompt the Smartsheet Connector (the MCP server) to get powerful insights and take action.
105: Prerequisites
106: The following items are required for you to use the Smartsheet Connector in Claude:
107: You are an active user on a Claude plan.
108: A Claude Owner must enable the integration for your organization. Refer to Claude’s instructions here.
109: The Claude Connector AI capability must be enabled. It's enabled by default for all eligible plans. If Claude access to Smartsheet appears to be blocked, contact your System Admin to activate it in the Smartsheet Admin Center.
110: Connect to Smartsheet
111: The following steps demonstrate how to connect Claude to Smartsheet:
112: Open Claude and sign in with your credentials.
113: Go to Customize > Connectors.
114: If the Smartsheet Connector doesn't appear, select the search icon (magnifying glass) and search for Smartsheet.
115: Once found, select it and then select Connect.
116: Claude prompts you for your credentials.
117: Log in with your Smartsheet credentials and select Allow.
118: When prompted, select the URL for your Smartsheet region:
119: US: https://mcp.smartsheet.com
120: EU: https://mcp.smartsheet.eu
121: AU: https://mcp.smartsheet.au
122: The Configure button and the server URL appear, confirming the connection.
123: Start a new chat.
124: Enable the Smartsheet Connector by selecting + > Connectors > Smartsheet.
125: You’re now connected to the Smartsheet MCP Server.
126: Manage Claude's permissions for Smartsheet functionality
127: You can configure permissions for individual Smartsheet tools, or apply them broadly to all read-only or write functions. In Claude, go to Customize > Connectors > Smartsheet > Configure. The following Smartsheet tools permission pages appears.
128: Brandfolder Image
129: When a prompt triggers a tool, the Smartsheet MCP Server Connector applies its designated permission level. Every tool operates under one of three permissions:
130: Always allow: Executes the tool automatically without asking.
131: Needs approval: Prompts you for confirmation before running. If you decline, the tool is skipped.
132: Blocked: Prevents the tool from running entirely and returns a notice that it is blocked.
133: See some examples on how you can use this Connector in your day-to-day work in Use the Smartsheet Connector with Claude.
134: FAQ
135: What access do Smartsheet and Claude have to my data via the integration?
136: Claude can access only the Smartsheet data you explicitly allow, including specific sheets, workspaces, or objects that you already have permission to view or edit, and only when you initiate a request. It cannot browse your account independently or access data outside the scope you select. Data is processed at runtime to generate a response and is not stored or used for model training. Smartsheet itself does not use customer data to train Claude or any other AI models, and does not access or process Claude-generated content, except for aggregated usage and reliability tracking.
137: How do I change the region for my Smartsheet MCP Connector?
138: When you set up the Smartsheet MCP Connector for the first time, you are prompted to select your region. This choice is cached to keep your connection stable.
139: If you need to switch to a different region later, you cannot simply change it in the settings or disconnect. You must fully reset the connection.
140: Follow these steps to reconfigure your region:
141: Remove the Connector.
142: Add the Connector again.
143: During Connector setup, select your new region.
144: How do I limit Smartsheet and Claude's access to my data and prompts?
145: You control access through existing Smartsheet permissions and Admin controls. Both Smartsheet AI features and Claude can access only the specific sheets, workspaces, and objects you already have permission to use, and only when you actively initiate a request. Organization sysadmins can turn on and off Read/Write permissions. Data and prompts are processed at runtime solely to fulfill your request and are not stored or used for model training.

1: Overview – Harvest API V2 Documentation
2: API V2 Documentation
3: Contact Us
4: Request new API
5: Welcome to the Harvest API v2 Help Center
6: Harvest API V2 Documentation
7: Introduction
8: Overview
9: This is the current API V2 documentation. You can still view the legacy API V1 documentation.
10: Help Topics
11: Overview
12: The Harvest V2 API is a REST API that allows you to interact with your Harvest account programmatically. You can track time, log expenses, create projects, and more.
13: API requests
14: Harvest requires applications to authenticate all requests with OAuth2 or Personal Access Tokens. The following HTTP methods are supported:
15: GET
16: POST
17: PATCH
18: DELETE
19: When issuing a GET request, parameters should be included in the URL query string:
20: curl https://api.harvestapp.com/v2/tasks?page=2&per_page=10 \
21: -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
22: -H "Harvest-Account-Id: $ACCOUNT_ID" \
23: -H "User-Agent: MyApp ([email protected])"
24: When issuing a POST or PATCH request, parameters should be included in the request body. Request parameters can either be formatted in JSON or submitted as form data. When submitting request parameters as JSON, you must pass application/json in the Content-Type header.
25: We also require that each request include a User-Agent header with both:
26: The name of your application
27: A link to your application or email address
28: We use this information to get in touch if you’re doing something wrong (so we can warn you before you’re blocked) or something awesome (so we can congratulate you). Here are examples of acceptable User-Agent headers:
29: User-Agent: Trello (http://trello.com/contact)
30: User-Agent: John's Harvest Integration ([email protected])
31: Notes about user agents
32: If you don’t include a User-Agent header, you’ll get a 400 Bad Request response.
33: If you use a non-standard User Agent or deviate from the pattern suggested above, you may encounter connectivity issues with Harvest’s API.
34: JSON
35: curl -X POST https://api.harvestapp.com/v2/tasks \
36: -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
37: -H "Harvest-Account-Id: $ACCOUNT_ID" \
38: -H "User-Agent: MyApp ([email protected])" \
39: -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
40: -d "{\"name\":\"My New Task\"}"
41: Form data
42: curl -X POST https://api.harvestapp.com/v2/tasks \
43: -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
44: -H "Harvest-Account-Id: $ACCOUNT_ID" \
45: -H "User-Agent: MyApp ([email protected])" \
46: -d name="My New Task"
47: API responses
48: Harvest formats response bodies in JSON and uses HTTP response codes to indicate the success or failure of an API request. The following are the HTTP status codes that you may encounter when using the API along with a brief explanation of when they occur.
49: Code
50: Explanation
51: 200
52: Your request was successful.
53: 201
54: A new object has been created. Its representation will be returned in the response body.
55: 403
56: The object you requested was found but you don’t have authorization to perform your request.
57: 404
58: The object you requested can’t be found.
59: 422
60: There were errors processing your request. Check the response body for additional information.
61: 429
62: Your request has been throttled. Refer to the Rate Limiting section for details.
63: 500
64: There was a server error. Contact [email protected] for help.
65: Rate limiting
66: We have an API throttle that blocks accounts that exceed our API rate limits. We reserve the right to tune the limitations, but they are always set high enough to allow a well-behaving interactive program to do its job.
67: The rate limit for general API requests is 100 requests per 15 seconds.
68: The rate limit for Reports API requests is 100 requests per 15 minutes.
69: For batch processes and API developers who still need to perfect their code, this throttle may be an inadvertent blocker. Just wait a bit, and try again. Since the throttle is reset with each call, the throttle will lift itself in a few minutes and API calls may resume.
70: When the rate limit is exceeded Harvest will send an HTTP 429 status code. The number of seconds until the throttle is lifted is sent via the Retry-After HTTP header, as specified in RFC 2616.
71: Please remember to write your application carefully, caching when possible. In case of abuse you may be blocked, disallowing further API access.
72: Conventions
73: When you encounter a value surrounded by curly braces, you should replace it with a value appropriate to your context.
74: For example, if your Harvest project’s ID is 1234 and the documentation provides the following URL:
75: https://api.harvestapp.com/v2/projects/{PROJECT_ID}
76: you would replace the {PROJECT_ID} with the actual project ID, like so:
77: https://api.harvestapp.com/v2/projects/1234
78: We also make use of shell variables in our example requests (e.g. $ACCESS_TOKEN). If your operating system supports shell variables, you can set shell variables like this:
79: ACCESS_TOKEN="my-access-token"
80: ACCOUNT_ID="my-account-id"
81: USER_AGENT="MyApp ([email protected])"
82: Then, you can reference them by prefixing them with a $:
83: curl -X POST https://api.harvestapp.com/v2/company \
84: -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
85: -H "Harvest-Account-Id: $ACCOUNT_ID" \
86: -H "User-Agent: $USER_AGENT"
87: This should allow you to copy/paste most of the example requests without needing to change anything aside from IDs.
88: Data types
89: Type
90: Example
91: Description
92: boolean
93: true
94: Either true or false.
95: string
96: "foo"
97: A double-quoted sequence of characters.
98: integer
99: 42
100: A non-negative integer value.
101: decimal
102: 6.8
103: A decimal value. The supported precision is field-dependent.
104: date
105: "2017-12-31"
106: An ISO 8601 formatted string containing just the date portion.
107: datetime
108: "2017-12-31T14:59:22Z"
109: An ISO 8601 formatted string containing a UTC date and time.
110: time
111: "14:59"
112: "2:59pm"
113: A string containing a 12-hour or 24-hour time depending on the Time Format configured for your account. You can check this on the Settings page in your Harvest account or the clock attribute the Company API.
114: array
115: [ 1, 2, 3 ]
116: A JSON array.
117: object
118: { name: "value" }
119: A JSON object.

1: Authentication – Harvest API V2 Documentation
2: API V2 Documentation
3: Contact Us
4: Request new API
5: Welcome to the Harvest API v2 Help Center
6: Harvest API V2 Documentation
7: Authentication
8: API
9: Authentication
10: This is the current API V2 documentation. You can still view the legacy API V1 documentation.
11: Help Topics
12: Authentication
13: Introduction
14: The V2 API requires an access token to authenticate requests. There are two options available to you:
15: A Personal Access Token which is tied directly to you and is the quickest way to start playing around with the API.
16: Implementing a full OAuth2 Authentication flow which allows other people to use your Harvest integrations.
17: Personal access tokens
18: The API can be accessed by creating a Personal Access Token from the Developers
19: section of Harvest ID. After creating it you’ll be provided with a random token and a list of your account IDs.
20: Personal Access Tokens are the preferred method when you want to write your own scripts that consume our API. Typical use cases
21: for Personal Access Tokens are scripts that build custom reports, sync data between different accounts, or automate tasks that
22: would otherwise take a long time when done manually.
23: Personal Access Tokens replace the Basic Authentication method that was used in our v1 API, as this is more secure. Within the Developers section you’ll see a list of all your Personal Access Tokens, when they were last used, and you’ll be able to easily revoke them if necessary.
24: Once generated, a Personal Access Token can be used to access the API by either providing the token in the Authorization header or including it in the query string. Each request will require your account ID as well, since you can use this Personal Access Token to access any of your Harvest or Forecast accounts.
25: Header authentication example
26: curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
27: -H "Harvest-Account-Id: $ACCOUNT_ID" \
28: -H "User-Agent: MyApp ([email protected])" \
29: https://api.harvestapp.com/v2/users/me
30: Query string authentication example
31: curl -H "User-Agent: MyApp ([email protected])" \
32: "https://api.harvestapp.com/v2/users/me?access_token=$ACCESS_TOKEN&account_id=$ACCOUNT_ID"
33: OAuth2 application
34: If you are interested in building integrations that other users can use, you will need to register an OAuth2 Application, also
35: known as an OAuth2 Client. The application can be created from the Developers section
36: of Harvest ID, and you will be required to provide some information:
37: Name–name of your application.
38: Redirect URL–the URL in your integration; successful authentications will be redirected to by default.
39: Multi Account–does your integration support multiple user account access or work with only one authenticated account.
40: Products–scope of access requested; can be either Harvest, Forecast or both. It is advised to pick the minimal scope
41: required for the integration to work.
42: OAuth2 authorization flow
43: For server-side applications
44: We use the Authorization Code flow for
45: server-side authorization. To start the authorization flow, you need to redirect the user to the following URL:
46: https://id.getharvest.com/oauth2/authorize?client_id={CLIENT_ID}&response_type=code
47: This URL allows the user to authenticate on Harvest ID and lets them authorize access to their account(s) depending on your OAuth2 Application settings and their choice.
48: This endpoint accepts other parameters:
49: state–(optional) used to pass any value that will get sent back to you when redirecting back to your application.
50: redirect_uri–(optional) the default Redirect URL can be further customized here if needed, but needs to start with the Redirect
51: URL registered with your Application.
52: After a successful authorization, the user will be redirected back to the Redirect URL you specified when registering your OAuth2
53: application, or the redirect_uri you provided. These parameters will be attached:
54: code–an authorization code that you will have to exchange for a set of Refresh and Access Tokens. You will be able to use this
55: Access Token to access the user’s account on their behalf.
56: state–(optional) contains the original value for the state parameter that was passed at the beginning of the authorization.
57: scope–contains a list of space-separated strings describing the granted access scope. See the Scopes section for further
58: explanation.
59: Once you have the Authorization Code, you can exchange it for a set of Access and Refresh Tokens:
60: curl -X POST \
61: -H "User-Agent: MyApp ([email protected])" \
62: -d "code=$AUTHORIZATION_CODE" \
63: -d "client_id=$CLIENT_ID" \
64: -d "client_secret=$CLIENT_SECRET" \
65: -d "grant_type=authorization_code" \
66: 'https://id.getharvest.com/api/v2/oauth2/token'
67: Response:
68: {
69: "access_token": "{ACCESS_TOKEN}",
70: "refresh_token": "{REFRESH_TOKEN}",
71: "token_type": "bearer",
72: "expires_in": 1209600
73: }
74: When your Access Token is about to expire, you can use the Refresh Token to get a new Access Token:
75: curl -X POST \
76: -H "User-Agent: MyApp ([email protected])" \
77: -H "Accept: application/json" \
78: -d "refresh_token=$REFRESH_TOKEN" \
79: -d "client_id=$CLIENT_ID" \
80: -d "client_secret=$CLIENT_SECRET" \
81: -d "grant_type=refresh_token" \
82: 'https://id.getharvest.com/api/v2/oauth2/token'
83: Response:
84: {
85: "access_token": "{NEW_ACCESS_TOKEN}",
86: "refresh_token": "{REFRESH_TOKEN}",
87: "token_type": "bearer",
88: "expires_in": 1209600
89: }
90: For client-side applications
91: We use the Implicit Grant flow for client-side authorization. These
92: are typically applications that run entirely on the browser and issue Cross-Origin requests to our API. The difference is that you’ll get a single Access Token back that you can use immediately.
93: If a backend server is available, we recommend the Authorization Code flow, because it’s more secure and the access token is never
94: visible by a browser.
95: To start the authorization flow, redirect the user to the following URL:
96: https://id.getharvest.com/oauth2/authorize?client_id={CLIENT_ID}&response_type=token
97: This URL allows the user to authenticate on Harvest ID and lets them authorize access to their account(s) depending on your OAuth2
98: Application settings and their choice.
99: This endpoint accepts other parameters:
100: state–(optional) used to pass any value that will get sent back to you when redirecting back to your application.
101: redirect_uri–(optional) the default Redirect URL can be further customized here if needed, but needs to start with the Redirect
102: URL registered with your Application.
103: After a successful authorization, the user will be redirected back to the Redirect URL you specified when registering your OAuth2
104: application, or the redirect_uri you provided. These parameters will be attached:
105: access_token–the Access Token token that can be used to authenticate the requests on the user’s behalf.
106: token_type–will always be bearer.
107: expires_in–time in seconds until the token expires.
108: state–(optional) contains the original value for the state parameter that was passed at the beginning of the authorization.
109: scope–contains a list of space-separated strings describing the granted access scope. See the Scopes section for further
110: explanation.
111: Scopes and account access
112: Personal Access Tokens have the all scope by default, so you have full access to all of your accounts. For OAuth2 Applications,
113: it can vary depending on the options you selected and the authorization the user might give you.
114: The scope can contain one or more of these values:
115: harvest:{ACCOUNT_ID}–a Harvest account ID that the user granted access to.
116: forecast:{ACCOUNT_ID}–a Forecast account ID that the user granted access to.
117: harvest:all–the user granted access to all of their Harvest accounts.
118: forecast:all–the user granted access to all of their Forecast accounts.
119: all–the user granted access to all of their accounts.
120: If you registered your app as needing access to just one account, the user will choose which account to authorize, and you’ll only
121: get one scope back, either harvest:{ACCOUNT_ID} or forecast:{ACCOUNT_ID}, depending on which products you chose to work with.
122: If your app can work with multiple accounts, you can get any combination of those scopes depending on what the user chose to
123: authorize. Use that list or consume Harvest ID’s accounts endpoint to figure out which accounts you can access:
124: GET https://id.getharvest.com/api/v2/accounts
125: Example Request (note that the account ID is not necessary):
126: curl "https://id.getharvest.com/api/v2/accounts" \
127: -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
128: -H "User-Agent: MyApp ([email protected])"
129: Example Response:
130: {
131: "user": {
132: "id": 1,
133: "first_name": "Albert",
134: "last_name": "Llop",
135: "email": "[email protected]"
136: },
137: "accounts": [
138: {
139: "id": 10254,
140: "name": "Sterling Cooper Advertising Agency",
141: "product": "harvest"
142: },
143: {
144: "id": 88888,
145: "name": "Iridesco",
146: "product": "forecast"
147: },
148: {
149: "id": 88903,
150: "name": "Sterling Cooper Advertising Agency",
151: "product": "forecast"
152: }
153: ]
154: }
155: Still have questions? We’re happy to help!

1: Getting started with Airtable's Web API | Airtable Help Center
2: Contact support
3: Sign up for free
4: All Collections›Integrating with Airtable›API
5: Getting started with Airtable's Web API
6: Last updated 3 months ago
7: Plan availability
8: All plan types with varying call limitations
9: Permissions
10: Generally, workspace Owner or base Creator permissions are useful for working with Airtable's Web API.
11: Enterprise Scale and Business customers will also find that having admin permissions is necessary to access certain information via API calls.
12: Platform(s)
13: Web/Browser, Mac app, and Windows app
14: API record limits
15: You can access the documentation for the Web API here, or directly from your base by clicking on the Help button in the upper right-hand corner while you are logged in on a laptop or desktop. This will bring up a list of additional resources. You will find a link to the API documentation at the bottom of that list.
16: When you list records with Airtable's API, you won't necessarily get all of them at once. Instead, you will receive them in pages of up to 100 records at a time. As soon as a table has more than 100 records, you will need to make multiple requests, one per page.
17: If your table has 501 records, the results will be spread across 6 pages, and therefore 6 HTTP requests are needed to fully capture all of that table's records. Your first request might look something like this with your base's app id appxxx and the table name:
18: https://api.airtable.com/v0/appxxx/TableName
19: You will get the first page of records (under the "records" key), but if there is another page, you'll also get an "offset" that would look something like this:
20: "offset": "itrSJ1l4jlPyxEG6c/recxxx"
21: To fetch the next page (in other words, the next 100 records), you'll include that offset as a query parameter. For example:
22: https://api.airtable.com/v0/appxxx/TableName?offset=itrSJ1l4jlPyxEG6c%2Frecxxx
23: This will give you the records from the next page. If there's another page, you'll repeat the process—grab the offset and put it in the offset query parameter. When the response doesn't include an offset anymore, you know you've reached the last page and can stop.
24: You can use the pageSize parameter to change the number from 100 to a smaller number like 50, but 100 is the maximum and most users do not change this.
25: FAQs
26: What can I do with the Airtable Web API?
27: Consult the Web API Scopes documentation where you'll find a list of the various Web API endpoints and how each one functions.
28: How do I get started with Airtable’s Web API?
29: We recommend that you start with the Web API introduction here.
30: Is there a Web API rate limit?
31: Yes, the Web API has a rate limit of 5 requests per second, per base. This limit is the same across all pricing tiers and increased rate limits are not currently available. For more information, see the "Rate Limits" section of the API documentation.
32: Are there API call limits?
33: Yes. These vary by plan type:
34: Free plan - 1000 calls per workspace per month
35: Team plan - 100,000 calls per workspace per month
36: Business and Enterprise plans - Unlimited API calls (Still subject to other limits such as the rate limits discussed above)
37: When I fetch records with Airtable’s Web API, some of my fields are missing. Why is that?
38: Returned records do not include any fields with "empty" values, e.g. "", [], or false. If you need to get the names of all fields in your table, you can create one record with all fields populated, and make a request to fetch that record.
39: Can I get information about my base, such as the base schema, with the Web API?
40: Yes. The base schema scope is covered here.
41: Can I create a new base using the Web API?
42: Yes. The "Create base" endpoint (POST /v0/meta/bases) is available on all plans — Free, Team, Business, and Enterprise Scale— when you authenticate with a Personal Access Token (PAT) or OAuth token. You can use it to create a new base in any workspace where you have the appropriate permissions.
43: For more information about the Web API and authentication methods, see the Airtable Web API documentation.
44: Legacy API key caveat: If you're still using the deprecated API key authentication method, the Create base endpoint is restricted to Enterprise accounts with the Enterprise API feature enabled. Airtable phased out API key auth in favor of PATs and OAuth, so migrating to one of those methods will remove this restriction.
45: Why does “GET /v0/meta/bases” returns an empty list {"bases":[]} when my PAT has schema.bases:read?
46: A correct scope with an empty result usually means the token can't see any bases, not that your request is malformed. For enterprise users, the most common cause is an org-level setting — "Block API access to organization-owned bases and workspaces" in the admin panel — which prevents your PAT from accessing organization-owned bases until you're on the allowlist. Importantly, this block returns an empty list rather than an error, which can look like a scope or query problem. A telltale sign: when editing your token's access, if the only option is "All Resources" and you can't add an individual base, your org's API restriction is likely in effect. To resolve it, ask an internal Airtable admin to add you (or your service account) to the allowlist for that setting (see Settings – Airtable admin panel). Also confirm the bases you expect to see are ones your user account can actually access, since the token can only return those
47: Is there an endpoint to read a single table's schema?
48: The only schema endpoint is GET /v0/meta/bases/{baseId}/tables, which returns the schema for every table in the base (requiring the schema.bases:read scope). There is no dedicated "get one table's schema" GET endpoint. On a large base this response can be big and slow, so to avoid timeouts:
49: Cache the schema instead of fetching it on every run. Table schemas change rarely compared to data. Fetch the base schema once, cache it, and refetch only on a schedule or when a write actually fails due to a schema mismatch — this removes the per-run cost entirely.
50: Parse out the one table you need from the response client-side. You still download the whole-base schema, but combined with caching the frequency is low.
51: Handle the request robustly: set generous timeouts and use retry with backoff, and stay within the 5 requests/second per-base limit.
52: If reading a single table's schema cheaply is important to your workflow, let support know so it can be added to the feature request for a per-table schema endpoint.
53: Related Articles

56: Airtable API: Common troubleshooting
57: Managing API call limits in Airtable
58: Airtable API Deprecation Guidelines

1: Managing API call limits in Airtable | Airtable Help Center
2: Contact support
3: Sign up for free
4: All Collections›Integrating with Airtable›API
5: Managing API call limits in Airtable
6: Last updated 1 month ago
7: Plan availability
8: All plan types
9: Permissions
10: Rate limits apply to all plans (via the workspace or workspaces under that plan)
11: Monthly limits apply to Free and Team plans only
12: Platform(s)
13: Web/Browser, Mac app, and Windows app
14: Related reading
15: Getting started with Airtable's Web API
16: Create records
17: Update multiple records
18: Delete multiple records
19: What is an Airtable API call?
20: An API call is a request sent from an application to Airtable's servers, asking it to perform a specific action—like retrieving records from a base, creating a new record, or updating existing data. When Airtable receives the request, it processes it and sends back a response containing either the requested data or confirmation that the action was completed.
21: Airtable's Web API is RESTful, meaning it uses standard web protocols and returns data in JSON format. Every API call targets a specific base and table using a URL structure like:
22: https://api.airtable.com/v0/{baseId}/{tableId}
23: Common examples of API calls in Airtable include:
24: List records — Retrieve records from a table, returned in pages of up to 100 at a time
25: Create records — Add new records to a table from an external form, app, or automation
26: Update records — Modify field values in existing records
27: Delete records — Remove records from a table programmatically
28: Get base schema — Retrieve information about a base's structure, including its tables and fields
29: What's included in an API call?
30: Each API call typically contains:
31: The endpoint URL specifying the base and table you're accessing
32: The HTTP method
33: Authentication via a personal access token in the request header
34: Optional parameters like filters, sort order, or field selections
35: A request body (for create and update operations) containing the record data in JSON format
36: Understanding rate limits
37: Airtable API allows you to integrate data in Airtable with any external system. The API closely follows REST semantics, uses JSON to encode objects, and relies on standard HTTP codes to signal operation outcomes.
38: Airtable enforces a rate limit of 5 requests per second (per base) to ensure optimal user performance across all pricing tiers. Additionally, there is a limit of 50 requests per second for all traffic using personal access tokens from a given user or service account. If you exceed this rate, you will receive a 429 status code and must wait 30 seconds before subsequent requests will succeed. API integrations should pause and wait before retrying the API request—behavior handled automatically by the official JavaScript client—with back-off and retry logic.
39: For other implementations, you may employ the following strategies to manage your API usage effectively and stay within this rate limit.
40: Web API requests are subject to a timeout that is separate from rate limits. A request that takes too long to process, often a complex filterByFormula or a large page size, can time out and return an error even when you're within your rate limit. If you hit timeouts, reduce the page size, simplify the formula, or narrow the query.
41: Monthly call limits for Free and Team plans
42: Free plan: 1000 API calls per month
43: Team plan: 100000 API calls per month
44: Monthly calls for Free and Team plans are also limited to 5 requests per second rate limit.
45: Detailed API usage analytics are only available for Free plans. Because Team, Business, and Enterprise Scale plans have high or unlimited API call allowances, granular usage tracking is not provided for these plan types.
46: Where can I find API usage analytics on Free plan workspaces?
47: You must be a workspace owner to access a particular workspace’s settings page.
48: Open your Airtable home screen.
49: Choose a workspace that you own from the sidebar on the left side of the screen.
50: Click the … icon and click Workspace settings.
51: In the “Summary” section you’ll see a total count of “Public API calls” made across the workspace for the current month.
52: If you’d like to view the API usage for individual bases, then click the Usage tab and scroll through the “Bases” section to find each base’s API call usage this month, if there is any.
53: Additionally, you can scroll until you find the “Public API Usage” section to see specific public API usage information.
54: What happens if I exceed limits on the Free plan?
55: API call limits are fixed per workspace plan and cannot be adjusted on a per-account basis. We're unable to grant additional API calls beyond your plan's monthly allowance or make exceptions to these limits. If you find you're consistently reaching your limit, we'd recommend upgrading to a plan with a higher allocation to better fit your needs.
56: The 30-day grace period is only available once. If you exceed call limits in the future, a new grace period is unavailable.
57: If you exceed your Free plan's call limit, a 30-day grace period is initiated, allowing you to continue using the API for that period. After the grace period ends, any API calls over the limit will be blocked until the month resets. API limits reset on the first day of each calendar month.
58: What happens if I exceed limits on the Team plan?
59: If you exceed your Team plan's call limit, any API calls will slow down to 2 requests per second until the month resets. API limits reset on the first day of each calendar month.
60: If you use a third-party integration with Airtable that performs API requests on your behalf, it is the third party's responsibility to handle rate limits appropriately. We suggest contacting the third-party support team for further details if you encounter rate limit errors.
61: Airtable may also update the enforced API rate limits or implement additional limitations, including changes based on pricing plans.
62: Rate limit management strategies
63: Batching overview - Airtable's API supports batching, allowing you to process multiple records per request instead of one at a time. Batching can handle up to 10 records per request, enabling you to update up to 50 records per second. To learn more about batching in Airtable, review our API documentation:
64: Create records
65: Update multiple records
66: Delete multiple records
67: Using the performUpsert parameter - The performUpsert parameter endpoint allows users to find, create, and update records in a single call, reducing the number of necessary API requests.
68: Avoiding duplicate actions - Avoid updating all records, including duplicates, as this can lead to unnecessary processing and transmission of unchanged records.
69: Using Sync API - The Sync API feature allows users to sync CSV data with up to 10,000 rows per request instead of 10 records per request using the regular create or update records JSON endpoints—which can significantly reduce the number of necessary API requests.
70: Caching - One approach for managing Airtable’s rate limit is using a caching mechanism to handle a high volume of read and list requests. Some developers choose to host a server running an API proxy that fetches and caches Airtable data. This approach can spread your requests over a longer period, helping you avoid hitting the API limits.
71: Managing API usage is crucial to ensure smooth and uninterrupted interactions with your Airtable data. By implementing the above-mentioned strategies, you can stay within the rate limit and optimize your API operations.
72: FAQs
73: What are the API call limits for each plan?
74: Airtable's API call limits vary by plan:
75: Free: 1,000 API calls per workspace per month. Once exceeded, a 30-day grace period begins.
76: Team: 100,000 API calls per workspace per month. Once the limit is reached, API calls are throttled to 2 requests per second.
77: Business / Enterprise Scale: No monthly call cap; rate limiting applies per base.
78: Why am I getting a 429 error even though my request rate is very low?
79: A 429 has two possible causes:
80: Monthly call cap: Applies to Free (1,000 calls/workspace/month) and Team (100,000/month) plans. If you're well under 5 requests/second but still seeing 429s, you've most likely reached your monthly cap. Check your usage on a Free-plan workspace via Workspace settings → Usage. Note that all Web API calls — including metadata/schema calls like GET /v0/meta/bases/{baseId}/tables — count toward these same limits; there is no separate, looser metadata allowance.
81: Per-base rate limit: 5 requests/second per base, or 50/second per personal access token, which is unlikely if you're only sending a few requests per minute.
82: Why am I receiving a 429 error on every API request, but my workspace usage shows very few calls?
83: The most common reason is that you're checking the wrong workspace. API call limits are counted per workspace (Free = 1,000 calls/month), and your integration is hitting whichever workspace contains the base it's actually calling — which may not be the workspace you opened. If one workspace shows near-zero usage but you're still 429ing on every request, another workspace likely holds the base being called and is over its monthly cap. To find it: identify the base your app/integration (Zite, Make, a script, etc.) connects to, open the Usage tab of that base's workspace (Workspace settings → Usage), and check the "Public API calls" figure. If that workspace is over its monthly limit, every request will return 429 until the workspace is upgraded or the monthly counter resets.
84: Receiving a 429 error on every request, continuing even with no activity, points to the monthly cap on the relevant workspace — not the per-second rate limit.
85: Once you've confirmed (in the correct workspace's Usage tab) that the workspace is over its monthly API allowance, the options are: wait for the monthly reset (the counter resets at the start of the next calendar month), or upgrade the workspace to a plan with a higher allowance — Team includes 100,000 calls/month, and Business and Enterprise Scale include unlimited calls. Note the monthly cap is fixed per workspace and can't be raised on a per-account basis, and any one-time grace period is available only once. To avoid recurring overages, reduce unnecessary calls (cache results, batch requests, and avoid frequent polling — for example, repeated login/credential-validation calls from an app each count as API calls).
86: Do third-party integrations count against my API quota?
87: Yes. Requests made by third-party integrations and tools that connect through your Airtable account consume the same monthly Public API quota as your own API calls. If you're approaching your limit, review which connected integrations are making requests on your behalf.
88: What happens if I downgrade from Team to Free mid-month after using more than 1,000 API calls?
89: API calls are counted per workspace for each calendar month (UTC), no matter which plan the workspace was on when the calls were made. A downgrade takes effect at the end of your current billing cycle, which can fall partway through a calendar month. From that date, every API call the workspace made earlier in the month, including calls made on the Team plan, counts toward the Free plan's limit of 1,000 calls per month.
90: If the workspace is already over 1,000 calls for the month when it moves to the Free plan, there are a couple of different possibilities of how Airtable will handle the exceeded limitation:
91: If the workspace hasn't used its one-time grace period, a 30-day grace period begins and we'll email you. API access continues during the grace period, so integrations that use bases in the workspace keep running.
92: If the workspace has already used its grace period, API requests to bases in the workspace return a 429 error until the monthly count resets on the first day of the next calendar month (UTC). Integrations that rely on those bases stop working until then. If you upgrade the workspace again, access comes back within a few minutes.
93: Airtable updates API usage and checks it against plan limits once a day, so the grace period or block may start a day or two after the downgrade takes effect.
94: To avoid interruptions, check which integrations are making API calls in the workspace before you downgrade (you can see current usage on the workspace settings page), and reduce or pause them if the workspace is likely to go over the Free plan's limit. Learn more in our Upgrading and downgrading your Airtable workspace plan article.

12: What is ClickUp MCP?
13: Your AI models and agents can use our official MCP (Model Context Protocol) server to access your ClickUp data in a simple and secure way. It's designed to work seamlessly with popular AI assistants like ChatGPT, Cursor, and Claude.
14: ClickUp MCP is available on all plans.
15: You can set up the ClickUp MCP server with any app that supports MCP servers, like Claude, Cursor, or VS Code.
16: Workspaces are being upgraded to our new plans. Not all Workspaces have been upgraded yet. Learn more
17: What can I do with the ClickUp MCP server?
18: Orchestrate task workflows: Create, enrich, and route tasks with assignees, Priorities, and due dates across Lists and Spaces.
19: Build executive reports: Produce release notes, status updates, and portfolio rollups consolidated from tasks, comments, and Docs.
20: Track time: Start and stop timers, log historical entries, and fetch entries.
21: Answer questions from work: Search tasks, Docs, and comments to deliver quick, context-rich answers.
22: Collaborate in comments and Chat: Summarize threads, extract action items, and post updates. Attach files and images to Channel messages, Posts, and Channel thread replies.
23: Available tools
24: ClickUp's MCP server enables AI assistants like ChatGPT, Claude, Cursor, or VS Code, to integrate with ClickUp's tools and data. This means your AI assistant can now execute actions, retrieve information, and provide intelligent, context-aware insights instantly.
25: For a full list of supported tools, read this developer article.
26: Before you connect an MCP client, review the rate limits section below to learn which rate limits apply to your Workspace and how usage is counted.
27: Example requests
28: Below are some examples of requests you could make after you've connected your AI assistant to ClickUp's MCP server:
29: Create a task for this bug we're working on.
30: Find all my incomplete tasks due this week.
31: List all milestones in the Product Launch project.
32: How many hours has the team spent on clients this month?
33: Setup instructions
34: For step-by-step setup instructions, read our MCP Server Setup Instructions article.
35: Rate limits
36: ClickUp's MCP Server has rate limits that depend on two criteria:
37: If your Workspace has purchased the Everything AI add-on.
38: Your Workspace plan.
39: MCP rate limits and public API rate limits are two separate limits. The public API limits requests per minute, per token. Without the Everything AI add-on, ClickUp MCP limits calls per rolling 24-hour period instead.
40: With the Everything AI add-on
41: If your Workspace has purchased the Everything AI add-on, your MCP rate limits are the same as the rate limits for our Public API which vary by plan.
42: On our new plans that include ClickUp AI, AI is included with your plan instead of as separate add-ons.
43: With the add-on, the rolling 24-hour limit no longer applies. Your MCP requests count toward the same per-minute, per-token limit as the public API:
44: Free Forever, Unlimited, and Business Plans: 100 requests per minute, per token.
45: Business Plus Plan: 1,000 requests per minute, per token.
46: Enterprise Plan: 10,000 requests per minute, per token.
47: On our new plans that include ClickUp AI, daily MCP limits differ by plan.
48: Without the Everything AI add-on
49: If your Workspace has not purchased the Everything AI add-on, your MCP usage is subject to the following daily rate limits by plan:
50: Free Forever Plan: 100 calls per 24 hours.
51: Unlimited Plan: 300 calls per 24 hours.
52: Business Plan: 1,000 calls per 24 hours.
53: Business Plus Plan: 2,500 calls per 24 hours.
54: Enterprise Plan: 5,000 calls per 24 hours.
55: Each person has their own daily limit. All the MCP clients you connect, such as Claude and Cursor, share that limit.
56: Every MCP request counts toward the limit, including everyday actions like reading, creating, and updating tasks. It isn't limited to AI-generated actions.
57: Rolling 24 hour rate limits
58: The rolling 24 hour rate limit begins with your first request.
59: For example, if your first MCP request on Monday is at 1pm and you reach your plan's daily limit by Tuesday at 11am, you will be rate limited until 1pm on Tuesday, 24 hours after your first request.
60: Attempting to send requests while rate limited does not extend the 24 hour window.
61: Rate limits cannot be reset.
62: When you reach the limit, MCP requests return a 429 RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED error until the rolling 24 hour window resets.
63: FAQ
64: Frequently asked questions about the ClickUp MCP server.
65: Can I monitor how many MCP calls my Workspace has used?
66: Not at this time.
67: Can I authenticate with my own API keys or access tokens?
68: No, only OAuth is supported. OAuth is an industry-standard protocol that provides secure, delegated access. It lets you grant limited access to your resources without sharing credentials, supports granular permissions, and makes it easy to revoke access.
69: API keys are less secure because they’re static, usually have broad access, and are harder to manage or revoke if compromised.
70: Can I use ClickUp MCP to search external apps I've connected to my ClickUp Workspace?
71: No, Connected Search can only be used from within your Workspace. For a list of all external apps that support Connected Search, read our Connected Search article.
72: Do admins need to take any action inside ClickUp before setting up an external tool like Claude or ChatGPT?
73: No action is needed inside ClickUp. ClickUp MCP will provide the list of available tools.
74: Will my custom LLM connect?
75: Yes, if your team builds an MCP client implementation that meets the following criteria:
76: Implements the JSON-RPC 2.0 protocol over HTTP
77: Supports OAuth 2.1 with PKCE authentication
78: Follows the MCP specification

13: Connect to the Coda MCP
14: The Coda MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a connection layer that enables AI clients - like Cursor, Claude, etc. - to read and write to your Coda docs using plain-language prompts. Instead of clicking through the Coda UI, you describe what you want in the chat window of your chosen client, and the AI carries it out directly in your doc. Think of it as giving an AI agent the same access to your Coda workspace that you have, and letting it act on your behalf based on your instructions.
15: The following article will walk you through the steps of connecting your preferred AI tool to the Coda MCP. Once you’ve connected, you can check out this article for some helpful guidance and examples on using the Coda MCP.
16: ℹ️ The Coda MCP is in beta. Behavior and available tools are subject to change.
17: Within this article, you’ll find...
18: Supported clients
19: Connect ChatGPT with Coda MCP
20: Connect Claude Chat & Cowork with Coda MCP
21: Connect Claude Code with Coda MCP
22: Connect Copilot Studio with Coda MCP
23: Connect Cursor with Coda MCP
24: Connect OpenAI Codex CLI with Coda MCP
25: Connect Google Antigravity with Coda MCP
26: FAQs
27: Supported clients
28: The table below lists the clients for which Coda MCP is currently well supported. We've also included the method of authentication available for each client. To learn more about these different authentication methods, refer to this article.
29: Supported client
30: Method of authentication
31: ChatGPT
32: OAuth 2
33: Claude (including Claude Code, Claude Cowork, and Claude Chat)
34: OAuth 2
35: CoPilot Studio
36: Personal Access Tokens
37: Cursor
38: OAuth 2

40: Personal Access Tokens
