42: Personal Access Tokens
43: You can find specific instructions for connecting to each of these clients in the subsequent sections.
44: Connect ChatGPT with Coda MCP
45: Follow the steps below to connect ChatGPT with Coda MCP:
46: Within ChatGPT, click into the Apps tab of the left panel
47: Enter "Coda" in the search bar
48: Select Coda from the search results, then click Connect
49: Note: If you see Disabled by admin instead of Connect, this likely indicates that the admin of your account has disabled connecting to new apps. We suggest contacting your admin and requesting they enable the Coda app for you or your org. Refer to this documentation to learn more.
50: Click Sign in with Coda
51: A new tab will open, where you will be prompted to sign into Coda and grant ChatGPT the necessary access.
52: Once authentication has been completed, you'll be redirected back to ChatGTP and should see a Coda is now connected confirmation.
53: You should now be successfully connected to the Coda MCP and can start using it within your chats.
54: Tip: If you would like to give ChatGPT more context when working with Coda, look for the Reference memories and chats setting during the connection process (right below the Sign in with Coda button). This setting is toggled off by default, but you can toggle it on if desired. And if you've already connected to Coda and want to change this setting retroactively, just click on your account name in the lower-left > Settings > Apps > Coda app > toggle on/off the Reference memories and chats option.
55: Connect Claude Chat & Cowork with Coda MCP
56: Whether you use Claude Chat or Claude Cowork, this section will help you connect Claude to the Coda MCP.
57: ℹ️ Before you begin: If you are using Claude Desktop for either Chat or Cowork, you must have Node.js v20.18.1 or higher installed on your device in order to complete the connection to Coda MCP.
58: To check your Node.js version, open Terminal (Mac) or Command Prompt (Windows) and run node --version. If the version is below v20.18.1, or you see command not found, then jump to the subsection below on installing Node.
59: Check if you have multiple Node versions by running nvm ls in Terminal (Mac) or nvm list in Command Prompt (Windows). If you see multiple versions, you must follow the steps described in the subsection below before continuing — setup will fail otherwise.
60: Node.js is not a requirement if accessing Claude Chat via web browser.
61: To connect Claude Chat or Cowork to the Coda MCP:
62: Open Claude
63: In the lower-left corner, click on your account name, then select Settings
64: Click into the Connectors section
65: If you're part of a Team or Enterprise plan on Claude, and your admin has configured Coda MCP as a connector, you may see Coda already in the list of connectors (see FAQ at the bottom of this article to learn more). If so, simply click the corresponding Connect button and follow the prompts to authenticate your account. If you do not see Coda already in the list of connectors, then jump to the next step to learn about adding custom connectors.
66: Scroll to the bottom of the list of connectors, and select Add custom connectors
67: Note that if an enterprise manages your Claude account, your administrators may have limited the ability to add custom connectors. In these cases, this button will be greyed out, and you will see this message: “Contact an organization owner to add custom connectors.” Before you can move forward, your admin will either need to 1) modify your permissions or 2) pre-configure Coda MCP for your org (see FAQ below) so that it shows up in the connector list.
68: Give your connector a name, then enter the following URL into the Remote MCP Server URL field: https://coda.io/apis/mcp
69: Click Add
70: Now find the newly added connector in the list, and click Connect
71: Follow the prompts to allow Claude access to Coda
72: Once authorized, you’re all set. You can start taking actions in Coda with Claude!
73: ℹ️ To learn more about adding custom connectors to Claude, refer to their documentation here.
74: Resolve Node issues when connecting to Claude desktop
75: Download the latest version of Node.js
76: Claude Desktop requires a tool called Node.js to run the Coda MCP connection. To install the latest version of Node, follow these steps:
77: Hit Cmd+Space → Terminal to open Terminal.
78: In Terminal, type or paste the following command:
79: /bin/bash -c "$(curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Homebrew/install/HEAD/install.sh)"
80: Hit Enter.
81: Terminal will ask for your Mac login password. When you type it, nothing will appear on screen — no dots, no asterisks, nothing. This is completely normal! Just type your password carefully and hit Enter.
82: The installation may take a few minutes. Make sure to pay attention to Homebrew's instructions for next steps. You'll likely need to run three individual commands in your terminal to add Homebrew to your PATH — two start with echo and one starts with eval.
83: Wait until you see the regular prompt again (ending with % or $). Then install Node.js by pasting the following command:
84: brew install node
85: Hit Enter.
86: Verify everything is installed correctly by pasting the following command:
87: npx --version
88: Hit Enter.
89: If you see a version number (like 10.8.2), you're good to move on. If it says command not found, try closing and reopening Terminal, then run npx --version again.
90: If Node is installed but you’re still running into errors...
91: For instance, you might be seeing "File is not defined," "Cannot find module 'node:path,'" or "Unsupported engine" errors when connecting the Coda MCP on Claude Desktop. This can happen if you have multiple Node.js versions installed and your system is defaulting to the wrong one. To resolve this, follow the steps below:
92: Step 1: Find your Node 20 path
93: Hit Cmd+Space → Terminal to open Terminal.
94: In Terminal, type or paste the following command:
95: nvm which 20
96: Hit Enter.
97: This should print a path like /Users/yourname/.nvm/versions/node/v20.x.x/bin/node. Copy everything up to and including /bin/ — you'll need it in the next step.
98: If this command says N/A or fails, install Node 20 first:
99: nvm install 20
100: Then run nvm which 20 again.
101: Step 2: Connect to the Coda MCP via the Claude UI
102: Follow the steps in the "Connect Claude Chat & Cowork to Coda MCP" section of this article.
103: Step 3: Clear the npm cache
104: Hit Cmd+Space → Terminal to open Terminal.
105: In Terminal, type or paste the following command:
106: rm -rf ~/.npm/_npx
107: Hit Enter.
108: Step 4: Restart Claude Desktop
109: Fully quit and reopen Claude Desktop.
110: The MCP Server should now connect successfully.
111: Windows users: The steps are the same, with a few differences:
112: To find your Node 20 path, run nvm which 20 in Command Prompt.
113: Open Command Prompt by hitting Win+R, typing cmd, and hitting Enter.
114: The path will look like C:\Users\yourname\AppData\Roaming\nvm\v20.x.x.
115: When updating your config, set "command" to that path followed by npx.cmd, and update the new "PATH" to use that same folder with semicolons instead of colons.
116: To clear the npm cache, run rmdir /s /q %LOCALAPPDATA%\npm-cache_npx.
117: Connect Claude Code with Coda MCP
118: To connect Claude Code to the Coda MCP, follow these steps:
119: To start, open a fresh terminal window and run the following block:
120: claude mcp add --transport http Coda https://coda.io/apis/mcp
121: Once the above has run, type Claude into your terminal and hit Enter
122: Then type /mcp into the terminal and hit Enter again.
123: You should now see a notice that Coda MCP needs authentication. Click Enter and select Authenticate.
124: This will open a browser window where you'll be asked to allow Claude Code access to Coda. You'll also see that the redirect URL is localhost, which is expected based on how Claude handles OAuth. Follow the prompts to accept and proceed. You should then see an Authentication Successful confirmation.
125: To confirm connection to the Coda MCP, return to your terminal window and enter the following:
126: Are you connected to the Coda MCP?
127: If successful, you’ll see a success message with Coda MCP tools. You can now start building in Coda using Claude Code!
128: ℹ️ Troubleshooting & Tips:
129: If you have already used another MCP that accesses Coda: Use claude mcp remove <mcp-name> in this case.
130: If you have directories named “Coda” in your filepath: Change the directory and try again.
131: Find more details in Claude’s MCP documentation.
132: Connect Copilot Studio with Coda MCP
133: To connect Copilot Studio with the Coda MCP, you will need to authenticate via Personal Access Tokens from your Coda account. Follow the steps below to learn more:
134: First, you’ll need to generate a personal access token from your Coda account page. You can click here (or scroll to the API settings section of your account page, then click Generate API token). Give your token a memorable name, ensure that the restriction type is MCP, and choose the type of access. Then click the Generate API token button to create. Once created, click the Copy token button to copy it to your clipboard.
135: Next, within Copilot Studio, open the agent you want to connect to the MCP.
136: From the menu across the top of the agent page, select Tools, then click the + Add a tool button.
137: Within the Create new options, select Model Context Protocol.
138: Enter the following info:
139: Server name and Server Description: fill these in as you see fit (for instance "Coda MCP" and "Coda MCP to read and write to docs"
140: Server URL: https://coda.io/apis/mcp
141: Authorization: Select the API Key option. Then for the Type choose Header, and for the Header name enter Authorization
142: Once all the above info has been entered, hit Create.
143: You'll then see the newly added tool, but you'll notice it's not yet connected. Click on Not connected and select Create new connection.
144: In the hidden field, enter the following string: Bearer Your-Coda-Auth-Token - making sure to replace Your-Coda-Auth-Token with the token you generated in step 1.
145: For instance, Bearer 1bxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx
146: Hit Create button to finalize the connection.
147: Connect Cursor with Coda MCP
148: To connect Cursor with Coda MCP, follow these steps:
149: Within your Cursor app, simply open up Cursor Settings and select the Tools & MCP section.
150: Then click New MCP Server. This will open a new mcp.json file.
151: Tip: Only enable the MCPs you are currently working with to save context and improve agent accuracy
152: Inside your mcp.json file in Cursor, insert the following code:
153: {
154: "mcpServers": {
155: "Coda": {
156: "url": "https://coda.io/apis/mcp"
157: }
158: }
159: }
160: Once you’ve made the above edits, the file should be saved automatically, and you should now be connected to the Coda MCP. You can verify by checking the tools list (under Tools & MCP) or asking Cursor about your tools in Coda.
161: Tip: If you don’t see your MCP show up at this stage, restart Cursor.
162: You can now use the Cursor agent to put the Coda MCP to work 🚀
163: ℹ️ To learn more about connecting MCPs in Cursor, please refer to Cursor’s documentation.
164: Connect OpenAI Codex CLI with Coda MCP
165: To connect OpenAI Codex with Coda MCP, you will need to use Personal Access Tokens from your Coda Account page. Follow the steps below to learn more.
166: To connect Codex CLI with Coda MCP, follow these steps:
167: First, you’ll need to generate an auth token from your Coda account page. You can click here (or scroll to the API settings section of your account page, then click Generate API token). Give your token a memorable name, ensure that the restriction type is MCP, and choose the type of access. Then click the Generate API token button to create. Once created, click the Copy token button to copy it to your clipboard.
168: Open a fresh terminal window and paste the block below into it, making sure to replace the Your-Coda-Auth-Token section with the auth token you generated and copied in the previous step.
169: codex mcp add Coda -- npx -y mcp-remote https://coda.io/apis/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer Your-Coda-Auth-Token"
170: Start Codex by typing codex into your terminal. You should be all set and can start using the Coda MCP!
171: ℹ️ For more details on connecting MCPs to OpenAI Codex, we suggest checking out their first-party documentation.
172: Connect Google Antigravity with Coda MCP
173: To connect Google Antigravity with Coda MCP, you will need to use Personal Access Tokens from your Coda Account page. Follow the steps below to learn more.
174: Follow these steps to connect Google Antigravity with Coda MCP:
175: First, you’ll need to generate an auth token from your Coda account page. You can click here (or scroll to the API settings section of your account page, then click Generate API token). Give your token a memorable name, ensure that the restriction type is MCP, and choose the type of access. Then click the Generate API token button to create. Once created, click the Copy token button to copy it to your clipboard.
176: Open Google Antigravity. Within the agent panel, click on the horizontal three-dot menu in the upper-right corner, and select MCP Servers. Then click Manage MCP Servers.
177: Now click the View raw config option at the top of the page and enter the following details - making sure to replace the Your-Coda-MCP-Auth-Token section with the auth token you generated and copied in the previous step.
178: {
179: "mcpServers": {
180: "Coda": {
181: "serverUrl": "https://coda.io/apis/mcp",
182: "headers": {
183: "Authorization": "Bearer Your-Coda-MCP-Auth-Token"
184: }
185: }
186: }
187: }
188: Save your settings, and hit refresh in Antigravity (if it doesn’t automatically refresh on its own). Coda should now appear as an available MCP tool in Antigravity.
189: ℹ️ For more details on connecting MCPs to Google Antigravity, please refer to their documentation.
190: FAQs
191: Can I connect Coda MCP to other AI tools not listed in this article?
192: You should be able to connect the Coda MCP to any AI client that supports creating custom MCP connections. In most cases, you will need to use Personal Access Tokens to complete the connection.
193: To acquire these access tokens from Coda, you can click here (or scroll to the API settings section of your account page, then click Generate API token). Give your token a memorable name, ensure that the restriction type is MCP, and choose the type of access. Then click the Generate API token button to create. Once created, click the Copy token button to copy it to your clipboard.
194: Do I have to be a Doc Maker to connect to the Coda MCP?
195: No - you do not have to be a Doc Maker to connect to the Coda MCP. Anyone can connect to the Coda MCP, but what you can do from there does depend on your role in Coda.
196: Doc Makers on paid Coda plans will have access to the full Coda MCP experience, including all of the available tools and endpoints.
197: Doc Makers on free plans can utilize a “free taste” of the Coda MCP (30 requests per week, with a max of 60 requests per month). During this “free taste,” you can utilize all of the tools of the MCP.
198: Editors also have access to a “free taste” of the Coda MCP (30 requests per week, with a max of 60 requests per month). However, they are limited to only the “read” type tools and actions. In other words, editors will not be able to use the MCP to update or add content, or to take other Doc Maker actions.
199: Can I configure Coda MCP as a custom connector in Claude, so the rest of my organization can easily connect?
200: Yes - if you are on a Team or Enterprise plan in Claude, an Owner or Primary Owner can configure Coda MCP as a custom connector on behalf of your org. Once this is done, organization members can easily find the Coda MCP in their available connectors and will be able to connect in a few short clicks.
201: To complete this configuration on behalf of your organization, follow these steps:
202: Ensure you're logged into Claude as an Owner or Primary Owner
203: Open Organization settings
204: Click into the Connectors tab
205: In the upper-right, click the Add button, hover over the Custom option, then select Web
206: Next, enter the following URL in the appropriate field: https://coda.io/apis/mcp
207: Finally, click Add
208: Now, when members of your org navigate to the Connectors section of their Claude settings, they will see Coda as an available connector (with a custom label). They'll just need to click the Connect button, then follow the prompts to authenticate.
209: Read more about configuring and connecting to custom connectors in Claude here.
210: Why am I getting a 401 error when trying to use my auth token to connect?
211: You may see this error when the auth token has the incorrect restriction type. To resolve this, we suggest creating a new auth token via your Coda account settings, this time ensuring that you select MCP for the restriction type. Then attempt the connection again using this new token.
212: What auth scopes are used when connecting to the Coda MCP?
213: When connecting the Coda MCP via OAuth 2 (as with ChatGPT, Claude, and Cursor) the auth scope will automatically be set to read and write.
214: When connecting via Personal Access Tokens (as described for Google Antigravity and OpenAI Codex), you have the option to choose between three scopes: read only, write only, read and write.
215: Therefore, if you wish to limit the scope to read only or write only, we recommend connecting via Personal Access Tokens instead of OAuth 2.
216: How do I submit bugs or feedback for the MCP?
217: Please submit any bugs or feedback via this form. Thank you in advance!
218: Can I connect the Coda MCP to Claude Code using Personal Access Tokens, rather than OAuth?
219: Yes! In this article, we describe the process of connecting the MCP to Claude Code via OAuth. But if you instead wish to connect to the MCP using Personal Access Tokens, you can do so by following these steps:
220: First, you’ll need to generate an auth token from your Coda account page. You can click here (or scroll to the API settings section of your account page, then click Generate API token). Give your token a memorable name, ensure that the restriction type is MCP, and choose the type of access. Then click the Generate API token button to create. Once created, click the Copy token button to copy it to your clipboard.
221: Next, open a fresh terminal window and paste in the following block, making sure to replace the Your-Coda-Auth-Token section with the auth token you generated and copied in the previous step.
222: claude mcp add --transport http Coda
223: https://coda.io/apis/mcp --header
224: "Authorization: Bearer Your-Coda-Auth-Token"
225: Confirm that your MCP got added correctly by pasting the following command into the terminal:
226: claude mcp list
227: Start Claude Code by typing claude . into your terminal and ask it to connect to the Coda MCP.
228: Connect to the Coda MCP
229: If successful, you’ll see a success message with Coda MCP tools. You can now start building in Coda using Claude Code!
230: Can I connect to Cursor using Personal Access Tokens, rather than OAuth?
231: Yes! In this article, we describe the process of connecting the MCP to Cursor via OAuth. But if you instead wish to connect to the MCP using Personal Access Tokens, you can do so by following these steps:
232: Within your Cursor app, simply open up Cursor Settings and select the Tools & MCP section.
233: Then click New MCP Server. This will open a new mcp.json file.
234: Tip: Only enable the MCPs you are currently working with to save context and improve agent accuracy
235: Next, you’ll need to generate an auth token from your Coda account page. You can click here (or scroll to the API settings section of your account page, then click Generate API token). Give your token a memorable name, ensure that the restriction type is MCP, and choose the type of access. Then click the Generate API token button to create. Once created, click the Copy token button to copy it to your clipboard.
236: Now, inside your mcp.json file in Cursor, insert the following code, making sure to replace the Your-Coda-Auth-Token section with the auth token you generated and copied in the previous step.
237: {
238: "mcpServers": {
239: "Coda": {
240: "url": "https://coda.io/apis/mcp",
241: "headers": {
242: "Authorization": "Bearer Your-Coda-Auth-Token"
243: }
244: }
245: }
246: }
247: Once you’ve made the above edits, the file should be saved automatically, and you should now be connected to the Coda MCP. You can verify by checking the tools list (under Tools & MCP) or asking Cursor about your tools in Coda.
248: Tip: If you don’t see your MCP show up at this stage, restart Cursor.

When a token passes that cap, requests using it fail with UNAUTHORIZED - Invalid authentication token. If you're on an enterprise organization and a token that previously worked stops being accepted, ask your admin whether a token lifetime policy is in effect. To resolve it, ask one of your internal Airtable admins to add you (or your service account) to the allowlist for that setting. If the admin needs guidance, point them to Settings – Airtable admin panel. The other documented causes remain worth ruling out: field/table editing permissions and an incorrect or inaccessible base/workspace ID.

evidence.observation: quote: Some MCP clients register themselves with Airtable using Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD) rather than dynamic client registration, and that path can be rejected at authorization. candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: In other clients, look for an equivalent OAuth setting that selects dynamic client registration — sometimes labeled DCR — as the registration method. evidence.observation: quote: Can I use MCP to access Airtable Interfaces?

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Yes, for supported page layouts. If you have interface-only access to a base, you can use MCP to discover your interface pages (list_pages_for_base), list records shown on a page (list_records_for_page), and drill into record details (get_record_for_page). The data returned respects the same permissions as your interface—you'll only see data that your interface pages make available to you. Not every interface page layout is supported yet. If a page's layout isn't supported, the request fails and your assistant may say that no matching records were found. See "Limitations and dependencies" above.

evidence.observation: quote: Expiration. Refresh an expired access token using a valid refresh token, or request a new client-credentials token. If the refresh token has expired, complete authorization again. See refresh an access token.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: The monday.com platform API utilizes personal V2 API tokens to authenticate requests and identify the user making the call. These tokens are unique to each user and have no explicit length.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Personal tokens allow you to interact with the API using your own user account. Their permissions mirror what you can do in the monday.com UI, ensuring that API access is consistent with your platform-level permissions.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: If you don't have a monday.com account yet, create a free developer account to get an API token and start testing.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: For example: If you don't have permission to access a certain workspace via the UI, you won't have permission using your personal API token either.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: You can access your API token in two ways, depending on your user type.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: All users with API access can follow these steps to access their API token:

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Click API token > Show.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Select Administration > Connections > Personal API token.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Once you have your token, you can make requests with the API by passing the token in the Authorization header.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: curl -X POST https://api.monday.com/v2 \

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: API tokens can be regenerated at any time. However, this will immediately invalidate your current token, so be sure to update any integrations using it.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Click API token > Regenerate.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Select Administration > Connections > Personal API token.

evidence.observation: quote: Monthly call cap: Applies to Free (1,000 calls/workspace/month) and Team (100,000/month) plans. Note that all Web API calls — including metadata/schema calls like GET /v0/meta/bases/{baseId}/tables — count toward these same limits; there is no separate, looser metadata allowance.

evidence.observation: quote: Why am I receiving a 429 error on every API request, but my workspace usage shows very few calls?

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: The most common reason is that you're checking the wrong workspace. API call limits are counted per workspace (Free = 1,000 calls/month), and your integration is hitting whichever workspace contains the base it's actually calling — which may not be the workspace you opened. If one workspace shows near-zero usage but you're still 429ing on every request, another workspace likely holds the base being called and is over its monthly cap. To find it: identify the base your app/integration (Zite, Make, a script, etc.) connects to, open the Usage tab of that base's workspace (Workspace settings → Usage), and check the "Public API calls" figure. If that workspace is over its monthly limit, every request will return 429 until the workspace is upgraded or the monthly counter resets.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: Once you've confirmed (in the correct workspace's Usage tab) that the workspace is over its monthly API allowance, the options are: wait for the monthly reset (the counter resets at the start of the next calendar month), or upgrade the workspace to a plan with a higher allowance — Team includes 100,000 calls/month, and Business and Enterprise Scale include unlimited calls. Note the monthly cap is fixed per workspace and can't be raised on a per-account basis, and any one-time grace period is available only once. To avoid recurring overages, reduce unnecessary calls (cache results, batch requests, and avoid frequent polling — for example, repeated login/credential-validation calls from an app each count as API calls).

From that date, every API call the workspace made earlier in the month, including calls made on the Team plan, counts toward the Free plan's limit of 1,000 calls per month.

candidate_excerpts.warning: Candidate excerpt only; do not promote automatically

evidence.observation: quote: If the workspace hasn't used its one-time grace period, a 30-day grace period begins and we'll email you. API access continues during the grace period, so integrations that use bases in the workspace keep running.

evidence_rules:
# Research format and evidence rules

Contract version 1.1, 2026-11-23 (updated in Task 06 from v1.0 based on verified Task 05 pilot findings; sealed v1.0 runs retain their frozen contract snapshots).

### Changelog (v1.0 → v1.1)
- Added `vendor_approval_required` to `credential_eligibility.{testing,production}` to separate platform/vendor API-access review (e.g., Google Ads Explorer/Basic/Standard application) from commercial/agency `partner_approval_required`.
- Clarified edition-matching for `mcp.discovery`: a community MCP targeting a different product edition (e.g., personal web/cookie scraping vs. Enterprise REST API) must not assert `found` for the Enterprise scope without explicit edition alignment.
- Reinforced per-claim attachment: every material detail in a claim (including `purpose` and MCP tool-list observations) must be anchored inside that claim's own attached evidence array and locator line range.

## Files and migration

- `data/apps.json` is the 100-app identity roster, in assignment order. Its provenance identifies the original conversation and user turn. Original app/hint Markdown is retained verbatim, including link targets and parenthetical hints. Categories and normalized names match the audited roster.
- `legacy_candidate_doc_urls` preserves the scaffold's URL leads with their separate provenance. Neither these URLs nor assignment hints establish auth, access, API or MCP findings. Do not inherit the old OAUTH/APIKEY/GATED/MCP lists, generic descriptions, breadth placeholders or buildability labels.
- `schemas/record.json` is a Draft 2020-12 schema for one app in one immutable run. `examples/unresearched-record.json` is a format example, excluded from research and accuracy totals.
- Initialize substantive claims as `not_researched`, with null values and empty evidence. Keep prior artifacts intact as legacy material; a migration must not relabel their guesses as documentary observations. Existing scripts do not yet consume or enforce this contract.
- Paygent Connect (84) is unresolved. Preserve the original `paygent (NMI-powered)` hint. The legacy paygentglobal.com lead has no established identity match. Resolve vendor/product/edition with primary evidence before attaching that domain's facts; do not substitute a similarly named payment company. The example intentionally leaves this unresolved.

## Claim states and evidence

Each scalar claim has a stable `claim_id`, `status`, `value`, `context`, `evidence`, `supporting_claim_refs` and `rationale`. Context names the edition, API version, account type, region and environment where relevant; say which details remain unknown. IDs remain stable across revisions for the same question. Split materially different scopes into distinct method/entry claims rather than merging them.

| Status | Meaning and counting |
| --- | --- |
| `observed` | Explicitly supported by captured source content; non-null value and evidence required. This means documentary observation, not verified truth or a successful API call. |
| `inferred` | Reasoned conclusion; non-null value, evidence, rationale and supporting claim references required. Report separately from documentary observations. |
| `unknown` | Attempted investigation did not resolve the question. Null value; explain the gap. |
| `disputed` | Conflicting content has not been reconciled. Null value; at least two evidence observations and an explanation required. |
| `not_researched` | No investigation yet. Null value; never count as a finding. |
| `not_applicable` | Evidence explains why the question does not apply to the stated scope. Null value; not a negative result or a correct auth/access claim. |
| `not_found_in_checked_sources` | A bounded search found no supported result. Null value and evidence identifying checked content/search scope required. Use for MCP discovery; never translate to 'no MCP exists'. |

`coverage_status` on auth/protocol/resource collections is workflow metadata: `not_researched`, `partial`, or `checked_sources`. `checked_sources` means only the listed sources were examined, never exhaustive coverage of the vendor. Empty arrays do not prove absence. Record unresolved questions in `notes`; a researched collection can still be incomplete.

For each evidence observation record:

- The actual source URL, source kind, exact heading/anchor, page/line range, or repository path plus commit and line range in `locator`.
- A short captured observation or faithful paraphrase supporting this specific claim. A homepage URL, search-result snippet, or a whole-page citation without a locator is a lead, not substantive evidence.
- `captured_on` (ISO date), capture method, and document date/version when known. Null document metadata means unknown, not current. Capture dates must reflect actual reading, not run creation.
- SHA-256 of the captured content and a relative `snapshot_ref` where feasible. Hash normalized/extracted content only if the snapshot is exactly that content and the extraction method is recorded. If no content snapshot/hash is available, use null and a specific `hash_unavailable_reason`; do not fabricate a digest. A hash proves content identity, not correctness. Never store credentials in snapshots.

For actual operational tests, use `source_kind: execution_receipt` and `capture_method: execution_log`. These require a real local receipt/log in `snapshot_ref` and its SHA-256; `source_url` may be null for a local log. Its locator identifies the run/tool call and relevant log lines; observation states the actual result. This is the only source kind that allows a null source URL. This format permits future receipts; it implements no execution functionality and the Task 02 example has no operational findings.

Prefer vendor developer/auth/pricing/access docs and official repositories. Community repositories support their own implementation claims, not vendor endorsement. Assignment text supports identity/category/hints only. Cite approval and pricing sources for eligibility claims; an API reference alone need not establish a free credential path. If official sources conflict, preserve both observations and their time, version and scope; do not silently pick one. `conflicts` links the affected claim IDs and explains the discrepancy; `disputed` claims may also hold both observations directly.

Evidence is attached per claim. Each auth method, API protocol, resource group and MCP entry has its own claim and evidence. A shared page may be cited repeatedly with the appropriate locator. One citation must not silently support other array members or scopes. When one claim necessarily includes several details (e.g. an auth method plus documented scopes), its evidence must support every detail; otherwise split the claim or omit unestablished optional details. For review, any unsupported material detail makes that whole claim unsupported; do not inflate the denominator by splitting punctuation into claims.

## Field rules

**Identity and purpose.** `identity.id`, `app` and `category` come from the roster; resolve product identity in `identity.resolution` using a cited product/edition description. Category is assignment metadata, not a researched auth claim. `purpose` is a short, single-line, cited description. Do not put placeholder prose in an observed value.

**Auth.** `auth.items` contains a separate claim per method and scope. Preserve OAuth2, API key, Basic and tokens separately; don't choose a single winner. `context` and `details` explain API/edition/actor, OAuth grant or signing scheme; `scopes` lists only documented scopes relevant to the described use. An empty scopes list means no scopes captured, not unrestricted permissions. For CLI/local software, only assert `none` or `not_applicable` when supported for that interface; lack of a REST API does not settle CLI buildability.

**Credentials.** `credential_eligibility.testing` and `.production` each contain independent boolean claims:

- `free_access`, `trial_access`, `sandbox_access`: true means a documented credential/use path is available for this environment; false requires evidence of its absence or inapplicability. Unknown stays null.
- `paid_required`, `admin_approval_required`, `vendor_approval_required`, `partner_approval_required`, `contact_sales_required`: true means this condition is required for the stated path/scope. False needs explicit support for proceeding without it; silence is unknown. Distinguish `vendor_approval_required` (vendor/platform API-access review or application, such as Google Ads Explorer/Basic/Standard) from `partner_approval_required` (commercial, agency, or technology partnership program gating) and `admin_approval_required` (customer tenant/organization admin role or approval).
- `self_serve`: a documented path allows the intended developer to obtain the relevant credentials without vendor/partner intervention. A paid path may be self-serve; an existing tenant's admin can still be required. State actor/plan/prerequisites in each claim's context. Never derive this by default or from 'Sign up'.

These conditions can coexist. A free sandbox can require admin approval; production may require a paid account and partner approval. For alternative credential paths, the context of each claim must identify exactly which path it describes. Do not collapse conflicting paths to one app-wide boolean: use unknown/disputed with explanatory evidence until a scoped answer is possible. A paid product does not automatically mean API access is gated, and a free trial does not establish production access.

**API surface.** Protocols, public documentation, resource groups and breadth are independent claims. A known REST protocol must survive even when breadth and resource groups are unknown. Record each documented protocol and resource group separately with supporting sections; a source can establish 'contacts' while leaving 'billing' unresearched. `public_documentation` refers to documentation visibility for this API scope, not credential eligibility or public data access. Public documentation does not mean anonymous API access.

`breadth` is an inference supported by resource-group claim IDs: `narrow` = one focused workflow/group; `moderate` = multiple related groups; `broad` = multiple distinct business domains. Explain the classification and captured examples in context/rationale. This is qualitative scope, not a fabricated endpoint inventory or a guarantee of completeness. Leave unknown if not enough resource documentation was read. REST/GraphQL/SDK/CLI can coexist; include other interfaces when relevant to agent-callable tools.

**MCP.** `mcp.discovery` is `observed` with value `found` only when at least one supported entry matching the record's declared product edition/scope is recorded. A community MCP targeting a separate consumer/personal edition (e.g., undocumented web-cookie scraping) does not establish `found` for an Enterprise API scope unless tested and documented for that edition; preserve such community entries only with explicit edition separation or leave Enterprise MCP discovery `not_found_in_checked_sources`/`unknown`. Otherwise use the appropriate null state. Each `mcp.entries` item is its own claim with `official`/`community`, source URL, scope, and repository/server URL where established (null otherwise). A server URL may be a hosted endpoint, while a local stdio server may have only a repository URL. No guessed URL. Vendor endorsement must be supported to call it official. Entries for outgoing MCP clients do not establish an app's callable server; record tool direction/scope. `operational_check` remains `not_researched` unless actual execution logs support the result. Docs, a server listing, or a GitHub README cannot establish successful connection, tool calls, or production readiness. This task runs no operational checks.

**Buildability.** This is an explicit inference for a stated agent workflow: `build_now`, `conditional`, `outreach_required` or `not_buildable_for_stated_scope`. Cite supported identity/auth/access/API/MCP or CLI claims through `supporting_claim_refs`, include relevant source evidence, explain the conclusion, list blockers and next steps. A public API can still require outreach; no MCP alone is not a blocker to building an API wrapper. Unknown identity/access/API details can leave buildability unknown. `build_now` is feasibility from evidence, not an implemented or tested integration. Blocker statements also require support; do not label an app unbuildable because a fetch failed.

## Fetch telemetry is separate

`fetches` records URL, attempt date, status, HTTP status, resolved URL, error and optional content digest. It never supplies claim truth. DNS/HTTP errors, login walls, robots blocks and timeouts do not establish no API, paid access, partner gating or nonexistent MCP. A 200 response does not establish a cited claim. Fetch outcomes can prompt follow-up but cannot promote research states automatically.

## Review, runs and accuracy

1. Every saved run gets a unique `run_id`, creation date and producer identity/type. Persist the run input roster hash, schema/rules versions, tool/model versions and configuration alongside that run in a run manifest. Never reuse a run ID or overwrite original records, evidence snapshots, logs or adjudications. The example's run ID is illustrative only.
2. Corrections create a new run with `parent_run_id` and `correction_refs` naming original run/claim IDs plus reasons. Keep the original value/evidence unchanged in the parent; revised claims reuse the same question ID where scope is unchanged. Record added/removed/split claims explicitly in the correction log. New evidence does not retroactively become first-pass evidence.
3. `review` is pending until actual claim adjudications exist. Completed means the listed adjudications are completed, not that every field/app was reviewed. Capture reviewer ID, `ai` or `human`, date, original run ID, each claim ID, judgment, rationale and review evidence. A tool/browser action or another AI is still AI review; only an actual identified person can sign human review. Producer and reviewer identities must be distinct for independent review; disclose shared model/context. Do not copy pending entries over completed reviews.

   An `unresolved` judgment may have an empty evidence array when no source content could be captured. Its required reason must name the actual fetch attempt (for example `fetches[0]` and its date/URL) or an existing failure-log path and describe why adjudication could not finish. Runtime review must resolve that reference. Do not fabricate a source observation for a DNS/access failure. `correct`, `incorrect`, `unsupported` and `not_applicable` judgments still require captured evidence; a failure-only review cannot establish any of them. A completed review containing unresolved judgments does not mean those claims have been verified and contributes no accuracy denominator for those judgments.
4. Before full-run verification, freeze a sampling manifest: manifest ID/path, target run, roster SHA-256, selection date, method/algorithm/version, seed, selected IDs, category counts, reviewer assignments and claim rubric. Use a deterministic seeded selection of two apps per category (20 total), without replacement; report all ten categories including Support and Helpdesk. Preserve pilot/targeted reviews separately from this sample. A seed alone does not reproduce an unspecified algorithm. Do not select actual sample IDs in Task 02.
5. Freeze the claim inventory and scoring rubric before review. Unit = each non-null `observed` or `inferred` claim object, identified by `(run_id, app_id, claim_id)`. Count auth methods, protocols, groups and MCP entries separately; nested operational checks are separate claims only if asserted. Score a compound claim correct only if all material details hold for its scope. Report documentary and inference results separately. Category/roster metadata, example fixtures, collection metadata, null states and bare URLs are not scored findings.
6. Each adjudication is `correct`, `incorrect`, `unsupported`, `unresolved`, or `not_applicable`. Unsupported is a failure to substantiate, not proof of factual falsity. Let C/I/U be completed correct/incorrect/unsupported judgments for asserted claims. Evidence-backed accuracy = C / (C + I + U); print those counts, with unresolved/pending/excluded totals alongside. If the denominator is zero, accuracy is null ('unmeasured'), not 0% or 100%. Exclude null-state claims and not-applicable judgments from this accuracy denominator; report any invalid applicability claims as audit issues. Do not drop incorrect or unsupported results after correction.
7. Report review coverage = completed C/I/U judgments / eligible asserted claims in the frozen sample, with unresolved and pending counts. Separately report research coverage across all 100: counts of observed, inferred and each null state for the six required research areas (purpose, auth, credentials, API, MCP, buildability), plus identity resolution. A collection is not covered just because it exists; distinguish partial protocol knowledge from missing breadth. Report area completion criteria and every denominator. Unknowns do not count as correct findings. No one overall 'accuracy' number should conceal missing research or missing review.
8. First-pass and corrected scores refer to immutable runs, the same sample and the frozen claim questions. Link changed/removed/split/new questions; publish paired results on comparable questions and the changed inventory separately. Do not claim improvement by deleting hard claims, changing denominators or relabeling a failure unknown. A corrected/previously reviewed sample is not an unbiased held-out estimate; disclose reuse. Report no accuracy or improvement until actual adjudication exists. Prepare a human checklist if no person has reviewed yet; do not claim human checks were performed.

## Publication contract (later tasks only)

A hosting config, Site registration, expected URL, local Git directory or ZIP is not proof of publication. Save a repository creation/write receipt, actual repository URL, commit SHA, source/README existence and readback evidence. Save the deployment ID/status, actual live URL, deployed commit or artifact SHA-256, date, and an independent fetch/browser result demonstrating the page is accessible to the intended reviewer. Record real errors/blockers when unsuccessful. No publication is attempted in Task 02.

## Validation and Task 03 handoff

No dependencies were installed. From the workspace root, the available PowerShell validates the example:

```powershell
Test-Json -Path examples/unresearched-record.json -SchemaFile schemas/record.json
$roster = Get-Content -Raw data/apps.json | ConvertFrom-Json
if ($roster.apps.Count -ne 100) { throw 'Expected 100 apps' }
if (($roster.apps.id -join ',') -ne ((1..100) -join ',')) { throw 'IDs/order changed' }
if (@($roster.apps | Group-Object category).Count -ne 10) { throw 'Expected 10 categories' }
if (@($roster.apps | Group-Object category | Where-Object Count -ne 10).Count) { throw 'Expected 10 apps per category' }
```

If `jsonschema` is already installed in another environment, this optional check verifies both the schema and example (do not install it for this task):

```console
python -c "import json,jsonschema; s=json.load(open('schemas/record.json')); jsonschema.Draft202012Validator.check_schema(s); jsonschema.Draft202012Validator(s, format_checker=jsonschema.FormatChecker()).validate(json.load(open('examples/unresearched-record.json'))); print('valid')"
```

Schema validation enforces required fields, value types, explicit states, local evidence minimums for assertions, reference presence for inferences, and pending/completed review shape. It cannot establish source truth, identity, evidence relevance, all reference integrity, actual human activity, or immutable run history. Validators may treat `format` as annotation: Task 03 must explicitly validate URLs/date values.

Runtime/reviewer checks to implement in Task 03 (not implemented here):

- Match IDs/names/categories to the roster; unresolved identity blocks promotion of product-specific claims.
- Ensure unique claim IDs (including nested checks), resolve all support/conflict/adjudication/correction references, reject self/circular support, and ensure buildability/breadth dependencies are supported and scoped consistently. Referenced IDs are claim IDs within this app/run unless explicitly paired with an original run ID.
- Require each asserted method/group/server and every material detail to be supported by its own evidence; inspect the actual cited content. Do not accept assignment hints or legacy leads as product evidence. `breadth` must use `inferred` and reference resource claims; `not_found_in_checked_sources` is restricted to MCP discovery.
- Require no asserted items under `not_researched` collection status; track partial knowledge and source scope. MCP `found` needs at least one supported entry and source-backed origin; operational success needs execution receipts. No nonempty MCP entries under an unknown/negative discovery state.
- Verify valid dates/URLs, content hashes/snapshot paths, document versions, primary/community attribution and conflicts. Keep fetch failures separate and ensure captures correspond to real reads.
- Enforce append-only runs/reviews and snapshot storage, parent/correction linkage, review identity/type, sample reproducibility/category coverage, frozen claim denominators and metric arithmetic. Retain unsupported results.
- Require publication receipts/readback before reporting repo/live-page success.

Coordinator acceptance should cover: honest unknown example passes; multi-auth and REST-only partial knowledge pass; evidence-free observed auth/purpose and unsupported inferred buildability fail; malformed dates/refs are flagged by runtime if the validator does not reject them; completed review with no reviewer/judgments fails. Passing a schema is not evidence that Task 03 or the assignment research is complete.

roster.purpose: Assignment identity inputs and source leads only; no researched app findings.

provenance.method: Original user assignment read via read_thread; hints preserved verbatim as Markdown; normalized app names, IDs, categories and order checked against research_agent.py RAW. No websites fetched.
provenance.legacy_warning: Candidate URLs are unverified source leads, not original assignment hints or evidence. Legacy auth/access/API/MCP/buildability guesses are excluded.

apps.identity_note: Original hint is paygent (NMI-powered). No evidence links this product to paygentglobal.com. Do not endorse that domain, substitute another Paygent product, or attach its docs until primary evidence resolves the identity.
